summary.title: Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440
summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey and Andrew Oldag
summary.type_of_paper: Observational study and radiative transfer modeling
summary.executive_summary: This study presents multi-spectral lunar occultation observations and subsequent radiative transfer modeling of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440. Utilizing the pMIRAS high-speed spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope, the authors observed the star over a continuous 1–4µm wavelength range. The primary objective was to resolve the spatial structure of the inner circumstellar dust shell, which is a critical component in understanding the mass-loss mechanisms of post-main-sequence stars. The study demonstrates that a single-size model cannot adequately fit the observed occultation fringes, necessitating a more complex approach. By employing the DUSTY radiative transfer code, the authors modeled a circumstellar shell and compared the results against both the observed occultation light curves and the known spectral energy distribution (SED). Key findings include a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum temperature (Tmax) of 950 K ± 50K, and an optical depth at 5µm of 0.5 ± 0.1. The results favor a radial density gradient of ρ ∝r−2, consistent with a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. Furthermore, the study identifies a discrepancy in the 60µm flux, which cannot be reconciled with the best-fit models unless a substantial abundance of graphite or a significantly higher historical mass-loss rate is assumed. The research also provides a derived dust mass-loss rate of 6.5 × 10−8 M⊙/yr. By successfully resolving the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the dust shell, this work provides essential constraints on the density and geometry of the innermost regions of AGB star envelopes, offering insights into the evolution of the interstellar medium.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents multi-spectral lunar occultation observations and subsequent radiative transfer modeling of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440. Utilizing the pMIRAS high-speed spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope, the authors observed the star over a continuous 1–4µm wavelength range. The primary objective was to resolve the spatial structure of the inner circumstellar dust shell, which is a critical component in understanding the mass-loss mechanisms of post-main-sequence stars. The study demonstrates that a single-size model cannot adequately fit the observed occultation fringes, necessitating a more complex approach. By employing the DUSTY radiative transfer code, the authors modeled a circumstellar shell and compared the results against both the observed occultation light curves and the known spectral energy distribution (SED). Key findings include a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum temperature (Tmax) of 950 K ± 50K, and an optical depth at 5µm of 0.5 ± 0.1. The results favor a radial density gradient of ρ ∝r−2, consistent with a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. Furthermore, the study identifies a discrepancy in the 60µm flux, which cannot be reconciled with the best-fit models unless a substantial abundance of graphite or a significantly higher historical mass-loss rate is assumed. The research also provides a derived dust mass-loss rate of 6.5 × 10−8 M⊙/yr. By successfully resolving the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the dust shell, this work provides essential constraints on the density and geometry of the innermost regions of AGB star envelopes, offering insights into the evolution of the interstellar medium.

Research Context
Mass loss from post-main-sequence stars contributes significantly to the heavy element abundance and solid particle content of the interstellar medium. The mechanisms of mass loss during the AGB phase involve radiation pressure and stellar pulsation, but specific details remain poorly understood. Studies of the spatial structure of circumstellar mass-loss shells can clarify many uncertainties in these processes. Recent imaging and molecular line studies have shown evidence for periodic variations in mass-loss rates, appearing as 'rings' in radial distributions. Studying the inner regions of these shells requires very high angular resolutions, specifically well under 1 arcsec. While speckle interferometry and adaptive optics provide some resolution, lunar occultations are required to reach milli-arcsecond levels.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to resolve the spatial structure of the dust shell around the carbon star AFGL 5440. The researchers seek to determine the constraints on the inner radius and the radial density gradient of the shell. It is hypothesized that multi-spectral lunar occultations can provide the necessary resolution to differentiate the central star from the innermost dust. The study specifically investigates whether a single-size model can explain the observed fringes or if a complex shell structure is required.

Methodological Details
The observations were conducted using the pMIRAS high-speed spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The study covered a continuous wavelength range from 1 to 4µm. The time resolution of the instrument was 8 msec, allowing for an effective angular resolution of a couple milli-arcsec. The spectral resolution varies from approximately R ~20 at the shortest wavelengths to R ~100 at the longest wavelengths. The spatial plate scale for the detector was 0.4 arcsec/pixel. The observation of AFGL 5440 occurred during an immersion occultation on 28 Aug 2001 at a lunar phase of 0.72. Two 'calibration' stars, IRC+00233 and HD 155292, were also observed to understand the limitations of the analysis process.

Procedures And Architectures
The data reduction process involved shifting images via a cross-correlation algorithm to minimize spectral blurring. Wavelength calibration was performed by fitting the NaCl dispersion function to atmospheric transmission maxima. The researchers used the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model the circumstellar shell and its energy distribution. The modeling process involved exploring more than 200 different model combinations to determine parameter effects. The dust composition was assumed to be carbon-rich, including amorphous carbon, silicon carbide, and graphite. Models were fit to both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED). The researchers varied the dust optical depth and the radial density gradient to find the best fit.

Key Results
The occultation fringes could not be adequately fit by any single-size model. The dust shell's maximum temperature was strongly constrained to 950 K ± 50K. The optical depth at 5µm was found to be 0.5 ± 0.1. The best-fit models demonstrated a radial density gradient of ρ ∝r−2. The dust mass-loss rate was derived as 6.5 × 10−8 M⊙/yr. Models with a maximum dust temperature below 900 K failed to fit the fringes at longer wavelengths. The best-fit dust composition included small amounts of SiC and comparable amounts of amorphous carbon and graphite.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The data imply that the density of grains in the 3–4µm region must be sufficiently large to produce the observed blurring. The results constrain the inner radius of the dust shell to an angular radius of 11 mas. The density gradient is consistent with that expected for a radiatively driven wind. The discrepancy in 60µm flux implies a potential decrease in the mass-loss rate from the time when far-IR emitting dust was ejected. The inclusion of graphite was necessary to fit the IRAS 60µm flux, despite evidence against its abundance in similar stars.

Contradictions And Limitations
Models could not fit the IRAS 60µm flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a higher historical mass-loss rate. The observations were limited by both spectral resolution and signal-to-noise ratios. The comparison star IRC+00233 showed a discrepancy in fit at wavelengths near 1.7µm. Absolute flux calibration was not attempted due to variable instrumental efficiency and non-photometric sky conditions.

Claims
AFGL 5440 possesses a complex circumstellar dust shell structure that cannot be modeled as a single uniform disk. The fringes cannot be fit by any single-size model. The 11 mas disk provides a passable fit in the mid-range but produces incorrect fringes at other wavelengths. For the comparison star HD 155292, uniform-disk models fit the data reasonably well. This necessitates the use of radiative transfer models to accurately describe the inner dust environment.
The inner edge of the dust shell is constrained to a temperature of approximately 950 K. The dust temperature at the inner radius was of order 950K ± 50K. Models with a maximum dust temperature below 900 K did not have enough hot dust. Some previous studies, like Ivezic & Elitzur (1996), derived a substantially lower temperature of ~750K. This provides a specific physical value for the inner radius of 3.7×10^14 cm.

Data And Code Availability
The study utilized the DUSTY radiative transfer code for modeling.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The researchers explored over 200 models to test the effects of varying input parameters. Ablation tests showed that density gradients of r-1.8 or r-2.2 could not simultaneously fit both the 5-20µm and 60µm distributions.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows observed and model light curves for a 4.5 mas uniform disk for IRC+00233. Figure 5 shows the observed light curves of AFGL 5440. Figure 7 and 8 show the fits to the spectral energy distribution and occultation light curves for the best-fit model. Figure 10 illustrates the spatial profiles of this best-fit model.

Three Takeaways
1. The study resolves the inner dust shell of the carbon star AFGL 5440 using milli-arcsecond lunar occultations. 2. The inner dust shell is constrained to a temperature of 950 K ± 50K with a ρ ∝r−2 density gradient. 3. The mismatch in 60µm flux suggests that mass-loss rates may have been higher in the recent past.

summary.title: Gluon Radiation of an Expanding Color Skyrmion in the Quark-Gluon Plasma
summary.authors: Jian Dai
summary.executive_summary:
This paper investigates the gluon radiation produced by a color skyrmion expanding during the hydrodynamic stage of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). The author employs a semiclassical method to calculate the density of states and the energy spectrum of this radiation. By modeling the transport of color charges using a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism, the study derives a nonabelian current corresponding to an expanding soliton solution. This soliton expands in a manner consistent with the fireball generated in RHIC experiments.

The calculation reveals three distinct regimes in the radiation spectrum: a fast fall-off in the UV side, a dominant smooth peak in the intermediate energy range, and a characteristic long tail in the IR. The results are compared with previous studies, notably showing that the IR behavior is softer ($\sim 1/\sqrt{k}$) than previous models ($1/k$) because the medium size is characterized by the soliton size rather than being infinite. The study provides a hydrodynamical approach to understanding radiation patterns, which may help characterize the hot QCD matter in the deconfined phase and potentially address the eccentricity of elliptic flow.

claims.description: The radiation spectrum of an expanding color skyrmion exhibits a characteristic long tail in the IR with a softer behavior than previously reported.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates the gluon radiation produced by a color skyrmion expanding during the hydrodynamic stage of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). The author employs a semiclassical method to calculate the density of states and the energy spectrum of this radiation. By modeling the transport of color charges using a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism, the study derives a nonabelian current corresponding to an expanding soliton solution. This soliton expands in a manner consistent with the fireball generated in RHIC experiments.

The calculation reveals three distinct regimes in the radiation spectrum: a fast fall-off in the UV side, a dominant smooth peak in the intermediate energy range, and a characteristic long tail in the IR. The results are compared with previous studies, notably showing that the IR behavior is softer ($\sim 1/\sqrt{k}$) than previous models ($1/k$) because the medium size is characterized by the soliton size rather than being infinite. The study provides a hydrodynamical approach to understanding radiation patterns, which may help characterize the hot QCD matter in the deconfined phase and potentially address the eccentricity of elliptic flow.

Research Context
The study addresses gluon radiation during the hydrodynamic stage of hot QCD matter. Medium induced radiation has been thoroughly explored in the context of jet quenching. The spatially extended nuclear matter affects the processes of fragmentation and hadronization. The time evolution of the RHIC fireball can influence the observable particle production spectra. The resulting state of matter is usually modeled as a relativistic fluid. Generalized fluid mechanics characterizes the transport of color charges. Recent discoveries include a type of single skyrmion solutions in color fluid. The pattern of gluon radiation pertains to the color current of these non-static configurations.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to calculate the radiation spectrum in a semiclassical approach. Specifically, the goal is to find the density of states and energy spectrum. The results are compared with those in literatures. The study examines how the time-dependent skyrmion expansion influences the radiation pattern. The primary hypothesis is that the spectrum will exhibit a fast fall-off in the UV side. Additionally, it is predicted that a smooth peak will dominate the intermediate energy. Finally, a long tail is expected to be the characteristic feature in the IR.

Methodological Details
The transport of color charges is modeled by a nonlinear sigma model. The model is expressed in a first-order formalism. The configuration of this fluid is described by a group element field U. The study considers the case where U takes value in an SU(2) group. The information about the equation of state is contained in the free energy density. At high temperature, the equation of state is approximated by \epsilon = 3p. The free energy density can be obtained by integrating the expression. The fluid system possesses a class of expanding soliton solutions. The expansion follows the form R(t) \approx R0(t/\tau+1)^{4/3}. A small parameter \lambda = \tau/R0 is defined for the expansion. The hedgehog ansatz is specified for the solution. A dimensionless coordinate s = x/R(t) is used to map the skyrmion.

Procedures And Architectures
The nonabelian charge current is related to the abelian current by Eckart factorization. The current is calculated using the trace of sigma matrices. The current takes a natural form of a multipole expansion. The calculation focuses only on the effect of the lowest mode. The lowest order semiclassical amplitude is calculated between the current and a free quantum field. The gluon factor is given by the wave function. The spatial Fourier transformation can be completed analytically. A specific polynomial Q4(x) appears in the Fourier transformation. The time-dependent expansion R(t) is inserted into the amplitude equation. The onshell condition is used to define the parameter \eta. The density of states n is calculated from the squared amplitude.

Key Results
The calculated radiation spectrum shows a fast fall-off in the UV side. A smooth peak dominates the intermediate energy range. In the IR, a long tail is the characteristic feature. The number density in small k follows a \sim 1/\sqrt{k} behavior. This IR behavior is softer than the 1/k form found in other studies. Numerical results are provided for \lambda = 1/15, 2/15, and 1/5. The results are visualized in Figure 1. The number density n/(1/\sqrt{k}) is shown in Figure 2.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The difference in IR behavior arises from the finite medium size. The medium size is characterized by the soliton size R0. Because of the finite size, the IR behavior is softer than in infinite models. The hydrodynamical approach provides a way to address the eccentricity of elliptic flow.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study only considers the effect of the lowest mode. The effects of higher polarization will be considered elsewhere. Gluon self-interaction is omitted to work with a free parton picture. The medium size is characterized by the soliton size rather than being infinitely large.

Claims
The radiation spectrum of an expanding color skyrmion exhibits a characteristic long tail in the IR with a softer behavior than previously reported. The spectrum shows a long tail in the IR. The number density in small k follows a \sim 1/\sqrt{k} behavior. The IR behavior in this case is softer. In other studies, the number density is of the 1/k form. The hydrodynamical approach could be used to address the eccentricity of elliptic flow.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Numerical results for three different lambda values are provided.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the density of states and energy spectrum for \lambda = 1/5, 2/15, and 1/15. Figure 2 shows the number density n/(1/\sqrt{k}) in small k for \lambda = 0.2.

Three Takeaways

summary.title: ARE THERE MACH CONES IN HEAVY ION COLLISIONS? THREE-PARTICLE CORRELATIONS FROM STAR
summary.authors: Jason Glyndwr Ulery for the STAR Collaboration
summary.field_subfield: Nuclear Physics; Heavy Ion Collisions; Quark Gluon Plasma
summary.executive_summary:
This study investigates the presence of Mach cones in heavy ion collisions by analyzing three-particle azimuthal correlations using data from the STAR experiment. The researchers focused on collisions at a center-of-mass energy of λNN = 200 GeV, specifically comparing pp, d+Au, and high-statistics Au+Au collisions. The primary goal was to distinguish between various physics mechanisms that explain the broadened away-side structure observed in two-particle correlations, such as large-angle gluon radiation, deflected jets, hydrodynamic conical flow (Mach-cone shock waves), and σCerenkov radiation.

The analysis utilized a trigger particle with 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c and two associated particles with 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c. A rigorous background subtraction method was employed, accounting for hard-soft background, soft-soft background, and trigger flow. The results showed that while pp and d+Au collisions exhibited standard kT broadening, central Au+Au collisions displayed an additional off-diagonal structure at approximately π ± 1.45 radians. This off-diagonal signal was found to increase with centrality and was consistent with conical emission.

To differentiate between hydrodynamic Mach cones and σCerenkov radiation, the team examined the dependence of the emission angle on the associated particle's transverse momentum (pT). While σCerenkov radiation predicts a sharply decreasing angle with increasing pT, the data showed that the emission angle remained constant as a function of pT. This finding supports the Mach cone emission model. Systematic uncertainties related to flow harmonics (v2 and v4) and normalization windows were investigated and found to be robust, with the signal remaining stable across different measurement methods.

The observed emission is consistent with Mach cones rather than σCerenkov radiation.

summary.title: A schematic model of scattering in PT −symmetric Quantum Mechanics
summary.authors: Miloslav Znojil
summary.executive_summary: This paper explores a one-dimensional scattering problem involving a complex, PT-symmetric short-range potential $V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x)$. The author aims to address a gap in existing literature, where PT-symmetric systems are well-studied in bound-state regimes but less so in scattering contexts. To analyze this, the author employs a Runge-Kutta-discretized version of the Schrödinger equation, transforming the differential equation into a difference-equation representation. The methodology allows for the derivation of analytical formulae for the reflection ($B$) and transmission ($C$) coefficients. A key technical innovation is the complexification of the potential-characterizing parameters, which distinguishes the non-Hermitian system from standard Hermitian models. The paper presents a step-by-step derivation: starting with a simple $M=1$ toy problem (which remains Hermitian), moving to an $M=2$ model where PT-symmetry is introduced, and finally developing a general matrix-inversion method for larger $M$. For systems where $M \ge 4$, the author notes that the algebraic complexity of the formulae grows significantly, necessitating symbolic manipulation. A central theoretical finding is that the 'dynamical input' of the scattering problem—the distinction between Hermitian and PT-symmetric cases—is entirely encoded in two specific coefficients, $\alpha$ and $\beta$. These coefficients are rational functions of the real coupling constants. The author argues that while PT-symmetry introduces a manifest asymmetry between 'in' and 'out' states, this asymmetry is merely formal. The scattering problem remains entirely tractable using standard linear algebra techniques, such as matrix inversion and partitioning the Schrödinger equation to isolate essential components. The work concludes by suggesting that this discrete model could be further applied to study the non-Hermitian inverse problem of scattering.

Standard quantum mechanics describes motion in real potential wells. The scattering regime involves specific boundary conditions. Recent developments have generalized these to non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. PT-symmetry has become a key source of these developments. The research intends to investigate a simple PT-symmetric scattering model. The study uses a Runge-Kutta-discretized difference-equation representation. The study aims to derive formulae for reflection and transmission coefficients. The model assumes the primary innovation is the complexification of parameters.

Methodological Details
The study considers a one-dimensional scattering problem. The potential $V(x)$ is complex and PT-symmetric. The potential consists of real parts $Z(x)$ and $Y(x)$. The Schrödinger equation is converted into a difference equation. The lattice step $h$ is a small parameter. The energy variable $\phi$ is defined by $2 \cos \phi = 2 - h^2E$. The matching method is used for the $M=1$ toy problem. For $M=1$, the problem is treated as Hermitian. The $M=2$ version introduces PT-symmetry into the equations. The system is reduced to a finite-dimensional non-square-matrix problem. The problem is further reduced to a non-homogeneous system of $2M-1$ equations. The final results are derived from the inverse matrix $R=T^{-1}$.

The reflection and transmission coefficients are derived as formulae. The coefficients are determined by the two functions $\alpha$ and $\beta$. The asymmetry between 'in' and 'out' states is merely formal. The scattering problem remains tractable by standard linear algebra techniques. The $O(h^4)$ discrepancy is a numerical uncertainty. This discrepancy disappears in the limit $h \to 0$. Formulae growth requires symbolic manipulations at higher dimensions.

Scattering in PT-symmetric systems is tractable using standard matrix inversion. The problem remains tractable by standard linear algebra. The construction of amplitudes reduces to a two-dimensional matrix inversion.  This allows for the solution of complex scattering models.

summary.authors: B.F.L. Ward and S.A. Yost
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical framework for QED×QCD resummation, designed to meet the stringent demands of precision LHC physics. Specifically, it addresses the necessity for a 0.67% theoretical precision tag for luminosity processes such as single W and Z production, where QED effects are shown to contribute approximately 0.3% of the error budget. The authors extend the Yennie-Frautschi-Suura (YFS) theory, providing an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series to allow for the simultaneous resummation of multiple gluon and photon radiative effects. The proposed theory is formulated such that it can be implemented in Monte Carlo (MC) methods on an event-by-event basis without the risk of double-counting effects. The cross-section is mathematically represented by a sum over residuals (̃β) and exponents, where the residuals are free of all infrared singularities. To ensure practical applicability, the authors discuss matching these exact calculations with standard parton shower Monte Carlo programs like HERWIG and PYTHIA. They propose two primary matching strategies: a pT matching approach that limits the scale of gluon radiation to avoid double-counting with the shower, and a more precise "shower-subtracted residuals" method that uses expanded shower formulas to match the exact cross-section order-by-order. Semi-analytical results for heavy gauge boson production demonstrate that the QED effect is consistently 0.3% at both LHC and Tevatron energies. This framework establishes a firm theoretical foundation for achieving the full O(α²s, α±²) results required for high-precision measurements at the LHC and other future colliders.

Executive Summary
This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical framework for QED×QCD resummation, designed to meet the stringent demands of precision LHC physics. Specifically, it addresses the necessity for a 0.67% theoretical precision tag for luminosity processes such as single W and Z production, where QED effects are shown to contribute approximately 0.3% of the error budget. The authors extend the Yennie-Frautschi-Suura (YFS) theory, providing an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series to allow for the simultaneous resummation of multiple gluon and photon radiative effects. The proposed theory is formulated such that it can be implemented in Monte Carlo (MC) methods on an event-by-event basis without the risk of double-counting effects. The cross-section is mathematically represented by a sum over residuals (̃β) and exponents, where the residuals are free of all infrared singularities. To ensure practical applicability, the authors discuss matching these exact calculations with standard parton shower Monte Carlo programs like HERWIG and PYTHIA. They propose two primary matching strategies: a pT matching approach that limits the scale of gluon radiation to avoid double-counting with the shower, and a more precise "shower-subtracted residuals" method that uses expanded shower formulas to match the exact cross-section order-by-order. Semi-analytical results for heavy gauge boson production demonstrate that the QED effect is consistently 0.3% at both LHC and Tevatron energies. This framework establishes a firm theoretical foundation for achieving the full O(α²s, α±²) results required for high-precision measurements at the LHC and other future colliders.

Research Context
The LHC requires 0.67% level precision for luminosity processes. QED contributions in the evolution of structure functions lead to effects of ~0.3%. This represents half of the error budget. Standard QCD resummation provides an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series. However, the current framework lacks simultaneous resummation of both QED and QCD.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The authors propose a QED×QCD resummation theory to control radiative effects. The theory aims to avoid double-counting when combining with parton showers. They hypothesize that QED effects will be significant for 1.0% precision. The framework is expected to allow systematic accuracy improvements.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on heavy gauge boson production. These processes involve decay into light lepton pairs. The theory uses the YFS theory framework. The QCD part is an exact rearrangement based on the N = 1 term. The cross-section is expressed using residuals free of all infrared divergences. The authors utilize semi-analytical methods and structure functions from Ref [23].

Procedures And Architectures
QED×QCD is obtained by simultaneously exponentiating QCD and QED IR terms. New residuals ̃βn,m represent successive application of YFS expansion. Functions SUMIR(QCED) and DQCED are determined via the substitutions. Two matching methods with HERWIG and/or PYTHIA are proposed. The first method is pT matching at factorization scale μ. The second method uses shower subtracted residuals.

Key Results
The QED effect is .3% at both LHC and FNAL. The results are stable under scale variations. The ratio rexp for QCED at LHC is 1.1901. The ratio rexp for QCD at LHC is 1.1872. The ratio rexp for QCED at Tevatron is 1.1911. The ratio rexp for QCD at Tevatron is 1.1879.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The theory provides an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series. It allows contact with parton showers without double-counting. QCD corrections happen an order of magnitude earlier than QED. The framework supports the desired theoretical precision tag.

Contradictions And Limitations
The current results are semi-analytical and not Monte Carlo. Analysis of W production is in progress. The results for the Nth Gatherall exponent are optional.

Claims
QED×QCD resummation allows for simultaneous exponentiation of QED and QCD radiative effects. The theory simultaneously exponentiates QCD and QED terms. The representation is exact and applicable to MC.  This enables the desired theoretical precision tag.
The QED effect is significant for precision LHC physics. QED is at the .3% level at both LHC and FNAL. QED is needed for LHC theory predictions at ≤1%.  It ensures accuracy of the calculations.

Key Figures Tables
Equation 8 provides the ratio rexp for different facilities.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the QED×QCD resummation theory. 2. The strongest evidence is the .3% QED effect. 3. The future path involves full MC event generator realization.

summary.authors: A.M. MATHAI and H.J. HAUBOLD
summary.executive_summary: The paper investigates the relationship between the product probability property (PPP), recursivity postulates, and the functional forms of entropy measures. The authors argue that while Shannon entropy is associated with additivity, this property is a direct consequence of the logarithmic functional form derived from a specific recursivity postulate, rather than a fundamental property of statistical independence. They distinguish between 'independence' and the 'product probability property' (PPP), noting that the former can be mathematically inconsistent with common expectations. The study introduces and examines five generalized entropies of order α: Rényi, Havrda-Charvát, Tsallis, Mathai entropy, and Mathai's additive entropy. By applying the Maximum Entropy Principle under various constraints—such as fixed moments or boundary conditions—the authors demonstrate that Mathai's entropy is uniquely versatile. It provides a unified pathway model that generates several significant physical distributions, including power laws, exponential forms, Maxwell-Boltzmann, Gaussian, and Weibull densities. Furthermore, the paper establishes non-additivity relations for multivariate joint distributions and derives specific differential equations for the pathway models. Finally, a theoretical connection is established between Mathai's entropy and Kerridge's measure of inaccuracy, positioning it as a form of directed divergence.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The paper investigates the relationship between the product probability property (PPP), recursivity postulates, and the functional forms of entropy measures. The authors argue that while Shannon entropy is associated with additivity, this property is a direct consequence of the logarithmic functional form derived from a specific recursivity postulate, rather than a fundamental property of statistical independence. They distinguish between 'independence' and the 'product probability property' (PPP), noting that the former can be mathematically inconsistent with common expectations. The study introduces and examines five generalized entropies of order α: Rényi, Havrda-Charvát, Tsallis, Mathai entropy, and Mathai's additive entropy. By applying the Maximum Entropy Principle under various constraints—such as fixed moments or boundary conditions—the authors demonstrate that Mathai's entropy is uniquely versatile. It provides a unified pathway model that generates several significant physical distributions, including power laws, exponential forms, Maxwell-Boltzmann, Gaussian, and Weibull densities. Furthermore, the paper establishes non-additivity relations for multivariate joint distributions and derives specific differential equations for the pathway models. Finally, a theoretical connection is established between Mathai's entropy and Kerridge's measure of inaccuracy, positioning it as a form of directed divergence.

Research Context
The study begins by examining product probability property, known in the literature as statistical independence. It notes that Mathai and Rathie (1975, 1976) consider various generalizations of Shannon entropy, called entropies of order α. A significant gap exists regarding the source of additivity in Shannon entropy. It is argued that the natural process is non-additivity, important for statistical mechanics. The text highlights that the term 'independence' of events is a misnomer. The property should have been called product probability property or PPP. The authors seek to clarify that simply because of PPP one need not expect additivity to hold. There is no reason to expect information in a joint distribution to be the sum of marginal contents. The nature of non-extensivity associated with various generalized entropies is pointed out even when PPP holds. The concept of statistical independence will be examined to illustrate that one should not expect this PPP should lead to extensivity. This is because the definition of independence becomes inconsistent with the common man’s vision of independence.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The primary research question examines how the nature of the recursivity postulate automatically determines the logarithmic functional form for Shannon entropy. The authors hypothesize that the recursivity postulate leads to a logarithmic function. It is further investigated whether Shannon entropy naturally gives rise to additivity when applied to situations having product probability property. A key objective is to explore situations where Mathai’s entropy leads to pathway models, exponential and power law behavior and related differential equations. The study also seeks to clarify the connection of Mathai’s entropy to Kerridge’s measure of 'inaccuracy'. The research also aims to show that maximization of the continuous analogue of Mk,α(P), denoted by Mα(f), gives rise to various functional forms for f, depending upon the types of constraints on f. Additionally, the study seeks to clarify the types of non-extensivity that can be expected from a multivariate distribution when PPP holds. Finally, the study investigates the types of differential equations satisfied by the various special cases of the pathway model, specifically focusing on the power law coming from Tsallis statistics.

Methodological Details
The study evaluates a multinomial population P = (p1, ..., pm) where pi > 0. It assumes symmetry in the outcomes to assign equal probabilities 1/n each to the elementary events. The authors analyze the product probability property P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) to define independence. The research considers five different generalized entropies of order α. These include Rk,α(P) for Rényi entropy, Hk,α(P) for Havrda-Charvát entropy, Tk,α(P) for Tsallis entropy, Mk,α(P) for Mathai entropy, and M*k,α(P) for Mathai’s additive entropy. Each entropy is defined as a function of a population P = (p1, ..., pk). For the continuous case, the study uses the density function f(x) of a real random variable x. The continuous analogues for these entropies are expressed as integrals involving f(x) raised to a power. The Maximum Entropy Principle is used to optimize these measures under various types of constraints. Constraints include the condition that the integral of f(x) from a to b equals 1. Another constraint is that the first moment E(x) is a given quantity for all functional f. The study also considers the constraint where f(a) and f(b) are the same for all functional f. The methodology employs the calculus of variation to solve the Euler equation. The Euler equation is derived by considering a functional U involving a Lagrangian multiplier λ. The study investigates the functional equation fα(x) + bα(x)fα(y/(1-x)) = fα(y) + bα(x)f(x/(1-y)). The form of bα(x) is determined by the recursivity postulate for each entropy measure. The authors examine bivariate situations of a discrete distribution pij > 0. The study also extends the analysis to trivariate populations pijk > 0. The methodology establishes non-additivity relations for multivariable situations when the product probability property holds. The study utilizes the escort density μ[f(x)]α in some cases of Tsallis statistics. The results are used to identify special cases such as the Maxwell-Boltzmann, Gaussian, and Weibull densities.

Procedures And Architectures
The authors begin by exploring the product probability property (PPP) and its relationship to statistical independence. They argue that the term 'independence' is a misnomer and should be called PPP. The procedure involves defining the recursivity postulate for a multinomial population. This postulate assumes that if an event is partitioned into independent events, the entropy becomes a weighted sum. From this postulate, the authors derive the logarithmic functional form for Shannon entropy. The study then presents several characterization theorems for Shannon entropy and its generalizations. The authors define five specific generalized entropies of order α, ranging from Rényi to Mathai's entropy. For each entropy, the authors derive the non-additivity relation for joint distributions. The authors use a specific bivariate formula to show that Fm,n,α(P, Q) = Fm,α(P) + Fn,α(Q) + a(α)Fm,α(P)Fn,α(Q). The coefficients a(α) are calculated for each of the five entropy measures. The analysis is then extended to trivariate and higher dimensional joint distributions. For the continuous case, the authors provide integral definitions for each generalized entropy. The authors then apply the Maximum Entropy Principle to determine the functional forms of f. They define a functional U and use a Lagrangian multiplier to derive the Euler equation. By assuming different types of constraints, such as the first moment or boundary values, they solve the Euler equation. This procedure leads to the derivation of the power law and Tsallis statistics. The authors specifically derive Mathai’s pathway model as a general functional form. The pathway model is shown to include various physical densities as special cases. Finally, the authors derive differential equations that the pathway model functional part satisfies. The differential equations are derived for specific values of the parameters γ, δ, and α.

Key Results
The study establishes that the recursivity postulate automatically determines the logarithmic functional form for Shannon entropy. It is shown that Shannon entropy naturally gives rise to additivity when applied to situations having product probability property. The authors derive the non-additivity relation for generalized entropies: Fm,n,α(P, Q) = Fm,α(P) + Fn,α(Q) + a(α)Fm,α(P)Fn,α(Q). The value of the parameter a(α) is specifically determined to be 0 for Rényi entropy and Mathai’s additive entropy. For the Tsallis entropy, the parameter a(α) is found to be 1 −α. For the Havrda-Charvát entropy, the parameter a(α) is calculated as 2^(1−α) −1. For Mathai entropy, the parameter a(α) is identified as α−1. The study demonstrates that maximizing Mathai’s entropy under specific constraints leads to Mathai’s pathway model. The pathway model is expressed by the functional form f(x) = c xγ−1[1 −s(1 −α)xδ]^(1/(1−α)). In the limit where α → 1, the model produces an extended or stretched exponential form f3 = c3e−s xδ. For specific parameters such as δ = 2, γ = 3, and α → 1, the model results in the Maxwell-Boltzmann density. When parameters are set to δ = 2, γ = 1, and α → 1, the model results in the Gaussian density. When parameters are set to γ = δ and α → 1, the model results in the Weibull density. The study also derives a power law equation for the pathway model when γ = 1 and δ = 1. Additionally, a differential equation for the pathway model is derived as x d/dx g(x) = (γ−1)g(x) −sδ[g(x)]α for δ = (γ−1)(α−1) for α > 1. Finally, the authors show that Mathai’s entropy can be looked upon as a type of directed divergence or inaccuracy measure. The study examines a trivariate population pijk > 0 and establishes the corresponding non-additivity relation. The study also demonstrates that optimizing under a fixed first moment E(x) results in a power law density. When optimizing under different moment-like expressions involving γ and δ, the authors obtain Mathai’s pathway model. The result for γ = 1, δ = 1 in the pathway model is the power law from Tsallis statistics.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The authors conclude that additivity is a result of the logarithmic functional form. This form is derived from the recursivity postulate rather than the PPP itself. The study highlights that 'independence' is a misnomer for the product probability property. The non-additivity of generalized entropies is shown to be important for statistical mechanics. Mathai's entropy is presented as a convenient tool for obtaining various probability models. The pathway model serves as a unified framework for various physical distributions. The results suggest that Mathai's entropy can be interpreted as a directed divergence. The derivation of differential equations allows for a dynamic analysis of pathway models.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors note that the definition of independence is inconsistent with common vision. There are no independent events for certain sample sizes like n = 3, 5, 7. The product probability property does not automatically lead to extensivity. One should not put too much importance on the additivity of joint distributions. The authors also acknowledge that producing densities can be difficult for some entropies.

Claims
Shannon entropy's additivity is a result of the recursivity postulate rather than the product probability property. The recursivity postulate automatically determines the logarithmic functional form. Shannon entropy naturally gives rise to additivity. Simply because of PPP one need not expect additivity. Logarithm of a product being the sum of logarithms.
Mathai's entropy provides a unified framework for various physical distributions via the pathway model. Mathai’s entropy is a convenient one to obtain various probability models. Mathai’s entropy leads to pathway models. It results in the Maxwell-Boltzmann density. It results in the Gaussian density.  The model gives the superstatistics of Beck.

Three Takeaways
1. The recursivity postulate determines the logarithmic form of Shannon entropy. 2. Mathai's entropy unifies various distributions into a pathway model. 3. Generalized entropies exhibit non-additivity under the product probability property.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The paper presents a theoretical extrapolation of the current λCDM cosmological model into the far future, arguing that as the universe expands under the influence of a dominant cosmological constant, the observational evidence for the Big Bang and the expansion of the universe will eventually vanish for any remaining observers. The authors posit that future observers, residing in a gravitationally bound 'island universe' consisting of the merged remnants of the Local Group, will find themselves in a state where the universe appears static. This occurs because structures outside this local cluster will be driven beyond the de Sitter event horizon or become exponentially redshifted to the point of invisibility. Furthermore, the cosmic microwave background (CMB) will be redshifted to wavelengths so large and intensities so low that it will become undetectable, potentially being screened by the interstellar medium's plasma frequency. The authors also demonstrate that general relativity is perfectly compatible with a static universe if the assumption of global homogeneity and isotropy is discarded, which would be the case for a future 'island universe.' Additionally, the signatures of Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) will be lost as primordial helium and deuterium abundances are overwhelmed by stellar evolution. The authors conclude that our current epoch is a unique 'cosmic coincidence' because we live at a specific time when the densities of dark matter and dark energy are comparable, allowing us to observationally verify the expansion of the universe—a privilege that future observers will not possess.

Research Context
The de Sitter model was historically marginalized after the discovery of the Hubble expansion. Current observational evidence supports a λCDM flat universe. This universe is composed of roughly 30% matter and 70% dark energy. All models with a non-zero cosmological constant will eventually approach a de Sitter universe.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The authors investigate whether future observers can perform any observation or experiment that infers the existence of an expanding universe or a Big Bang. They hypothesize that the universe will effectively be over for such observers as evidence vanishes. They predict that the static universe will have returned with a vengeance.

Methodological Details
The study extrapolates the current λCDM universe forward in time. The model accounts for a universe with roughly 30% matter and 70% dark energy. The analysis considers the implications of a non-zero cosmological constant. The study explores the transition to a de Sitter universe in the far future.

Procedures And Architectures
The authors analyze the de Sitter metric using a static coordinate system. The de Sitter space-time is defined as a four dimensional hyperboloid. The model assumes expansion is dominated by dark energy. The study calculates the redshift of the CMB peak wavelength. The authors model the screening of radiation by the interstellar medium's plasma frequency.

Key Results
The Local Group remains gravitationally bound despite accelerated expansion. More distant structures will be driven outside of the de Sitter event horizon. This horizon crossing occurs on a timescale of 100 billion years. Light from these distant objects will be exponentially redshifted. Future observers will see a single galaxy as the merger product of the Local Group. The universe will appear to be empty and static. The CMB intensity will be redshifted by about 12 orders of magnitude. The CMB peak will be redshifted to roughly 1 m. This occurs at a frequency of roughly 300 MHz. Screening will occur when the expansion factor is less than 50 times the present age. The mass fraction of helium is predicted to reach Y = 0.6. The matter density relative to dark energy will be ρM/ρΛ ≈ 10⁻¹².

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The universe will appear to be empty and static to future observers. This is because observers will lack probes of the length scales over which Λ dominates. Our current epoch is special because we can observationally verify the expansion. Future observers will be hard pressed to know they live in an expanding universe.

Contradictions And Limitations
The analysis is restricted to observers within a bound gravitational system. The study assumes the universe is dominated by dark energy.

Claims
The evidence for the Hubble expansion will disappear for future observers. The Local Group remains gravitationally bound. Distant structures will cross the de Sitter event horizon. Light from distant objects will be exponentially redshifted.  The universe will appear static. The static universe will have returned.
The Cosmic Microwave Background will become unobservable. The CMB intensity will decrease by 12 orders of magnitude. The CMB will redshift to roughly 1 m. The CMB will be screened by plasma frequency.  Observers will come up empty-handed.
General Relativity allows for a static universe description. The static universe is not inconsistent. An empty static universe can prevail.  Cosmology will effectively be over.
Primordial nucleosynthesis evidence will be lost to stellar pollution. The helium mass fraction will reach Y = 0.6. The relic deuterium will be destroyed.  Inferring the original BBN will be difficult.

Three Takeaways
1. Future observers in a bound system will see a static universe. 2. Evidence like the CMB and Hubble expansion will disappear. 3. Our current era is uniquely positioned to observationally verify the expansion.

summary.authors: Natalya A. Zimbovskaya
summary.field_subfield: Condensed Matter Physics / Quantum Hall Effect
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a theoretical investigation into the temperature and magnetic field dependencies of Coulomb drag transresistivity in double-layer two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) systems, specifically in the quantum Hall regime near half-filling of the lowest Landau level (ν ≈ 1/2). The primary motivation for the study is to explain experimental findings where the transresistivity appears nearly independent of the interlayer spacing (d) and exhibits a specific quadratic enhancement with the filling factor deviation (Δν = ν - 1/2). Executive Summary
This paper presents a theoretical investigation into the temperature and magnetic field dependencies of Coulomb drag transresistivity in double-layer two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) systems, specifically in the quantum Hall regime near half-filling of the lowest Landau level (ν ≈ 1/2). The primary motivation for the study is to explain experimental findings where the transresistivity appears nearly independent of the interlayer spacing (d) and exhibits a specific quadratic enhancement with the filling factor deviation (Δν = ν - 1/2). Initial calculations within the standard RPA framework fail to account for the observed distance-independence, as the calculated parameter α (the ratio of the Thomas-Fermi screening length to the layer separation) remains below unity. To resolve this, the author incorporates Fermi-liquid interaction effects, specifically renormalizing the CF liquid's compressibility using the f0 and f1 interaction parameters. These corrections significantly reduce the compressibility, leading to α > 1. This condition ensures that intralayer interactions predominate over interlayer interactions, providing a physical explanation for the lack of sensitivity to interlayer spacing. The final model successfully reproduces the experimental temperature dependence (T^4/3) and the quadratic magnetic field dependence near ν = 1/2. The study provides strong evidence for the existence of significant Fermi-liquid interactions in the Composite Fermion system near the half-filled Landau level.

Research Context
Double-layer 2DEG systems are of significant interest. Coulomb drag occurs via interlayer interactions. At ν = 1/2, transresistivity is proportional to T^4/3. This originates from the ballistic contribution. Recent experiments showed quadratic enhancement with Δν. Drag was insensitive to the distance d. The present work is motivated by these experiments.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study calculates transresistivity near ν = 1/2. It examines temperature and magnetic field dependences. The goal is explaining the independence of spacing. The author hypothesizes Fermi-liquid interactions provide a significant effect. The results are expected to agree with evidence.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on the quantum Hall regime. The filling factor is near half-filling. Drag relates to density-density components of polarization. The Composite Fermion (CF) approach is used. The Random Phase Approximation (RPA) is adopted. The layers are assumed to be identical. The Boltzmann transport equation provides CF conductivity. Conductivity components are calculated for ν slightly away from 1/2. The ballistic regime assumes ql ≫ 1 and ωτ ≫ 1.

Procedures And Architectures
The 2x2 polarizability matrix uses the CF response. Density-density response functions are derived from the CF response. The conductivity tensor is related to response functions. Fermi-liquid interaction terms f0 and f1 are kept. Compressibility is replaced with a renormalized quantity.

Transresistivity is proportional to T^4/3 at ν = 1/2. The correction δρD is proportional to (T/T0)^2/3. Transresistivity enhances nearly quadratically with Δν. The study considers the collisionless limit. The analysis omits terms for simplicity.

summary.authors: Theo M. Nieuwenhuizen
summary.executive_summary: The paper explores the fundamental nature of gravitation by reconciling the Einsteinian view (curvature of space) and the Maxwellian view (a field in flat space). Starting with a field-theoretic approach in Minkowski space, the author derives the gravitational energy-momentum tensor from the Einstein equations, demonstrating that they can be represented as an acceleration tensor proportional to the total energy-momentum tensor. A key result is that in flat-space cosmology, the negative gravitational energy perfectly cancels the material energy, leading to a total energy of zero. The author then develops the Relativistic Theory of Gravitation (RTG), which introduces a bimetric coupling between the Riemann and Minkowski metrics, thereby breaking general coordinate invariance. This framework produces a singularity-free solution for the Schwarzschild black hole where metric components remain positive in the interior, allowing time to retain its standard role. In cosmology, the RTG accommodates the ΛCDM model while allowing for a positive curvature-type contribution and predicting an inflation scenario at early times starting at t = -∞. The author concludes that while the field-theoretic and curved-space descriptions are equivalent in standard GTR, the bimetric nature of RTG makes the view of gravitation as a field in flat space more natural. Furthermore, the theory suggests that the quantization of gravity should involve the quantization of fields rather than the quantization of space itself.

Furthermore, the theory suggests that the quantization of gravity should involve the quantization of fields rather than the quantization of space itself.

Research Context
Einstein made the step to go from flat space to curved space. A fundamental difficulty is dealing with the quasi energy-momentum tensor. Babak and Grishchuk recently derived a proper energy-momentum tensor. Their approach used a field-theoretic method in a Minkowski background. Nathan Rosen considered a bimetric theory involving Minkowski and Riemann metrics.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper asks if gravitation is a curvature of space or a field in flat space. It investigates how energy can be faithfully transferred from waves to detectors. The hypothesis is that a field-theoretic approach allows the derivation of the gravitational energy-momentum tensor. The study explores if bimetric coupling can provide a singularity-free version of black holes. The author predicts that the total energy and zero point energy vanish.

Methodological Details
The study starts with a field-theoretic approach in Minkowski space. The Minkowski metric is denoted by γμν. The Riemann metric tensor gμν is defined via kμν. The acceleration tensor Aμν is defined using Minkowski covariant derivatives. The combination τμν is calculated from Aμν and Rμν. The Einstein equations are rewritten in the Newton shape. Matter is included by adding the stress-energy tensor Tμν to τμν.

Procedures And Architectures
The author considers the FLRW metric for flat space cosmology. A bimetric coupling is introduced to break general coordinate invariance. A positive cosmological constant Λ is chosen for the RTG. The theory imposes a harmonic constraint Dν hμν = 0. The metric functions U, V, and W are scaled to identify small parameters. A parametric solution of the equations is derived for the black hole.

Key Results
In flat space cosmology, the gravitational energy is negative. The gravitational energy cancels the material energy. The Schwarzschild black hole solution is singularity-free. Metric components in the interior remain positive. The theory yields a ΛCDM model for large scale factors. The ρ2 term allows a positive curvature-type contribution. An initial inflation scenario occurs starting at t = -∞. The zero point energy vanish in the presence of ρΛ and ρbi.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Curvature is a geometric description of the gravitational field in flat space. Coordinate space is the physical space. The expansion is interpreted as a decrease in the cosmic speed of light. Quantization of the RTG will involve fields but not space. RTG forces a Maxwellian view of gravitation as a field in flat space.

Contradictions And Limitations
The RTG has self-repulsive properties for matter falling into a black hole. Logunov's choice of ρbi leads to an imaginary mass graviton. The theory requires an inflaton field to counteract a negative cosmological constant. The harmonic condition severely reduces the gauge invariance of GTR. The Schwarzschild black hole cannot obey energy-momentum conservation if the central mass is smeared.

Claims
Gravitation can be treated as a field in flat space. The gravitational energy-momentum tensor is derived in Minkowski space. Standard GTR is a step to curved space. This supports the Maxwellian view of gravitation.
The RTG provides a singularity-free black hole solution. The solution is singularity free. Metric components remain positive in the interior. Standard solutions are Schwarzschild black holes. Time maintains its standard role in the interior.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows black hole functions U, V, and W for αμ = 0.1.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the derivation of a gravitational energy-momentum tensor in Minkowski space. 2. The strongest evidence is the singularity-free black hole where time remains valid. 3. The future path involves the quantization of fields rather than space.

summary.title: Differential recursion and differentially algebraic functions
summary.authors: Akitoshi Kawamura
summary.executive_summary: Moore introduced a class of real-valued "recursive" functions intended to bridge the gap between digital and analog computation, specifically referencing Shannon’s General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC). The GPAC was shown to be capable of generating differentially algebraic functions, leading Moore to propose that his "real primitive recursive" functions were also differentially algebraic (Claim 1). However, this paper identifies technical inaccuracies and ambiguities in Moore’s original work, particularly his lack of formal treatment for partial functions. The author reformulates Moore's theory by defining real primitive recursive functions through three primary operators: juxtaposition (jx), composition (cm), and a rigorously defined differential recursion operator (dr). The dr operator is designed to pick a "unique" solution from the set of all solutions to an integral equation while preserving analyticity. Through this rigorous framework, the author proves that Moore's Claim 1 is false. The paper provides a specific counter-example: the function ̄Γ is shown to be real primitive recursive but, as demonstrated by Hölder, it is not differentially algebraic. This result implies that Moore's classes do not have the intended relationship with Shannon's model of analog computation. Furthermore, the paper examines other operations like minimization (mn), noting that they can lead to discontinuous functions, and discusses the limitations of using these for modeling digital computation. The work emphasizes the necessity of dealing with partial functions seriously to avoid the erroneous statements found in early literature.

Executive Summary
Moore introduced a class of real-valued "recursive" functions intended to bridge the gap between digital and analog computation, specifically referencing Shannon’s General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC). The GPAC was shown to be capable of generating differentially algebraic functions, leading Moore to propose that his "real primitive recursive" functions were also differentially algebraic (Claim 1). However, this paper identifies technical inaccuracies and ambiguities in Moore’s original work, particularly his lack of formal treatment for partial functions. The author reformulates Moore's theory by defining real primitive recursive functions through three primary operators: juxtaposition (jx), composition (cm), and a rigorously defined differential recursion operator (dr). The dr operator is designed to pick a "unique" solution from the set of all solutions to an integral equation while preserving analyticity. Through this rigorous framework, the author proves that Moore's Claim 1 is false. The paper provides a specific counter-example: the function ̄Γ is shown to be real primitive recursive but, as demonstrated by Hölder, it is not differentially algebraic. This result implies that Moore's classes do not have the intended relationship with Shannon's model of analog computation. Furthermore, the paper examines other operations like minimization (mn), noting that they can lead to discontinuous functions, and discusses the limitations of using these for modeling digital computation. The work emphasizes the necessity of dealing with partial functions seriously to avoid the erroneous statements found in early literature.

Research Context
Several different kinds of models talk about "computability" and "complexity" of real functions. Analog computation takes place in continuous time. Shannon’s General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC) models the Differential Analyzer. The GPAC was shown capable of generating all and only the differentially algebraic functions. Moore [13] addressed this question for his new function classes. These classes are defined as closures under operators supposedly real-number versions of primitive recursion and minimization. Moore’s work lacked formality in some ways. The definition of the classes suffers from ambiguity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper seeks to reformulate Moore’s theory in a mathematically sound way. It investigates technical inaccuracies in Moore's work regarding the behavior of the differential recursion operator. The author focuses on the behavior of the differential recursion operator on partial functions. The central hypothesis is that Moore's Claim 1 is incorrect. The author aims to show that the purported relation to Shannon’s model fails.

Methodological Details
The study analyzes functions f: ⊆Rm →Rn which may be partial functions. The domain of f is allowed to be a proper subset of Rm. A function is said to be analytic if a family of n-tuples of real numbers allows a sum to converge. The study uses the Identity Theorem and Baire Category Theorem for proofs. Differentially algebraic functions are defined through polynomial relations of derivatives. The study characterizes differentially algebraic functions using transcendence degree.

Procedures And Architectures
Real primitive recursive functions are defined through three operators: juxtaposition, composition, and differential recursion. Juxtaposition and composition are defined precisely to specify the domain of the functions constructed. The differential recursion operator dr(f, g) is formulated to pick a unique solution. The unique solution is defined as the function h such that restrictions of any other solution are restrictions of h. The operator dr is designed to preserve analyticity. The author employs the Cauchy–Kowalewsky Theorem to simplify the uniqueness discussion.

Key Results
Theorem 3 proves that several characterizations of differentially algebraic functions are equivalent. Lemma 5 shows that a function is differentially algebraic if its derivatives stay within a field of finite transcendence degree. Theorem 8 proves that the property of being differentially algebraic is preserved by juxtaposition and composition. The author proves that Claim 1 fails. The function ̄Γ is shown to be real primitive recursive. The function ̄Γ is not differentially algebraic, contradicting Moore's claim.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results show that the purported relation to Shannon’s model of analog computation fails. The paper argues that partial functions must be dealt with seriously. Moore’s lack of formality led to ambiguous and erroneous statements. The failure of Claim 1 means the classes are not necessarily GPAC-generable. Certain operators, like minimization, produce non-smooth functions. These non-smooth functions no longer enjoy the analyticity properties of the core class.

Contradictions And Limitations
Moore's original work lacked formality and the definition of the classes suffers from ambiguity. The author notes that Moore’s definition of minimization is left ambiguous. The class of real recursive functions is probably not well-behaved. Because minimization can produce non-smooth functions, the class no longer enjoys Theorem 12.

Claims
Moore's Claim 1, stating that real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic, is false. The function ̄Γ is shown to be real primitive recursive. The function ̄Γ is not differentially algebraic. The limit as R goes to infinity yields a contradiction to H"{o}lder. Moore's original work suggested these functions were differentially algebraic. The purported relation to Shannon’s model fails.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the concept of a unique solution to an integral equation. Figure 2 shows an integrand with a singularity.

Three Takeaways
1. Moore's Claim 1 is false. 2. The function ̄Γ serves as the primary counter-example. 3. Partial functions must be dealt with seriously.

summary.authors: D. DeMille, S. Sainis, J. Sage, T. Bergeman, S. Kotochigova, and E. Tiesinga

summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a novel laboratory methodology to detect potential spatial or temporal variations in the electron-to-proton mass ratio ($\mu \equiv m_e/m_p$). While variations in fundamental constants have been hypothesized in string-inspired models and quintessence theories to explain dark energy, direct laboratory verification remains challenging. Most current constraints come from cosmological observations of distant sources, which provide bounds around $\sim 10^{-15}/\text{year}$ but are limited by significant systematic uncertainties. The authors suggest that $\mu$ variation could be significantly larger (by a factor of $\sim 30$) than variations in the fine structure constant $\alpha$, making it a high-priority target for precision spectroscopy. The core of the proposal involves using molecular vibrational levels in the Cs$_2$ molecule, specifically identifying nearly-degenerate levels in overlapping electronic potentials. By selecting a high-vibrational level of the $X^1\Sigma^+_g$ ground state and a lower-vibrational level of the $a^3\Sigma^+_u$ state, the researchers can create a system where the energy splitting ($\Omega$) is small but the sensitivity to $\mu$ ($\partial_\mu \Omega$) remains large. The paper provides spectroscopic evidence for such a degeneracy between the $v_a = 37$ and $v_X = 138$ levels in Cs$_2$. Using two-color photoassociation (PA) spectroscopy on ultracold Cs atoms ($T \sim 100 \mu\text{K}$), the authors identified specific sublevels and performed a global fit of the potentials. They calculate that the energy sensitivity $\partial_\mu \Omega$ for these transitions is approximately $5 \times 10^{12}$ Hz. This level of sensitivity allows for a fractional change $\Delta\mu/\mu \lesssim 10^{-17}$ to be detected in roughly one day of integration, requiring an accuracy comparable to current atomic clocks. The proposal highlights the use of long-lived states and high density of states in Cs$_2$ to minimize linewidths and maximize sensitivity.

While variations in fundamental constants have been hypothesized in string-inspired models and quintessence theories to explain dark energy, direct laboratory verification remains challenging. The paper provides spectroscopic evidence for such a degeneracy between the $v_a = 37$ and $v_X = 138$ levels in Cs$_2$. Using two-color photoassociation (PA) spectroscopy on ultracold Cs atoms ($T \sim 100 \mu\text{K}$), the authors identified specific sublevels and performed a global fit of the potentials. They calculate that the energy sensitivity $\partial_\mu \Omega$ for these transitions is approximately $5 \times 10^{12}$ Hz. This level of sensitivity allows for a fractional change $\Delta\mu/\mu \lesssim 10^{-17}$ to be detected in roughly one day of integration, requiring an accuracy comparable to current atomic clocks. The proposal highlights the use of long-lived states and high density of states in Cs$_2$ to minimize linewidths and maximize sensitivity.

Research Context
The study explores the possible spatial or temporal variation of the electron-to-proton mass ratio $\mu$. Theoretical motivation comes from string-inspired models including space-time with extra dimensions. Light scalar fields whose variable amplitude couples to ordinary matter are also considered. These scalar fields are potential candidates dubbed “quintessence” to explain the observed dark energy. Measurements can only detect variation in dimensionless constants. To date, most attention has focused on the fine structure constant $\alpha$. However, variations in $\alpha$ are no more likely than in any other fundamental dimensionless parameter. Within the context of grand unified theories, variation in $\mu$ should be larger than $\alpha$ by a factor of $\sim 30$. Study of $\mu$ is a potentially more sensitive method to observe any variation. Most sensitive tests have come from examining molecular spectra from cosmologically distant sources. These measurements yield stringent bounds at the level $\sim 10^{-15}/\text{year}$ on the time variation of $\mu$. However, systematic errors associated with these measurements can be significant. These errors are difficult to eliminate due to the uncertainty in the structure, environment, and dynamics of the sources.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to perform a laboratory experiment to search for variation of $\mu$ with high sensitivity. The authors propose using molecular vibrational levels where energy can be highly sensitive to changes in $\mu$. Specifically, the study hypothesizes that pairs of closely-spaced levels can be used to enhance sensitivity relative to the level splitting. The authors argue that the splitting between pairs of levels in Cs2 could be measured precisely enough to sense a fractional change $\Delta\mu/\mu \lesssim 10^{-17}$. The sensitivity is governed by the absolute change $\partial_\mu \Omega$ of the energy splitting $\Omega$. The primary figure of merit is the ratio $\partial_\mu \Omega/\Gamma$. Additionally, the relative change $\partial_\mu \Omega/\Omega$ provides an important secondary figure of merit. Ultimately, $\Omega$ must be measured with respect to some reference clock. Many systematic effects are proportional to $\Omega$.

Methodological Details
The study proposes experiments using the Cs2 molecule to detect small variations in $\mu$. The system relies on the nearly-degenerate pair of molecular vibrational levels. Each state is associated with a different electronic potential. The study demonstrates the existence of such pairs of levels in Cs2. Ultracold atoms were cooled and confined in a dark SPOT magneto-optic trap. A sample of ultracold ($T \sim 100 \mu\text{K}$) Cs atoms was used. Atoms were optically pumped into the $6s_{1/2} F = m_F = 4$ state. Two-color photoassociation (PA) spectroscopy was used to determine positions of deeply bound $a^3\Sigma^+_u$ levels. A CW laser excites the atoms into a bound state of the Cs2 (2)0-g potential. This excited state decays to a manifold of $a^3\Sigma^+_u$ vibrational levels. A second CW (probe) laser is applied to search for resonances. Binding energies are reported relative to the hyperfine (HF) barycenter.

Procedures And Architectures
The analysis assumes both $m_e$ and $\alpha$ remain constant while $\mu$ varies. This corresponds to a variation of $m_p$. Molecular electronic potentials are independent of $\mu$ because they depend only on the Rydberg energy. The vibrational energy levels $E_v$ are approximated via the WKB quantization condition. Varying Eq. (1) with respect to $\mu$ and v yields the energy sensitivity $\partial_\mu E_v$. Near its minimum, a typical potential is harmonic, where $\partial_\mu E_v = E_v/2$. For higher values of v, the density of states becomes large, and $\partial_\mu E_v$ becomes small. Therefore, $\partial_\mu E_v$ is maximized at an intermediate value of v. For a generic Morse potential, the maximum value of $\partial_\mu E_v$ is obtained for levels with $E(max)_v \approx 3D/4$. The study identifies a degeneracy between the $v_a = 37$ and $v_X = 138$ levels in Cs2. A global fit of the potentials was performed to all known levels. For spectral regions with no data, the potentials were modeled using the “Hannover” analytic form. The fit accounts for the SO2 interaction.

Key Results
The study explicitly calculates $\partial_\mu E_v$ for all vibrational levels in the X and a states of Cs2. The energy sensitivity $\partial_\mu \Omega$ for transitions of this type is $\sim 5 \times 10^{12}$ Hz. This allows for a detection of $\Delta\mu/\mu \lesssim 10^{-17}$ in $\sim 1$ day. A magnetic dipole transition can be driven at $\Omega \approx 6.3$ GHz. Alternatively, an E1 transition can be driven at $\Omega \approx 9.8$ GHz. The energy sensitivity $\partial_\mu E(X)v_X$ increases monotonically with $|E_b|$.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The mechanism for amplifying $\partial_\mu \Omega$ involves using levels in overlapping electronic potentials. In this situation, two electronic potentials X and Y overlap. An excited level of X with $v_X \gg 1$ can be near in energy to a lower level of Y with $v_Y \ll v_X$. The energy difference $\Omega$ is small, but it retains a large sensitivity because $\partial_\mu \Omega \approx \partial_\mu E(X)v_X$. The large mass of Cs yields a high density of states. The incommensurate vibrational splittings and high density of states make near-degeneracies likely. The strong HF mixing reduces the value of $\partial_\mu E_v$ for the directly observed X sublevel. However, the position of other nearby, unobserved X state sublevels can be accurately predicted for use in the experiment.

Contradictions And Limitations
Systematic errors associated with cosmological measurements can be significant and are difficult to eliminate. The sensitivity of the proposed measurement is governed by several key parameters. The ratio $\partial_\mu \Omega/\Gamma$ provides a primary figure of merit. The relative change $\partial_\mu \Omega/\Omega$ is an important secondary figure of merit. Ultimately, $\Omega$ must be measured with respect to some reference clock. It is impossible to determine $\Omega$ to better than $\delta\Omega_{min} = \Omega(\delta\Omega_c/\Omega_c)$. Many systematic effects are proportional to $\Omega$. The proposed experiment requires $\delta\Omega/\Omega \sim 10^{-14}$ accuracy. This is over ten times less accuracy than the best atomic clocks. The details of the data and fit are not provided in this text.

Claims
The Cs2 molecule is an ideal system for detecting $\mu$ variation due to overlapping potentials and high density of states. Cs2 has two low-lying, overlapping potentials. The large mass of Cs yields a high density of states. All rovibrational levels of both potentials have extremely long radiative lifetimes. Strong HF mixing reduces the value of $\partial_\mu E_v$ for the directly observed X sublevel. The system can yield spectral lines with narrow width $\Gamma$.
Near-degenerate levels in Cs2 provide a way to achieve a fractional change sensitivity of $\Delta\mu/\mu \lesssim 10^{-17}$. The splitting between pairs of levels in Cs2 could be measured precisely enough to sense a fractional change $\Delta\mu/\mu \lesssim 10^{-17}$. The energy sensitivity $\partial_\mu \Omega$ for transitions of this type is $\sim 5 \times 10^{12}$ Hz. Measurement requires $\delta\Omega/\Omega \sim 10^{-14}$ accuracy. Detection could be achieved in $\sim 1$ day.

Data And Code Availability
Details of the data and the fit will be given elsewhere.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
For spectral regions with no data, the potentials were modeled using the “Hannover” analytic form.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows energy sensitivity vs. binding energy for both potentials. Figure 2 shows data indicating a degeneracy between the deeply bound a3$\Sigma^+$u (va = 37) and X1$\Sigma^+$g (vX = 138) levels.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is proposing a laboratory experiment using nearly-degenerate molecular vibrational levels in Cs2 to detect variations in $\mu$. 2. The strongest evidence is the identification of a degeneracy between the $v_a = 37$ and $v_X = 138$ levels with a calculated sensitivity of $\partial_\mu \Omega \sim 5 \times 10^{12}$ Hz. 3. summary.authors: Alfredo Braunstein, Roberto Mulet, Andrea Pagnani
