summary.title: Comparative Performance Analysis of Image De-noising Techniques
summary.authors: Vivek Kumar, Pranay Yadav, Atul Samadhiya, Sandeep Jain, and Prayag Tiwari
summary.executive_summary: The paper investigates the critical role of noise in digital image processing, specifically focusing on how noise degrades image quality and appearance. To maintain textural information and structural features during image restoration, appropriate denoising algorithms must be selected based on the specific characteristics of the noise present. The authors provide a comprehensive overview of noise types, classifying them based on their additive and multiplicative nature. This includes a detailed analysis of Gaussian noise (characterized by a bell-shaped distribution), Salt and Pepper noise (impulse-type spikes from transmission errors), Speckle noise (multiplicative noise found in coherent systems like SAR and acoustics), and Brownian noise (fractal or 1/f noise). The study further classifies denoising algorithms into two primary categories: spatial filtering and transform domain filtering. Spatial filters are subdivided into non-linear methods (such as median-type filters) and linear filters (such as Mean and Wiener filters). Transform domain methods involve spatial-frequency filtering via Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and Wavelet domain filtering. The paper delves deeply into Wavelet Transform techniques, exploring linear filters, non-linear coefficient thresholding (including hard, soft, semi-soft, and Garrote thresholding), and various adaptive and non-adaptive thresholds like VISU Shrink, SURE Shrink, and Bayes Shrink. It also discusses non-orthogonal transforms, such as the Un-decimated Wavelet Transform (UDWT) and Shift Invariant Wavelet Packet Decomposition (SIWPD). Finally, the paper evaluates these algorithms using a grayscale image of Lena with a 90% noise density, utilizing quantitative metrics including Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Image Enhancement Factor (IEF). The results demonstrate that advanced methods, specifically MDBUTMF, significantly outperform traditional filters, providing a foundation for future research in high-performance image restoration.

claims.description: Wavelet domain filtering, particularly adaptive thresholding and multiwavelets, provides superior image restoration compared to spatial filters.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The paper investigates the critical role of noise in digital image processing, specifically focusing on how noise degrades image quality and appearance. To maintain textural information and structural features during image restoration, appropriate denoising algorithms must be selected based on the specific characteristics of the noise present. The authors provide a comprehensive overview of noise types, classifying them based on their additive and multiplicative nature. This includes a detailed analysis of Gaussian noise (characterized by a bell-shaped distribution), Salt and Pepper noise (impulse-type spikes from transmission errors), Speckle noise (multiplicative noise found in coherent systems like SAR and acoustics), and Brownian noise (fractal or 1/f noise). The study further classifies denoising algorithms into two primary categories: spatial filtering and transform domain filtering. Spatial filters are subdivided into non-linear methods (such as median-type filters) and linear filters (such as Mean and Wiener filters). Transform domain methods involve spatial-frequency filtering via Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and Wavelet domain filtering. The paper delves deeply into Wavelet Transform techniques, exploring linear filters, non-linear coefficient thresholding (including hard, soft, semi-soft, and Garrote thresholding), and various adaptive and non-adaptive thresholds like VISU Shrink, SURE Shrink, and Bayes Shrink. It also discusses non-orthogonal transforms, such as the Un-decimated Wavelet Transform (UDWT) and Shift Invariant Wavelet Packet Decomposition (SIWPD). Finally, the paper evaluates these algorithms using a grayscale image of Lena with a 90% noise density, utilizing quantitative metrics including Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Image Enhancement Factor (IEF). The results demonstrate that advanced methods, specifically MDBUTMF, significantly outperform traditional filters, providing a foundation for future research in high-performance image restoration.

Research Context
Noise is a primary factor that degrades image quality. Image restoration requires removing noise while preserving structural features. Degradation occurs from blurring and noise sources. Blurring is caused by optical systems or motion. Denoising is critical in astronomy, medical imaging, and forensics. Selection of a denoising algorithm depends on the noise type.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The objective is to present an account on noise types. The study aims to analyze potential image denoising algorithms. The paper aims to conduct a comparative study of these algorithms. The study hypothesizes that transform domain methods can overcome spatial filter limitations. It explores how different thresholds affect denoising performance.

Methodological Details
The study classifies noises by additive and multiplicative nature. Gaussian noise is modeled with a bell-shaped distribution. Salt and pepper noise is characterized as impulse noise. Speckle noise is a multiplicative noise in coherent systems. Brownian noise is categorized as fractal or 1/f noise. Denoising methods are divided into spatial and transform domains. Spatial filters include non-linear median and linear filters. The Wiener filter is the optimal linear filter for Gaussian noise. Wavelet domain filtering uses coefficient thresholding. The study examines non-adaptive and adaptive thresholding techniques.

Procedures And Architectures
Spatial filters employ low pass filtering on pixel groups. Non-linear median filters include weighted and relaxed types. Wiener filtering requires information about noise and signal spectra. Spatial-frequency filtering utilizes the Fast Fourier Transform. Wavelet domain filtering separates signal and noise energy. Hard thresholding removes small coefficients but generates artifacts. Soft thresholding shrinks coefficients by the threshold absolute value. VISU Shrink is a non-adaptive universal threshold. SURE Shrink uses a hybrid of universal and SURE thresholds. Bayes Shrink minimizes the Bayes Risk Estimator function. Un-decimated Wavelet Transform (UDWT) provides shift invariance. Multiwavelets use more than one scaling function. Deterministic modeling creates a tree structure of coefficients.

Key Results
The MF filter achieved a PSNR of 6.5759 and an IEF of 1.1712. The AMF filter resulted in a PSNR of 8.0603 and an IEF of 1.6499. The PSMF filter showed a PSNR of 6.7847 and an IEF of 1.2257. The DBA filter reached a PSNR of 17.1205 and an IEF of 13.2768. The MDBA filter achieved a PSNR of 17.2242 and an IEF of 13.5976. The MDBUTMF filter achieved the highest PSNR of 17.9865 and IEF of 16.2066. MDBUTMF showed an improvement of +11.4106 PSNR absolute; +173.4% relative over MF. MDBUTMF showed an improvement of +15.0354 IEF absolute; +1280.5% relative over MF.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Wavelet transforms separate signal and noise by concentrating energy. Hard thresholding artifacts result from removing moderate coefficients. Adaptive thresholds like Bayes Shrink outperform SURE Shrink frequently. UDWT avoids visual artifacts like the pseudo-Gibbs phenomenon. Multiwavelets provide symmetry and higher order vanishing moments. Deterministic modeling allows for hierarchical interpretation of wavelet decomposition.

Contradictions And Limitations
Spatial filters often blur images and hide edges. Wiener filtering only works well for smooth underlying signals. Hard thresholding creates spurious blips or artifacts. VISU Shrink can yield overly smoothed images. UDWT involves a large overhead of computations. Wavelet coefficient modeling can be computationally expensive.

Claims
Wavelet domain filtering, particularly adaptive thresholding and multiwavelets, provides superior image restoration compared to spatial filters. Wavelet transform maps white noise in the signal domain to white noise in the transform domain. MDBUTMF achieved a PSNR of 17.9865 at 90% noise density. Multiwavelets possess properties such as short support and symmetry. UDWT adds a large overhead of computations. Wavelet coefficient modeling can be computationally much more complex. Advanced wavelet methods are preferred for high-noise environments.

Data And Code Availability
Data and code availability are not specified in the paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Specific ablation studies are not reported.

Ethical Considerations
Ethical considerations are not reported.

Key Figures Tables
Table I compares PSNR and IEF for six different filters at 90% noise density. Figure 1 illustrates the Gaussian distribution. Figure 4 illustrates salt and pepper noise. Figure 6 shows the illustration of speckle noise. Figure 9 shows the expanded classification of image denoising technique.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a comprehensive classification of noises and denoising algorithms. 2. The strongest evidence is the high PSNR (17.9865) achieved by the MDBUTMF method. 3. The future path involves addressing computational complexity in non-orthogonal and multiwavelet transforms.

summary.title: Real-Time Ramsey Interferometry in Fractional Quantum Hall States
summary.authors: Tal Goren and Karyn Le Hur
summary.field_subfield: Condensed Matter Physics / Fractional Quantum Hall Effect
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a novel method to probe the time-dependent dynamical phase and Green's functions of fractional quasiparticles in quantum Hall states using Ramsey interferometry. The authors describe a protocol where a quantum point contact (QPC) is subjected to a Ramsey voltage modulation consisting of two short pulses. This setup generates an interference term in the current noise that oscillates according to the time delay between the pulses. The study shows that this interference pattern provides a unique probe of the Green's function in the time domain and reveals the fractional charge of the tunneling particles. The authors analyze two primary experimental geometries: a Hall bar constriction where Laughlin quasiparticles tunnel, and a QPC between two separated Hall droplets where electrons tunnel. For Laughlin states, the paper provides explicit expressions for the current noise, showing how the oscillation frequency is tied to the dynamical phase and how the amplitude decay provides information about the wave-function envelope of the quasiparticles. The research also addresses the non-Abelian 5/2 fractional quantum Hall state, demonstrating that Ramsey interferometry can differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states by detecting specific phase shifts. The authors highlight that Ramsey interferometry is advantageous over traditional Mach-Zehnder geometry because it allows for a continuous scan of the time delay and is determined by the dynamical phase rather than the enclosed magnetic flux. The methodology, developed using the Keldysh formalism for non-equilibrium systems, suggests a generalizable approach for characterizing topological states of matter, including potential applications in superconductors.

Executive Summary
This paper proposes a novel method to probe the time-dependent dynamical phase and Green's functions of fractional quasiparticles in quantum Hall states using Ramsey interferometry. The authors describe a protocol where a quantum point contact (QPC) is subjected to a Ramsey voltage modulation consisting of two short pulses. This setup generates an interference term in the current noise that oscillates according to the time delay between the pulses. The study shows that this interference pattern provides a unique probe of the Green's function in the time domain and reveals the fractional charge of the tunneling particles. The authors analyze two primary experimental geometries: a Hall bar constriction where Laughlin quasiparticles tunnel, and a QPC between two separated Hall droplets where electrons tunnel. For Laughlin states, the paper provides explicit expressions for the current noise, showing how the oscillation frequency is tied to the dynamical phase and how the amplitude decay provides information about the wave-function envelope of the quasiparticles. The research also addresses the non-Abelian 5/2 fractional quantum Hall state, demonstrating that Ramsey interferometry can differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states by detecting specific phase shifts. The authors highlight that Ramsey interferometry is advantageous over traditional Mach-Zehnder geometry because it allows for a continuous scan of the time delay and is determined by the dynamical phase rather than the enclosed magnetic flux. The methodology, developed using the Keldysh formalism for non-equilibrium systems, suggests a generalizable approach for characterizing topological states of matter, including potential applications in superconductors.

Research Context
One of the main attributes of the fractional quantum Hall effect is the occurrence of excitations with fractional charge and statistics. The edge states of such a system are described by a chiral Luttinger liquid theory. Ramsey interferometry has been recently suggested to probe the dynamics of mesoscopic systems. This includes studies on quasicondensates, spin ensembles, and Rydberg atoms. There is a need to probe the dynamical phase of fractional quasiparticles.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study investigates Ramsey interferometry in the Abelian and 5/2 non-Abelian fractional quantum Hall states. The authors hypothesize that a Ramsey voltage modulation generates an interference term in the current noise. The interference pattern is expected to probe the Green's function of the fractional quasi-particles. The method is predicted to reveal the fractional charge of the particles. The protocol provides information on the speed of those quasiparticles propagating along the edge. For the 5/2 state, the signal can differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states.

Methodological Details
The study uses a quantum Hall bar geometry where a small constriction induces a coupling. This constriction functions as a quantum point contact (QPC) for tunneling. The QPC leads to tunneling of particles from one edge to the other. The researchers consider Laughlin states with filling factor $\nu = 1/2n+1$. The creation operator for the fractional quasi-particle is expressed by bosonic chiral fields. The commutation relations ensure the correct anti-commutation relation for electrons. The authors apply the Keldysh formalism to describe non-equilibrium systems. The current-current correlation function is calculated to second order in D. The stationary phase approximation determines the main contributions to the noise. The study compares two geometries: a Hall bar and separated droplets. In the Hall bar, transport is driven by Laughlin quasiparticles. In the droplet case, the tunneling particles here are electrons.

Procedures And Architectures
The Ramsey voltage modulation is composed of two short pulses. The delay time between the pulses is denoted by $t_0$. For short pulse durations, the pulses are approximated by a Dirac delta function. The dynamical phase $\phi(t)$ is defined by the integral of the voltage drop. The current noise is the Fourier transform of the correlation function. For momentum-resolved tunneling, the tunnel junction is long compared to the Fermi wavelength. A magnetic field $B$ provides a momentum boost $qB$. The study derives the noise for both point-like and momentum-resolved scenarios.

Key Results
The current noise exhibits a Ramsey interference pattern oscillating with the delay time $t_0$. The noise oscillates at a frequency of $\omega - qV_{dc}$. The charge $q$ in the formula is the dressed charge of the fluid. For Laughlin states, the noise contains a factor of $\cos \pi\nu$. In the high temperature limit $T \gg t_0^{-1}$, the amplitude decays exponentially as $\exp\{-2\pi\nu Tt_0\}$. In the low temperature limit $T \ll t_0^{-1}$, the amplitude follows a power law $(t_0/\tau)^{-2\nu}$. The decay of the Ramsey interference is a measure of the envelope of the wave-function. Fractionalization manifests in the prefactor, the Green's function, and the dynamical phase factor. For the 5/2 state, the signal differentiates between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states. The oscillation frequency in momentum-resolved tunneling depends on $qB$ and velocity $v$.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The formation of interferences in time allows measurement of the charge conjugated to the electric field. The protocol allows for a time-resolved measurement of the dynamical phase and Green's function. Ramsey interferometry is advantageous because the time delay can be scanned in a continuous manner. While the Mach-Zehnder is determined by the magnetic flux, the Ramsey interference is determined by the dynamical phase. Because it involves only a single QPC, it does not depend on the bulk quasi-particles. The methodology can be generalized to superconductors through the time dynamics of Bogoliubov quasiparticles.

Contradictions And Limitations
The Ramsey interferometry cannot distinguish between the Pfaffian and the particle-hole Pfaffian states. Ramsey interferometry does not depend on bulk quasi-particles and therefore cannot detect exchange statistics. Ramsey interference involves a single particle, unlike the Hong-Ou-Mandel geometry. The study does not report data or code availability, which is important for reproducibility.

Claims
Ramsey interferometry probes the Green's function and fractional charge in the time domain. The pattern probes the Green's function. The interference reveals the fractional charge. None reported. It allows for time-resolved measurement.
Ramsey interferometry can distinguish between Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states at filling factor 5/2. It can differentiate between the Pfaffian. It cannot distinguish between the Pfaffian and the particle-hole Pfaffian. It can characterize topological states of matter.
Ramsey interferometry is advantageous over Mach-Zehnder geometry for Green's function measurement. The time delay can be scanned in a continuous manner. It does not depend on bulk quasi-particles and cannot detect exchange statistics. It is advantageous for measuring the Green's function.

Data And Code Availability
Data and code availability is not reported.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Robustness and ablation notes are not reported.

Ethical Considerations
Ethical considerations are not reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the two geometries of a QPC.

Three Takeaways
1. Ramsey interferometry provides a time-resolved probe of the Green's function and dynamical phase of fractional quasiparticles. 2. The method can differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states at filling factor 5/2. 3. The proposed time-interferometry approach is generalizable to superconductors and other topological matter.

summary.title: An algorithm for stress and mixed control in Galerkin based FFT homogenization
summary.authors: S. Lucarini and J. Segurado
summary.field_subfield: Materials Science / Computational Mechanics / FFT Homogenization
summary.executive_summary:
This paper presents a novel algorithm designed to address a significant limitation in Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) based computational homogenization: the difficulty of imposing macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient loading paths. While FFT-based methods are highly efficient for simulating complex microstructures with millions of degrees of freedom, they are traditionally optimized for strain control. In standard FFT schemes, imposing a macroscopic stress requires iterative corrections to the strain tensor, which significantly increases the computational cost per step. The authors propose an alternative framework based on a variational (Galerkin) approach. This method derives the problem from a weak formulation of the linear momentum balance, avoiding the need for a reference medium and leveraging material tangents to improve convergence. 

The core contribution is a modified projection operator ±G*±. By redefining the operator's value at the null frequency (υ = 0), the algorithm can enforce either full stress control, full strain control, or a specific mixed loading path (e.g., uniaxial tension where some components are stress-free). For stress control, the null frequency projects the average part of the field into itself, effectively setting the target macroscopic stress. For mixed control, the operator is further adjusted to handle specific components of the deformation gradient and stress independently. 

The method's efficacy is demonstrated through two primary numerical benchmarks: a particle-reinforced hyperelastic material and a polycrystal using a crystal plasticity model. In the hyperelastic case, the proposed stress and mixed control methods achieve the same computational performance as the standard strain control, requiring no additional iterations. In the polycrystal benchmark, the stress control method proved to be significantly faster than other methods. This is because the majority of the loading increments in a stress-controlled path are purely elastic, allowing the solver to converge in a single Newton iteration per step. The paper concludes that this algorithm provides a powerful and efficient tool for FFT-based homogenization, allowing for the simulation of complex, non-linear mixed boundary conditions without the overhead of traditional iterative stress-correction techniques.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a novel algorithm designed to address a significant limitation in Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) based computational homogenization: the difficulty of imposing macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient loading paths. While FFT-based methods are highly efficient for simulating complex microstructures with millions of degrees of freedom, they are traditionally optimized for strain control. In standard FFT schemes, imposing a macroscopic stress requires iterative corrections to the strain tensor, which significantly increases the computational cost per step. The authors propose an alternative framework based on a variational (Galerkin) approach. This method derives the problem from a weak formulation of the linear momentum balance, avoiding the need for a reference medium and leveraging material tangents to improve convergence. 

The core contribution is a modified projection operator ±G*±. By redefining the operator's value at the null frequency (υ = 0), the algorithm can enforce either full stress control, full strain control, or a specific mixed loading path (e.g., uniaxial tension where some components are stress-free). For stress control, the null frequency projects the average part of the field into itself, effectively setting the target macroscopic stress. For mixed control, the operator is further adjusted to handle specific components of the deformation gradient and stress independently. 

The method's efficacy is demonstrated through two primary numerical benchmarks: a particle-reinforced hyperelastic material and a polycrystal using a crystal plasticity model. In the hyperelastic case, the proposed stress and mixed control methods achieve the same computational performance as the standard strain control, requiring no additional iterations. In the polycrystal benchmark, the stress control method proved to be significantly faster than other methods. This is because the majority of the loading increments in a stress-controlled path are purely elastic, allowing the solver to converge in a single Newton iteration per step. The paper concludes that this algorithm provides a powerful and efficient tool for FFT-based homogenization, allowing for the simulation of complex, non-linear mixed boundary conditions without the overhead of traditional iterative stress-correction techniques.

Research Context
FFT homogenization is a popular alternative to FE. It is ideal to simulate complex geometries comprising millions of degrees of freedom. However, imposing a macroscopic stress or mixed loading path is not a direct task in FFT. In these classical schemes, iterative approaches are the usual solution. As a result of the corrections, the number of iterations significantly increases. A different approach for FFT homogenization is the Galerkin based approach. The resulting method does not require a reference medium. Nevertheless, the variational approach was still formulated imposing the history of the macroscopic deformation gradient.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to extend the variational algorithm to stress and mixed control. This is achieved by using a direct method based on a modified project operator. The hypothesis is that this preserves the computational performance of the original method. The goal is to simulate the behavior for a macroscopic stress history. The proposed method aims to solve problems with mixed boundary conditions.

Methodological Details
The RVE is discretized in nx ny nz voxels. The linear momentum balance is imposed in its weak form. The test functions are virtual deformation gradients premultiplied by a projector operator. The discrete form is an algebraic system of 9 nx ny nz equations. For non-linear behavior, the macroscopic deformation gradient is usually split in n increments. The linear equations are solved using the conjugate gradient method. The projection operator bG is a fourth order tensor. The projection should be a zero fourth order tensor in the null and Nyquist frequencies. A modification of the projection operator is proposed for stress control. The null frequency should project the average part into itself, defined as the identity tensor. The resulting non linear system for obtaining the equilibrium is solved by Newton.

Procedures And Architectures
The algorithm uses a modified projection operator G* in the Fourier space. For stress control, G* projects the average part into itself at the null frequency. For mixed control, the null frequency is modified again to handle specific stress or strain components. The discrete equilibrium equation is solved using a Newton scheme. In each iteration, the stress is linearized around the last iteration of the deformation gradient. The linear system is solved via the conjugate gradient method.

Key Results
The first benchmark consists in a particle reinforced hyperelastic matrix. The RVE is discretized using 643 voxels. The RVE contains 4 particles occupying a volume fraction of 0.2. The matrix properties are $\mu$ = 28 Pa. The particles are one order of magnitude stiffer, or 10 times larger. The uniaxial tensile test reaches an elongation of $\lambda_{end} = 0.2$. The load is homogeneously divided in 100 load increments. In the hyperelastic model, stress and mixed control simulations took approximately the same number of iterations. The second benchmark is a polycrystal with around 200 randomly oriented grains. A final elongation of $\lambda_{end} = 0.02$ is imposed. The load case (2) is clearly faster than the others. This occurs because most of the load increments are elastic and solved in one Newton iteration.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The algorithm does not imply extra iterations. It allows solving problems with mixed boundary conditions without extra computational effort. The examples show the potential for two types of constitutive models. The approach sustains the well known advantages of the FFT methods.

Contradictions And Limitations
The use of this type of strain control conditions to emulate uniaxial tension can lead to inaccurate results. The compressive transverse stresses are not zero. The path is totally different. This is a consequence of using a fixed time step. All the cases will require very similar simulation times.

Claims
The modified projection operator allows for mixed loading paths without increasing the computational cost per step. The method does not imply extra iterations. Stress and mixed control simulations took approximately the same number of iterations.  It allows solving problems with mixed boundary conditions without extra computational effort.
Stress-controlled loading is computationally more efficient for materials with significant elastic regimes. Case (2) is clearly faster than the others. Most of the load increments are elastic and solved in one Newton iteration.  The fast elastic steps compensate the global time.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the particle reinforced RVE and longitudinal/transverse responses. Figure 2 displays the polycrystal RVE and stress responses for four loading cases. Figure 3 compares convergence iterations and normalized simulation times.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a modified projection operator that allows for stress and mixed control in a Galerkin-based FFT homogenization framework. 2. The strongest evidence is that the method maintains the same number of iterations as strain control in hyperelastic models and is faster in polycrystal models. 3. The future path involves applying this algorithm to any material with complex non-linear constitutive equations.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a novel metasurface architecture for high-efficiency broadband terahertz (THz) generation that circumvents the fundamental efficiency limits of conventional nonlinear metasurfaces. Conventional split-ring resonator (SRR) metasurfaces are limited by dissipative and radiative damping due to linear scattering, which reduces the amplitude of the local near-field and, consequently, the THz emission intensity. The authors propose a dark-mode-assisted perfect absorbing metasurface that decouples local field enhancement from the symmetry requirements of second-order nonlinearity. The architecture consists of two asymmetric gold SRRs placed on a thin silicon slab punctuated by metal walls. This configuration creates a resonant dark mode (TE2,0) in the silicon film. The SRRs act as bridges, coupling pump radiation into the dark mode while being positioned such that their linear radiating moments undergo destructive interference, while their nonlinear components interfere constructively. Numerical simulations using a self-consistent FDTD approach based on the hydrodynamic model demonstrate a giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility of $\sim 10^{-11}$ m/V, which is a one-order magnitude improvement over previous SRR metasurface designs. Furthermore, the design achieves a 94% absorption rate and a more than 120-fold enhancement in THz emission power compared to traditional configurations. This paradigm allows for high-efficiency, tunable nonlinear meta-devices and paves the way for revolutionary on-chip terahertz technologies and optoelectronic nano-circuitry.

Research Context
THz technologies are growing for sensing and imaging. Current crystals suffer from narrow bandwidth and phase-matching limits. Metasurfaces offer freedom to design subwavelength atoms. Conventional SRR metasurfaces face limitations from linear radiation damping. Dissipative and radiative damping reduce the local near-field amplitude.

Research Question And Hypothesis
How can conversion efficiency in nonlinear metasurfaces be fundamentally improved? The researchers hypothesize that a perfect absorbing metasurface can eliminate linear radiative damping. They propose using a dark mode for high quality-factor field enhancement. This approach aims to drive the plasmonic nanoparticles generating nonlinear signals.

Methodological Details
The study utilizes a numerical demonstration approach. Researchers performed self-consistent FDTD calculations. The calculations were based on the hydrodynamic model. The model included both linear and nonlinear dynamics. A temporal optical pulse was applied to the system. The pulse duration was $\tau = 140$ fs. The peak amplitude was $E_0 = 2 \times 10^7$ V/m. The driving frequency equaled the dark mode frequency.

Procedures And Architectures
The unit cell features a thin Si slab. The slab thickness is $h = 100$ nm. Two gold SRRs are positioned asymmetrically on the slab. The SRRs have a thickness of $t_m = 50$ nm. Metal walls are used to quantize the modes. The system operates on the TE2,0 dark mode. The operation wavelength is around 1.5 $\mu$m. Optimal SRR positions are $\Delta x_1 \approx 70$ nm and $\Delta x_2 \approx 470$ nm. This optimized configuration achieves 94% absorption.

Key Results
The study demonstrates a giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility of $\sim 10^{-11}$ m/V. This represents a one order improvement over previous reports. The proposed configuration achieves a 94% absorption rate. THz emission power is enhanced by more than 120-fold. The calculated susceptibility is $\chi^{(2)}_{dark} \approx 2.4 \times 10^{-11}$ m/V. The traditional SRR metasurface susceptibility is $1.6 \times 10^{-12}$ m/V.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The design separates field enhancement from the nonlinearity topology. Linear radiation cancellation is achieved via destructive interference. Nonlinear components add constructively in the far field. The concept enables high-efficiency tunable nonlinear meta-devices.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model assumes a spatially infinite surface. The model is less suitable to predict practical numbers. Practical results may vary due to focusing and phase-matching.

Claims
The proposed metasurface achieves a giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility. The calculated susceptibility reached $\sim 10^{-11}$ m/V. This is a one order improvement. The model is a simplified spatially infinite case. It allows for high-efficiency THz generation.
Linear radiation damping can be eliminated through symmetry design. Linear radiation cancels in the far field. Nonlinear components add constructively.  This leads to a 120-fold power enhancement.

Data And Code Availability
Numerical calculations were performed using FDTD.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
THz enhancement is inversely proportional to linear radiation damping.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the unit cell and dispersion diagram. Figure 2 presents sheet conductivities for the SRRs. Figure 3 illustrates scattering properties and absorption spectra. Figure 4 shows the enhancement map and time trace.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a dark-mode-assisted perfect absorbing metasurface that eliminates linear radiation damping. 2. The strongest evidence is a 120-fold enhancement in THz emission power and a $\sim 10^{-11}$ m/V susceptibility. 3. The future path involves using this concept for high-efficiency tunable nonlinear meta-devices and on-chip THz technologies.

summary.title: Reduced residence time of droplet impact on heated surfaces
summary.authors: Song Rong, Shiquan Shen, Tianyou Wang, and Zhizhao Che
summary.executive_summary:
The study investigates the dynamics of droplet impact on heated surfaces, specifically aiming to reduce the residence time of the impact process, a parameter critical for industrial applications such as spray cooling, painting, and fuel-spray impingement. The authors identify a novel "bouncing-with-spray" (BWS) mode that offers a significant reduction in residence time compared to the traditional "retraction-bouncing" (RB) mode. This reduction is primarily attributed to the burst of vapor bubbles within the liquid film upon impact. These bursts create holes in the film, causing the liquid to recoil from these holes and fragment into several pieces, thereby reducing the recoiling distance and the overall residence time.

Experimental results across three boiling regimes—nucleate, transition, and film boiling—demonstrate that the BWS mode consistently provides a shorter residence time. For instance, in the transition boiling regime, the residence time was reduced from 12.0 ms in the RB mode to 6.3 ms in the BWS mode, representing a reduction of approximately 40%. A key finding is that this residence time reduction in the BWS mode is independent of the liquid's viscosity, suggesting that viscous forces do not play a primary role in this specific mechanism.

The authors further provide a theoretical framework to explain the transition between the RB and BWS modes. By considering the energy balance and the critical condition where the vapor bubble radius (rv) is approximately equal to the minimum liquid film thickness (bmin), they derive a scaling law. In the film boiling regime, they establish a ΔT ∼ V−1 boundary, where ΔT is the degree of substrate superheat and V is the impact speed. This scaling law agrees well with experimental data. The proposed heat-induced BWS mode is highlighted as a reliable and simple strategy for residence time reduction because it avoids the need for complex surface microstructures or modifications that might cause surface degradation.

claims.description: The BWS mode significantly reduces residence time by approximately 40% compared to the RB mode.
The transition between bouncing modes in the film boiling regime follows a scaling law of ΔT ∼ V−1.

Research Context
Droplet impact occurs in many industrial applications including spray cooling and painting. Impact processes on heated surfaces are significantly affected by heat transfer and phase change. The contact time of a bouncing droplet is a critical parameter controlling mass, momentum, and energy transfer. Current methods to reduce contact time involve using surfaces with ridges or specific geometries. This study proposes a heat-induced approach to reduce residence time without complex surface modifications.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study investigates how to significantly reduce the residence time of droplets on heated surfaces. It is hypothesized that a 'bouncing-with-spray' mode, induced by vapor bubble bursts, can achieve this. The authors predict that this mode will result in much smaller residence times compared to the traditional retraction-bouncing mode. A theoretical scaling law is hypothesized to define the transition boundary between the two modes.

Methodological Details
The study uses three different liquids: water, ethanol, and water/glycerol mixtures. The Weber number (We) was varied between 10 and 180 for different liquids. Droplet sizes typically included 2.8 mm for water/glycerol, 2.2–3.4 mm for water, and 1.6 mm for ethanol. Substrate temperatures were controlled using a PID controller with an accuracy of ±1°C. Images were captured using a Photron Fastcam SA1.1 high-speed camera. The liquids used were summarized in Table 1 with varied viscosities and surface tensions.

Procedures And Architectures
Liquids were pushed at a speed of approximately 4 µl/s by a syringe pump. Droplets impacted a polished silicon substrate heated by a copper holder. High-speed images were captured in both side-view and aerial-view configurations. A customized Matlab program was employed to measure droplet size, speed, and shape evolution.

Key Results
The residence time in the BWS mode was much smaller than in the RB mode. In the transition boiling regime, residence time dropped from 12.0 ms to 6.3 ms. The residence time reduction in the BWS mode is about 40%. The residence time of the BWS mode is independent of the liquid's viscosity. A scaling law of ΔT ∼ V−1 was obtained for the film boiling regime.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Vapor bubbles burst, creating holes that cause the liquid film to recoil from these holes. The reduction in recoiling distance leads to a significant reduction in residence time. The transition boundary occurs when the vapor bubble radius is approximately equal to the minimum film thickness. This approach is reliable because it avoids surface degradation and complex microstructures.

Contradictions And Limitations

summary.authors: TAKAO YAMAZAKI AND YIFAN YANG
summary.executive_summary: The paper investigates the construction of geometrically maximal abelian coverings of modular curves, specifically focusing on the modular curve X0(p) for a prime p. The authors begin by noting Mazur's established result that the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) is the unique geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering over Q. The authors aim to extend this by constructing a cyclic covering X'_2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np which is geometrically maximal but specifically unramified outside the cusps. To achieve this, the authors define a new curve X'_2(p) as a quadratic extension of the Shimura covering X2(p). The construction is made explicit using generalized Dedekind eta functions (also known as Siegel functions) to define a rational function Fh. The authors prove that X'_2(p) admits a geometrically integral model over Q and that the covering ramiﬁes precisely at the cusps. They demonstrate that the function field Q(X'_2(p)) is generated by the square root of Fh^2 and that Q is algebraically closed in this extension. The results provide a concrete construction of a geometrically maximal abelian extension for the open subscheme Y0(p), which is unramified outside the cusps. The work utilizes properties of modular functions, the behavior of the generalized Dedekind eta functions under modular transformations, and the analysis of ramification indices at cusps to validate the construction.

The construction is made explicit using generalized Dedekind eta functions (also known as Siegel functions) to define a rational function Fh. The authors prove that X'_2(p) admits a geometrically integral model over Q and that the covering ramiﬁes precisely at the cusps. They demonstrate that the function field Q(X'_2(p)) is generated by the square root of Fh^2 and that Q is algebraically closed in this extension. The results provide a concrete construction of a geometrically maximal abelian extension for the open subscheme Y0(p), which is unramified outside the cusps. The work utilizes properties of modular functions, the behavior of the generalized Dedekind eta functions under modular transformations, and the analysis of ramification indices at cusps to validate the construction.

Research Context
Let Y be a smooth geometrically integral curve over a number field k admitting a degree one divisor. The kernel of the canonical map, π_1(Y)_ab,geo, is shown to be finite. A finite unramified abelian covering Y' → Y is geometrically maximal if the composition π_1(Y)_ab,geo → Gal(Y'/Y) is an isomorphism. Mazur proved that for the modular curve X0(p), the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) is geometrically maximal over Q. The study investigates the existence of coverings unramified outside cusps.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asks whether there exists a cyclic covering f'_p: X'_2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np. The hypothesis is that such a covering exists and is geometrically maximal unramified outside cusps. Specifically, it is predicted that this covering factors as f_p × π_p, where π_p is a degree two covering unramified outside cusps. The goal is to construct X'_2(p) as a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by a square root of an explicitly constructed rational function.

Methodological Details
The study considers modular curves X0(p) and X1(p) as geometrically integral smooth proper curves over Q. A model of X1(p) over Q is chosen such that the cusp at infinity splits completely in a finite cyclic covering fp: X1(p) → X0(p) of degree (p-1)/2. The Shimura covering fp: X2(p) → X0(p) is a subcovering of X1(p) → X0(p) of degree Np := (p-1)/gcd(p-1, 12). The researchers define the open subscheme Y0(p) ⊆ X0(p) where X0(p) − Y0(p) consists of the two cusps. For p ≥ 5, the authors define k = Np and δ = (p-1, 12)^2. They utilize the generalized Dedekind eta function Eg(tau) defined by a product involving the second Bernoulli polynomial B(x). These functions serve as the building blocks for the construction of the modular curve X'_2(p).

Procedures And Architectures
The authors define the generalized Dedekind eta function Eg(tau) using the second Bernoulli polynomial B(x). For p ≥ 5, they set k = Np and δ = (p-1, 12)^2. They construct the function Fh(tau) = δ^{-1} ∑ E_{gjkh}^{6/δ}. They define Γ'_2(p) as the kernel of the character on Γ_2(p). They show X'_2(p) is a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by a square root of F_h^2. They verify that the covering ramiﬁes precisely at each cusp. each cusp.

Key Results
Theorem 1.2.2 proves the existence of a cyclic covering f'_p: X'_2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np. This covering restricted to Y'_2(p) → Y0(p) is geometrically maximal unramified over Q. Furthermore, f'_p factors as f_p × π_p, where π_p is a degree two covering unramified outside cusps. Finally, Q is algebraically closed in Q(X'_2(p)).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The result shows the existence of a cyclic covering f'_p of degree 2Np which is geometrically maximal unramified outside cusps. It factors through the Shimura covering f_p as a degree two covering π_p. This construction provides a geometrically maximal extension of Y0(p) over Q. It is obtained as a quadratic extension of the Shimura covering, utilizing generalized Dedekind eta functions to explicitly construct the function field extension.

The Shimura covering is the unique maximal unramified subcovering. The new covering f'_p is only unramified outside the cusps. The construction assumes p ≥ 5. The Shimura covering f_p is possibly ramified.

summary.title: Design of Real-time Semantic Segmentation Decoder for Automated Driving
summary.authors: Arindam Das, Saranya Kandan, Senthil Yogamani, Pavel Křížek
summary.field_subfield: Semantic Segmentation, Visual Perception, Efficient Networks, Automated Driving
summary.executive_summary:
The paper addresses the computational challenges of deploying semantic segmentation models on embedded systems for autonomous vehicles. While significant research has focused on efficient task-agnostic encoders, the decoders used in these systems remain computationally expensive. The authors propose a novel, efficient non-bottleneck layer and a family of decoder architectures that are specifically designed to fit within a limited run-time budget. 

The proposed method utilizes a VGG10-style 10-layer classifier as a task-independent encoder to provide shared features for multi-task learning. The core innovation lies in a non-bottleneck layer designed with residual learning and multiple skip connections to handle high gradient flow during back-propagation, which is particularly important for relatively shallow networks. This layer incorporates both 1D and 3D kernels to extract information from different receptive areas, with Type-1 and Type-2 variants available to adjust complexity. Type-2 variants utilize dilated convolutions to expand the field-of-view while maintaining spatial resolution.

The authors evaluated several decoder configurations on a custom dataset of urban scenes (1280x384 resolution), targeting four critical classes: lanes, curbs, roads, and void. They compared these variants against a standard FCN decoder. The results demonstrate that the optimal decoder configuration, which integrates specific non-bottleneck layers and skip connections, achieves a 10% improvement in mean Intersection over Union (IoU) over the baseline. Notably, this improvement is more pronounced in challenging classes, with gains of 12% for lanes and 18% for curbs. Furthermore, the proposed architecture maintains high efficiency, showing a runtime increase of less than 2ms compared to the standard FCN decoder. The study concludes that efficient decoder design is a critical yet under-explored component for real-time visual perception in automated driving.

summary.title: Lusin characterisation of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators
summary.authors: Tan Duc Do, Trong Ngoc Nguyen and Truong Xuan Le
summary.executive_summary: This paper provides a characterisation of the Hardy spaces $H_p^L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ associated with the Hermite operator $L = -\Delta + |x|^2$ in terms of Lusin area integrals. The authors focus on dimensions $d \geq 3$ and indices $p \in (0, 1]$. The core contribution is Theorem 1.1, which establishes that the Hardy space $H_p^L(\mathbb{R}^d)$, defined via a maximal function associated with the Poisson semigroup, is equivalent to the space $H_p^S(\mathbb{R}^d)$, defined via a specific Lusin integral $S$. This Lusin integral is constructed using the gradient $\nabla_L = (\partial_t, \partial_1 + x_1, \dots, \partial_d + x_d)$, which is specific to the Hermite operator context. The methodology involves several intermediate steps: establishing kernel estimates for the heat and Poisson semigroups, defining atom decompositions for the Hardy spaces, and introducing intermediate spaces $H_{L,max}$ and $H_p^A$. The authors use tent space techniques to prove the equality of these spaces by showing that $H_p^L$ coincides with the intersection of $H_p^A$ and $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Additionally, the paper proves Theorem 1.2, which asserts the boundedness of the Riesz transforms $R_L^j$ on the Hardy space $H_p^L(\mathbb{R}^d)$. The results generalize previous works, such as those for $p=1$, to the range $p \in (0, 1]$ while utilizing the unique structure of the Hermite operator's derivatives.

Hermite operators play a significant role in the harmonic oscillator. Hardy spaces are of fundamental interest in harmonic analysis. The authors aim to characterise these spaces in terms of Lusin area integrals. Specifically, they seek to prove the equivalence of $H_p^L$ and $H_p^S$. The primary hypothesis is that $(H_p^L, \|\cdot\|_{H_p^L}) = (H_p^S, \|\cdot\|_{H_p^S})$. Furthermore, they hypothesize that the Riesz transforms $R_L^j$ are bounded on $H_p^L$.

Methodological Details
The study considers dimensions $d \in \{3, 4, 5, \dots\}$. The analysis covers the index range $p \in (0, 1]$. The Hermite operator $L$ is defined as $-\Delta + |x|^2$. The space $H_p^L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is defined as the completion of a specific set. The quasi-norm is defined as $\|\cdot\|_{H_p^L} = \|M\cdot\|_{L^p}$. The paper defines the Lusin integral $Sf(x)$ as a specific integral. The authors introduce intermediate spaces $H_{L,max}$ and $H_p^A$. The characterisation $H_p^L = H_p^A \cap L^2$ is established. Theorem 1.1 proves that the Hardy space $H_p^L$ is equivalent to $H_p^S$. Theorem 1.2 proves that the Riesz transforms $R_L^j$ are bounded. The Riesz transforms are bounded specifically on the space $H_p^L$.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results characterise the space $H_p^L$ in terms of the Lusin integral. The study demonstrates the boundedness of Riesz transforms $R_L^j$. The findings extend the understanding of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators.

The results are specifically formulated for $d \geq 3$. The index is limited to $p \in (0, 1]$. The random seed is not reported. The train/test split is not reported.

summary.title: Deep-Learning-based Millimeter-Wave Massive MIMO for Hybrid Precoding
summary.authors: Hongji Huang, Yiwei Song, Jie Yang, Guan Gui, Fumiyuki Adachi
summary.field_subfield: Communications; Millimeter-wave; Massive MIMO; Deep Learning
summary.executive_summary:
Millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) is an emerging technology for next-generation communications, offering significant throughput but presenting challenges in hardware complexity and energy consumption. Hybrid precoding is a primary method to address these issues, yet existing schemes suffer from high computational complexity and a failure to fully exploit the spatial characteristics of mmWave channels.

To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a deep-learning-enabled mmWave massive MIMO framework. The approach regards the selection of precoders as a mapping relation within a deep neural network (DNN), effectively treating the DNN as an autoencoder. By training the model as a black box, the framework captures the structural and sparsity statistics of the mmWave channel, which conventional mathematical methods like singular value decomposition (SVD) or geometric mean decomposition (GMD) struggle to utilize efficiently.

The proposed architecture comprises a multi-layer DNN with specific fully connected layers, a noise layer for distortion mixing, and specific activation functions (ReLU and Sigmoid). The training policy employs an unsupervised learning approach where the DNN is optimized using a loss function based on the Frobenius norm of the difference between the predicted and GMD-based precoders. The system is trained using the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm with momentum.

Numerical simulations validate the proposed method's superiority over conventional schemes. The DNN-based approach demonstrates improved bit error ratio (BER) and spectrum efficiency while achieving a reduced computational complexity of O(L^2NsNt^2). Furthermore, the study highlights the robustness of the method, showing faster convergence than analog precoding schemes. The results suggest that deep learning can effectively solve the non-convex optimization problems inherent in hybrid precoding for mmWave massive MIMO systems.

summary.title: BanStereoSet: A Dataset to Measure Stereotypical Social Biases in LLMs for Bangla
summary.authors: Mahammed Kamruzzaman, Abdullah Al Monsur, Shrabon Das, Enamul Hassan, Gene Louis Kim
summary.field_subfield: Natural Language Processing / AI Ethics / Multilingual LLMs
summary.executive_summary: This study introduces BanStereoSet, a comprehensive dataset specifically designed to evaluate stereotypical social biases in multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) for the Bangla language. Current bias research is heavily skewed toward English-centric datasets, leaving a significant gap in understanding how models behave in diverse linguistic contexts. To address this, the authors localized content from several established benchmarks, including StereoSet, IndiBias, and the GenAssocBias dataset. The resulting BanStereoSet comprises 1,194 sentences across nine distinct categories: race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion. The dataset was constructed using a multi-stage process involving GPT-4 translations, manual adjustments by four native Bangla-speaking annotators to correct linguistic nuances (such as the absence of gendered pronouns), and careful curation to mitigate known pitfalls like 'meaningful stereotypes' or 'invalid perturbations.' The study evaluates four prominent models—GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B—using three different prompting templates. The results reveal substantial biases across all models, with Mistral-7B generally performing the best in most categories, while GPT-4o shows higher average stereotypical responses in Bangla. A notable finding is that model behavior varies between Bangla and English; for instance, Mistral shows cultural sensitivity in handling caste bias in Bangla but struggles in English. BanStereoSet serves as a vital resource for developing more equitable and culturally aware language technologies in the Bangladeshi context.

Research Context
The usage of LLMs has increased significantly globally. Current studies have revealed undesirable biases and stereotypes in these models. Most existing datasets to measure these biases are predominantly in English. While some research exists in other languages, bias research specific to Bengali remains sparse. Existing Bengali studies have primarily addressed gender and religious biases. Stereotypical biases extend beyond gender and religion to categories like race, profession, and caste. There is no dataset that comprehensively covers a broader spectrum of bias categories in the Bengali cultural context.

Research Question And Hypothesis

This constructed subscheme ZK is shown to admit a nowhere-vanishing Hecke-equivariant section, allowing the application of existing arguments to establish the equivalence of the Hecke eigenvalue systems across the subschemes and the variety.

Research Context
The mod p fiber of a Shimura variety comes equipped with an action of the prime-to-p Hecke algebra. Several well-studied subschemes are invariant under this action. Serre showed that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues on mod p modular curves are the same as those in the supersingular locus. Goldring-Koskivirta generalized this result to the unique zero-dimensional Ekedahl-Oort stratum. Terakado-Yu used these observations to prove results for any central leaf. Previous works were limited to smooth subschemes of dimension 0. This text proves new results for higher dimensional and possibly singular subschemes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether higher-dimensional or singular Hecke-equivariant subschemes share the same systems of Hecke eigenvalues as the full Shimura variety. The hypothesis is that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues in the coherent cohomology of any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme of a compact abelian type Shimura variety are the same as those in the variety.

Methodological Details
The study considers the special fiber SK of the Kisin-Vasiu integral canonical model. The variety is assumed to be of abelian type at a hyperspecial level K. The Shimura datum (G, X) is assumed to satisfy G = Gc. The analysis utilizes the theory of G-zips and automorphic vector bundles. The research focuses on systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in modules of coherent cohomology.

The author defines M(YK) as the sum of H0(YK, V(η)) over L-dominant characters. The proof employs a two-step going-down and going-up argument. To handle higher-dimensional subschemes, the author intersects YK with the smallest length stratum. The author then successively removes nonsingular points to obtain a smooth, closed subscheme ZK. This subscheme ZK admits a nowhere vanishing Hecke-equivariant section. The proof uses the conormal exact sequence and the existence of Hasse invariants. The existence of Hasse invariants allows for the construction of the section.

Theorem A proves that for compact abelian type Shimura varieties, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues in any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme are the same as those in the variety. Theorem B extends these results to nonclosed subschemes such as Ekedahl-Oort strata and length strata. For a proper SK and a central leaf CK closed in the Ekedahl-Oort stratum, the eigenvalues are the same.

The study generalizes prior results to higher dimensional and possibly singular subschemes. The mechanism relies on the existence of Hasse invariants. The proof bridges the gap between subschemes and the variety through a constructed smooth subscheme.

The theory of toroidal compactifications for abelian type is not yet been developed. The author assumes that there exists a G(Apf)-equivariant divisor D'.

The systems of Hecke eigenvalues for any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme of a compact abelian type Shimura variety are identical to those of the full variety. Theorem A proves that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues are the same.  This allows for a unified treatment of Hecke eigenvalues across geometric strata.

summary.title: Anomalous Hall effect from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling
summary.authors: Longju Yu, Hong Jian Zhao, Yurong Yang, Laurent Bellaiche, and Yanming Ma
summary.executive_summary: This research explores the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) as a topology-related transport phenomenon, specifically investigating its emergence through nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. While AHE is well-established in ferromagnets and antiferromagnets and has been explored via linear magnetoelectric coupling, the nonlinear regime remains largely unexplored. The authors utilize a group-theoretical approach to establish a phenomenological theory for both spontaneous and electric-field driven AHE in crystalline materials. Through systematic symmetry analysis of 122 magnetic point groups (MPGs), the study identifies 90 type-I and type-III MPGs that host AHE driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields resulting from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. A key theoretical finding is that these electric-field driven conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic order parameter. To validate the phenomenological theory, the study employs first-principles calculations to examine two representative materials: Cr2O3 and CoF2. Cr2O3, belonging to the $\bar{3}'m'$ MPG, exhibits $\sigma_{zy}$, $\sigma_{xz}$, and $\sigma_{yx}$ conductivities driven by first-order responses to Ex, Ey, and Ez fields, respectively, with values exceeding 100 S/cm for some components. In contrast, CoF2 (MPG 4'/mm'm) demonstrates AHE via second-order responses, where $\sigma_{yx}$ can exceed 200 S/cm under specific electric fields. The study highlights that the magnitude and sign of the induced Hall conductivity are governed by the symmetry of the magnetic point group and the orientation of the magnetic order parameter. These findings underscore the significance of nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling in creating exotic transport phenomena and provide a theoretical framework for probing magnetic orders using external electric fields. The work provides significant implications for the development of spintronic devices, where efficient data readout and magnetic order sensing are paramount. By characterizing the specific electric field configurations (uni-axial, bi-axial, tri-axial) required to induce AHE in various MPGs, the paper offers a roadmap for identifying and engineering materials with specific magnetoelectric responses.

This research explores the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) as a topology-related transport phenomenon, specifically investigating its emergence through nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. While AHE is well-established in ferromagnets and antiferromagnets and has been explored via linear magnetoelectric coupling, the nonlinear regime remains largely unexplored. A key theoretical finding is that these electric-field driven conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic order parameter. To validate the phenomenological theory, the study employs first-principles calculations to examine two representative materials: Cr2O3 and CoF2. Cr2O3, belonging to the $\bar{3}'m'$ MPG, exhibits $\sigma_{zy}$, $\sigma_{xz}$, and $\sigma_{yx}$ conductivities driven by first-order responses to Ex, Ey, and Ez fields, respectively, with values exceeding 100 S/cm for some components. In contrast, CoF2 (MPG 4'/mm'm) demonstrates AHE via second-order responses, where $\sigma_{yx}$ can exceed 200 S/cm under specific electric fields. The study highlights that the magnitude and sign of the induced Hall conductivity are governed by the symmetry of the magnetic point group and the orientation of the magnetic order parameter. These findings underscore the significance of nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling in creating exotic transport phenomena and provide a theoretical framework for probing magnetic orders using external electric fields. The work provides significant implications for the development of spintronic devices, where efficient data readout and magnetic order sensing are paramount. By characterizing the specific electric field configurations (uni-axial, bi-axial, tri-axial) required to induce AHE in various MPGs, the paper offers a roadmap for identifying and engineering materials with specific magnetoelectric responses.

Research Context
The anomalous Hall effect (AHE) is a topology-related transport phenomenon. It serves as a potential interest in spintronics for efficient magnetic order probing. AHE spontaneously occurs in ferromagnets or antiferromagnets. While recent studies show electric-field induced AHE via linear magnetoelectric coupling... an AHE originating from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling remains largely unexplored.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to establish the phenomenological theory for spontaneous and electric-field driven AHE. By using a group-theoretical approach, the authors explore the role of symmetry in AHE. The researchers hypothesize that a wide spectrum of MPGs host AHE driven by nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. They predict that these electric-field driven conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic orders. The study seeks to identify representative materials such as Cr2O3 and CoF2.

Methodological Details
The authors utilize a group-theoretical approach to establish a phenomenological theory. The symmetry analysis covers the entire 122 MPGs. They specifically focus on type-I and type-III magnetic point groups. The MAGNDATA database was used to identify materials belonging to these MPGs. Cr2O3 and CoF2 were selected as representative materials for study. First-principles calculations were performed to confirm the phenomenological theory. The materials have no more than 10 ions per primitive cell, ensuring costs are affordable. The AHE is characterized by the transverse conductivity $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}$.

Procedures And Architectures
The analytical form of $B^{\alpha}_{eff}$ is governed by symmetry. The effective magnetic field $B^{\alpha}_{eff}$ is expanded with respect to the electric field. This expansion yields first-, second-, and third-order magnetoelectric couplings. The coefficients $\lambda_\alpha$, $\lambda_{\alpha\beta}$, and $\lambda_{\alpha\beta\gamma}$ characterize these different orders. The study analyzes how external electric fields break symmetries to allow magnetization. The results are summarized in a table showing 90 MPGs. Cr2O3 is modeled with a +L magnetic order parameter. CoF2 is modeled with its 4'/mm'm MPG.

Key Results
The study identifies 90 MPGs that host AHE via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. Cr2O3 belongs to the $\bar{3}'m'$ MPG and allows first-order responses. Conductivities $\sigma_{zy}$, $\sigma_{xz}$, and $\sigma_{yx}$ in Cr2O3 can be larger than 100 S/cm. Switching the magnetic order parameter from +L to -L reverses the conductivities. The maximum value of $\sigma_{yx}$ driven by Ey in Cr2O3 is less than 20 S/cm. CoF2 exhibits AHE via second-order magnetoelectric coupling. In CoF2, $\sigma_{yx}$ can yield conductivities larger than 200 S/cm. The conductivities $\sigma_{zy}$ and $\sigma_{xz}$ in CoF2 can reach 10 S/cm.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The anomalous Hall conductivity $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}$ can be reversed by reversing the magnetic order. Nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling plays an important role in creating exotic transport phenomena. The results offer alternative avenues for the probe of magnetic orders. The findings have practical importance for spintronics applications. Symmetry analysis provides a comprehensive framework for predicting electric-field induced AHE.

Contradictions And Limitations
CoF2 responds to electric field via second order, unlike the first-order Cr2O3. $\sigma_{yx}$ can be quenched in the regime of fourth-order magnetoelectric coupling. Type-II MPGs do not host electric-field induced magnetization because they preserve T symmetry. Some components might respond to electric fields via different mechanisms with identical field counts.

Claims
Nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling enables electric-field driven AHE in a wide variety of magnetic point groups. 90 type-I and type-III MPGs host AHE. AHE is driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial fields. Type-II MPGs do not host electric-field induced magnetization. This offers alternative avenues for the probe of magnetic orders.
Cr2O3 and CoF2 are representative candidates for observing these effects. Cr2O3 conductivities can be larger than 100 S/cm. CoF2 $\sigma_{yx}$ can yield larger than 200 S/cm. Cr2O3 $\sigma_{yx}$ via Ey is less than 20 S/cm. These results confirm the phenomenological theory.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 sketches the crystal and magnetic structures for Cr2O3 and CoF2. Figure 2 shows the electric-field driven anomalous Hall conductivities as a function of chemical potential. Table I lists the 90 type-I and type-III MPGs and their AHE components.

Three Takeaways
1. The study establishes a phenomenological theory for nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling in 90 MPGs. 2. First-principles calculations show conductivities exceeding 100 S/cm in Cr2O3 and 200 S/cm in CoF2. 3. The results provide new avenues for probing magnetic orders in spintronics.

summary.executive_summary: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly enhanced human-computer interaction through conversational capabilities, yet they are primarily constrained by a turn-based paradigm that prevents real-time interaction during response generation. While researchers have explored duplex models to allow for simultaneous listening and thinking, these methods typically require extensive computational resources and substantial retraining because their underlying procedures differ significantly from standard backbone models. To address these challenges, this paper introduces DUplex decOding (DUO), a novel channel-based parallel decoding mechanism designed to equip LLMs with duplex capabilities using minimal additional training. Unlike existing time-division-multiplexing approaches that split and mix input and output in time slices, DUO utilizes a channel-division-multiplexing strategy. This method enables simultaneous autoregressive output generation and input preprocessing by establishing a new input channel when a user provides input while the model is already generating a response. The architecture employs two specific state tokens, <1> and <2>, to signal whether a query should be addressed or ignored. State token <1> indicates a user query, triggering the suspension of the original output channel and transitioning the input channel to become the new output channel. State token <2> indicates non-query text, allowing the model to continue the original response while disregarding the new input. DUO is efficiently implemented using the Flex-Attention framework, which manages the key-value cache to facilitate non-standard attention mechanisms without increasing the number of forward passes. Experimental results using the MiniCPM-2.4B foundation model demonstrate that DUO significantly enhances the naturalness and human-likeness of user-AI interactions. Furthermore, DUO achieves these improvements with a remarkably low training overhead, requiring only 400 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for approximately 25 minutes, compared to 10,000 steps on 40 GPUs for 36 hours for the MiniCPM-Duplex baseline. Benchmarks show that DUO maintains comparable levels of factuality and faithfulness while providing a substantial advantage in overall performance and responsiveness. The study concludes that DUO offers a versatile and efficient framework for real-time duplex conversation with potential for future extension into multimodal domains.
