judge_context:
Executive Summary
This research presents a novel synthetic methodology for the production of high-value cyclobutane dimers, specifically targeting 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB) and the anti-inflammatory lignan natural product magnosalin. The study utilizes a radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition pathway, which has traditionally been hindered in batch reactors by excessive reaction times, the requirement for cryogenic temperatures, and high catalyst loadings. By integrating homogenous, sustainable organophotoredox catalysis—specifically employing a pyrillium catalyst—with continuous flow technology, the authors demonstrate a significant improvement in synthetic efficiency and scalability. The core of the paper involves a comparative analysis between traditional batch reactions and a continuous flow platform. In the batch synthesis of t-DCzCB, an 82% isolated yield was achieved, but the process necessitated deoxygenated acetone, cryogenic conditions, and long durations. In contrast, the optimized continuous flow system utilized a flow rate of 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ and remarkably low catalyst loadings of 0.1 mol% to achieve high yields. The study expands the scope of this methodology to include a diverse range of functionalized carbazoles and electron-rich styrenes. Significant improvements were noted for brominated vinylcarbazoles, where flow conditions drastically reduced reaction times compared to batch methods, which sometimes required up to 5 days for completion. For instance, the dimerization of 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (12a) was improved to a 64% isolated yield under flow. Furthermore, the synthesis of magnosalin was successfully performed on a 10 mmol scale with a 40% isolated yield under flow conditions without requiring cryogenic temperatures. The researchers attribute the advantages of flow to more efficient irradiation of substrates and the mitigation of potential reaction reversibility. Ultimately, the methodology offers a robust, environmentally friendly, and scalable route for the synthesis of new functional materials and natural products, showcasing the distinct advantages of flow chemistry over conventional batch processes.

Research Context
The dimerization of electron-rich alkene building blocks such as enamines and styrenes provides a convenient synthetic route to cyclobutane functional materials and natural products. Vinyl carbazole serves as a valuable monomer for the formation of conductive polymers and a precursor for 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB). Naturally occurring styrenes like E-asarone can be seen as precursors of dimeric cyclobutyl natural products such as the anti-inflammatory lignan magnosalin. Synthesis of these cyclobutanes is accomplished via a radical cation-induced [2+2]-cycloaddition process. The key alkene radical cation intermediate can be generated through chemical oxidation or by utilizing photochemical methods. Previous organophotoredox catalyzed dimerizations were excessive in some cases and required cryogenic conditions for certain substrate classes. Furthermore, the catalysis loadings were not as low as those obtained using Ru-and Ir-photoredox catalysed systems. The use of continuous flow technology provides advantages in photoredox transformations by allowing for more efficient irradiation of starting substrates. A scalable route to magnosalin was previously reported using a heterogenous photoredox fixed bed flow chemical process. This study aims to provide a convenient, environmentally beneficial methodology that showcases the advantages of a continuous flow over existing conventional batch chemistry.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to compare the performance of continuous flow versus traditional batch reaction conditions for the synthesis of t-DCzCB. It was anticipated that continuous flow technology would provide a convenient synthetic route to the host material t-DCzCB. The researchers hypothesized that merging homogenous small molecule, sustainable, organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology would deliver cyclobutane functional materials and natural products. The study investigates whether flow conditions can achieve high yields while significantly reducing catalyst loadings and reaction times. A central research question is whether a continuous flow platform can deliver a general, robust, and scalable route to valuable carbazole host materials. The researchers hypothesized that this protocol would demonstrate distinct advantages over traditional batch chemistry, specifically regarding scalability and reduced reaction times. The scope of the inquiry includes the expansion of the cyclobutyl carbazole products available through this specific transformation. The study also seeks to provide a scalable synthesis of the styrene based lignan dimeric natural product magnosalin. The researchers anticipate that the proposed methodology will provide an environmentally beneficial synthetic approach. Ultimately, the research explores if continuous flow can overcome the excessive reaction times and cryogenic requirements inherent in batch organophotoredox dimerization.

Methodological Details
The study focused on the dimerization of electron rich alkenes, including vinyl carbazoles and various styrenes. A commercial, off-the-shelf, continuous flow platform was selected for its excellent useability and improved availability. The batch synthesis of t-DCzCB was performed using organophotoredox catalysts at a loading of 3 mol%. Batch reaction conditions required the use of deoxygenated acetone and cryogenic temperatures. Optimization of the continuous flow synthesis was conducted using HPLC-analysis with p-terphenyl as an internal standard. The flow system required calibration of the vinyl carbazole and the dimer t-DCzCB. Optimal flow synthesis of 1 was realized at a flow rate of 0.5 mL.min -1 with a catalyst loading of 2 mol%. Irradiation was applied at a wavelength of 450 nm during the flow process. The scope was expanded to include brominated t-DCzCB substrates to serve as potential building blocks for transition metal cross coupling. Vinyl carbazoles were synthesized using the methodology established by Obora and coworkers. Continuous flow dimerization was performed at a reduced concentration of 0.2 M in acetone for certain substrates. The researchers examined several mono-and disubstituted carbazoles using solely continuous flow conditions. Electron rich styrenes were dimerized using anthracene or diethylaniline as an electron relay. The lignan magnosalin was dimerized on a 10 mmol scale. Flow rates were adjusted, including a rate of 0.2 mL.min -1 for specific dimerizations. HPLC analysis was utilized to confirm the formation of products and investigate byproduct formation.

Procedures And Architectures
The protocol merges homogenous small molecule, sustainable, organophotoredox catalysis with a continuous flow technology. A commercial flow platform was chosen due to its excellent useability and improved availability. The batch synthesis utilized organophotoredox catalyst 10 at a 3 mol% loading. Flow irradiation was conducted at wavelengths of 450 nm, 405 nm, and 420 nm. Flow rates were varied from 0.1 mL.min -1 to 5 mL.min -1 to probe the reversibility of the dimerization. Residence times were adjusted, with specific values including 20 min and 100 min. A flow rate of 0.5 mL.min -1 was used for primary optimization studies. Starting materials were maintained at either a 0.4 M or 0.2 M concentration in acetone. Anthracene was added as an electron relay (0.25 eq.) to the styrene solution before introduction into the flow apparatus. The catalyst loading was significantly reduced to 0.1 mol% for the 10 mmol scale synthesis. Palladium mediated Suzuki coupling and subsequent vinylation were used to prepare 2-arylated vinylcarbazoles. Specific flow rates of 0.2 mL.min -1 were applied to the dimerization of brominated substrates. All substrates were dissolved in acetone at the specified concentrations for the flow reactions. HPLC was employed to monitor conversion and identify the formation of carbazole. The flow system was designed to facilitate the dimerization of several classes of electron rich alkenes.

Key Results
The batch synthesis of t-DCzCB achieved an 82% isolated yield. In the continuous flow system, a catalyst loading of 1 mol% resulted in a yield of 93%. A catalyst loading of 2 mol% at a flow rate of 0.5 mL.min -1 provided the target product. Reducing the flow rate to 0.1 mL.min -1 caused the yield of 1 to drop to 53%. A significant amount of carbazole was observed under the low flow rate conditions of 0.1 mL.min -1. The dimerization of 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (12a) provided an improved isolated yield of 64% under flow. For 2,7-dibromo-9vinylcarbazole (17a), the batch reaction conditions slightly outperformed the flow conditions. The 2-chloro-9-vinylcarbazole and 2-methoxy-9-vinylcarbazole provided yields of 61% and 45%, respectively, under flow. The 4-fluoroarylated vinyl carbazole (22a) was isolated in a 65% yield. The tetra-alkyl substituted cyclobutyl dimer (23b) was provided in a 57% yield. The 3,6-bisarylated 9-vinyl carbazole (24a) provided a modest yield of 50% under flow. The flow protocol delivered the lignan magnosalin (4) in 40% isolated yield on a 10 mmol scale. Flow reaction times were reduced significantly compared to the traditional batch conditions. The batch dimerization of 12a required significantly longer reaction times of 5 days. The continuous flow reaction of 12a was completed in under 1h.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reduction in yield at low flow rates is attributed to the possible reversibility of the dimerization reaction. The formation of carbazole is linked to background oxidation by adventitious oxygen within the flow system. The use of continuous flow leads to more efficient irradiation of the starting substrates. Flow technology enables the synthesis of functionalized carbazole dimers that are difficult to produce via electrophilic substitution. The protocol provides a robust and scalable route to valuable host materials. Flow chemistry avoids the requirement for cryogenic temperatures in the dimerization of electron rich styrenes. The results demonstrate that flow technology can significantly decrease catalyst loadings to near-state-of-the-art levels. The methodology provides a convenient and environmentally beneficial route to natural products and functional materials.

Contradictions And Limitations
At very low flow rates (0.1 mL.min -1), the yield of t-DCzCB dropped significantly to 53%. The formation of carbazole was observed under these extended residence time conditions. The substrate 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (15a) proved challenging and yielded no observed cyclobutane product. The solubility of certain substituted vinyl carbazoles in acetone was challenging at a 0.4 M concentration. The dimerization of 21a resulted in a modest isolated yield of only 25%. The solubility of 21a was poor in acetone, which was reflected in the moderate isolated yield.

Claims
Continuous flow significantly improves the synthesis of cyclobutane dimers compared to batch processes. Flow reaction times were reduced significantly. The 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole provided an improved isolated yield of 64%. The 13b dimer yielded 71% under flow. Batch conditions slightly outperformed flow for 17a. No cyclobutane product was observed for 15a. It provides a scalable route to magnosalin. It offers a convenient, environmentally beneficial methodology.
The methodology enables the synthesis of highly functionalized carbazole dimers that are difficult to access via traditional substitution. Flow delivered functionalized carbazoles. Flow conditions provided 65% yield for 22b. Substrate 21a yielded only 25%. These materials are well placed for exploitation as novel functional materials.

Data And Code Availability
The details of the calibration for the flow system can be found in the supporting information.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study probed potential reversibility by lowering the flow rate. The study probed different wavelengths including 405 nm and 420 nm. The use of an electron relay, anthracene, greatly improved product outcome.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents the optimization study for the continuous flow synthesis. Scheme 4 compares the batch and flow conditions for VCZ dimerization. Scheme 5 illustrates the expansion of the carbazole product scope. Scheme 6 explores the synthetic potential of brominated cyclobutanes. Scheme 7 demonstrates the application of the flow protocol to styrenes.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a robust, scalable continuous flow protocol for organophotoredox catalyzed dimerization of vinylcarbazoles and styrenes. 2. The strongest evidence is the significant reduction in reaction times and catalyst loadings (to 0.1 mol%) while maintaining high yields. 3. The future path involves using this scalable flow chemistry to synthesize new photophysical materials and natural products.

summary.title: A New Organocatalytic Desymmetrization Reaction Enables the Enantioselective Total Synthesis of Madangamine E
summary.authors: Shinya Shiomi; Benjamin D A Shennan; Ken Yamazaki; Ángel L Fuentes De Arriba; Dhananjayan Vasu; Trevor A Hamlin; Darren J Dixon
summary.executive_summary: The study presents a 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of the marine natural product madangamine E, achieved through the development of a novel organocatalytic desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition reaction. This key transformation involves a prochiral ketone reacting with a tethered $\beta,\beta'$-disubstituted nitroolefin to construct a chiral bicyclic core. The reaction is highly efficient, providing near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity while simultaneously establishing three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon. The researchers utilized Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst (9f) as the primary catalyst, which proved uniquely effective for this challenging transformation. To understand the reaction's selectivity, the team employed density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The computations identified a specific transition state (TS1) as the most energetically favorable, with a $\Delta\Delta G^\ddagger$ of 3.0 kcal mol$^{-1}$, which correlates perfectly with the experimental 99% ee. The transition state is stabilized by a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism involving several hydrogen bonding interactions with the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties. Beyond the primary catalytic step, the total synthesis involved several strategic maneuvers: a scalable synthesis of the nitroolefin precursor 17, a mild one-pot oxidation-lactamisation to build the B and D rings, and a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone. Furthermore, the study addresses the challenges of macrocyclization, noting that the spatial arrangement of alkenes significantly impacts ring-closing metathesis outcomes. The synthesis concludes with a final double amide reduction to yield madangamine E. This work highlights the utility of organocatalytic desymmetrization as a powerful tool for the rapid and atomoeconomical generation of complex stereochemical motifs in natural product synthesis.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The study presents a 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of the marine natural product madangamine E, achieved through the development of a novel organocatalytic desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition reaction. This key transformation involves a prochiral ketone reacting with a tethered $\beta,\beta'$-disubstituted nitroolefin to construct a chiral bicyclic core. The reaction is highly efficient, providing near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity while simultaneously establishing three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon. The researchers utilized Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst (9f) as the primary catalyst, which proved uniquely effective for this challenging transformation. To understand the reaction's selectivity, the team employed density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The computations identified a specific transition state (TS1) as the most energetically favorable, with a $\Delta\Delta G^\ddagger$ of 3.0 kcal mol$^{-1}$, which correlates perfectly with the experimental 99% ee. The transition state is stabilized by a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism involving several hydrogen bonding interactions with the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties. Beyond the primary catalytic step, the total synthesis involved several strategic maneuvers: a scalable synthesis of the nitroolefin precursor 17, a mild one-pot oxidation-lactamisation to build the B and D rings, and a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone. Furthermore, the study addresses the challenges of macrocyclization, noting that the spatial arrangement of alkenes significantly impacts ring-closing metathesis outcomes. The synthesis concludes with a final double amide reduction to yield madangamine E. This work highlights the utility of organocatalytic desymmetrization as a powerful tool for the rapid and atomoeconomical generation of complex stereochemical motifs in natural product synthesis.

Research Context
The madangamine family is isolated from marine sea sponges. These products are characterized by a complex pentacyclic fused-ring system. While some syntheses exist, there are only two reports of total syntheses of family members. The first synthesis employed a stereoselective cyclocondensation of phenylglycinol. A subsequent synthesis used a key N-acyl-iminium cyclization. The authors proposed using an enantioselective desymmetrization reaction to install stereochemical information in a single step.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The authors sought to install all the ensuing stereochemical information from a single chirality inducing step. They hypothesized that a desymmetrization reaction would provide a rigid scaffold for elaboration. The strategy aims to enable the conversion of relatively simple achiral starting materials to high-value products.

Methodological Details
A nitroolefin 7 was selected as an ideal model substrate. The researchers investigated a range of chiral single enantiomer organocatalysts. Tested catalysts included trans-cyclohexanediamine and proline-derived scaffolds. The reactions were conducted at 20 mol% loading. Benzoic acid was included as a co-catalyst for the reaction. The synthesis of nitroolefin 17 was scaled up to 17 g.

Procedures And Architectures
A new route for nitroolefin 17 involved reductive amination. Selenoxide elimination chemistry was used to install the nitroolefin. Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f provided an uniquely efficient reaction profile. The reaction pathway was investigated computationally using DFT calculations. TS1 emerged as the most energetically favorable transition structure. The RCM was performed using a Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst.

Key Results
The model compound 8 was obtained in 70% yield. The experimental enantioselectivity for model 8 was 99% ee. The desymmetrization of 17E provided intermediate 18 in excellent yield. Intermediate 18 was obtained with >99% ee. Computational analysis showed $\Delta\Delta G^\ddagger = 3.0$ kcal mol$^{-1}$ for TS1. The yield of desired aldehyde 23 was improved to 86%.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reaction follows a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism. TS1 is stabilized by several hydrogen bonding interactions. Mechanism differences result from the pKa difference between nitronate and enolate.

Contradictions And Limitations
The application of Amat's Wittig reaction was largely unsuccessful. RCM resulted in no desired cyclisation due to spatial arrangement. The initial yield of aldehyde 23 was low. The reaction for ketone 3 was highly capricious.

Claims
The organocatalytic desymmetrization reaction enables the construction of the bicyclic madangamine core with high selectivity. Intermediate 18 was reached in 95% yield. The result provided >99% ee. RCM resulted in no desired cyclisation. This enables the conversion of relatively simple materials.
DFT calculations successfully rationalized the observed enantioselectivity of the desymmetrization. TS1 showed $\Delta\Delta G^\ddagger = 3.0$ kcal mol$^{-1}$. The calculated ee is in excellent agreement.  The mechanism benefits from several hydrogen bonding.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A depicts the pentacyclic fused-ring system. Figure 1B illustrates the madangamine A structure. Figure 1C presents the retrosynthetic analysis. Figure 2A shows the previous intramolecular Michael addition. Figure 2B summarizes the catalytic cycle. Figures 2C and 3 provide the DFT calculations.

Three Takeaways
1. A new catalytic and highly enantioselective desymmetrization reaction was developed. 2. The desymmetrization of 17E provided intermediate 18 in excellent yield. 3. The spatial organisation of reacting alkenes should guide future macrocyclization campaigns.

summary.title: Tuning the Dielectric Response in a NC Material through Nanoparticle Morphology
summary.authors: Archita Adluri; Brett Henderson; Irina Paci
summary.executive_summary:
This study investigates the dielectric response of nanocomposite (NC) materials, specifically focusing on how the morphology of molecular-scale silver (Ag) nanoparticle inclusions affects the dielectric permittivity of a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix. As modern electronics demand higher-κ materials for energy storage and processing power, traditional silicon dioxide (SiO2) gate materials are reaching their physical limits due to significant current leakage and tunneling effects at the few-nanometer scale. To address this, the authors explore nanocomposites where small, highly polarizable molecular nanoparticles (mNPs) are embedded in a high-κ matrix. Unlike bulk metallic nanoparticles, mNPs behave like molecules, offering a source of polarizable electron density without the low percolation thresholds and tunneling issues of traditional metallic structures. 

Using Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) and the Modern Theory of Polarization within the Quantum Espresso code, the research models several inclusion types, including rod-like and disk-like structures of varying sizes. The methodology includes structural relaxation and polarization calculations under a static field (0.001 a.u.). Key findings demonstrate that dielectric permittivity enhancements are not merely a function of inclusion volume but are significantly influenced by shape and orientation. For instance, while an Ag8 inclusion provides a ~30% increase in dielectric constant (εr), multi-layer disk-like inclusions (e.g., disks 332, 432, and 442) can achieve over 70% enhancement. The study identifies that the 'reach' of the induced polarization field is strongest when inclusions are oriented parallel to the applied field and identifies the matrix-nanoparticle interface as the critical site of dielectric enhancement. Furthermore, the study highlights that 2D disk-like nanoparticles show a decrease in polarization because electrons cannot move in the z-direction. The results provide a foundational understanding of quantum polarization effects in nanoscale composites, suggesting that precise control over nanoparticle geometry can be used to engineer next-generation high-κ dielectrics.

claims.description: Nanoparticle morphology (shape and orientation) significantly enhances dielectric response beyond simple volume-ratio expectations.
The dielectric enhancement is primarily driven by induced fields at the matrix-inclusion interface.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the dielectric response of nanocomposite (NC) materials, specifically focusing on how the morphology of molecular-scale silver (Ag) nanoparticle inclusions affects the dielectric permittivity of a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix. To address this, the authors explore nanocomposites where small, highly polarizable molecular nanoparticles (mNPs) are embedded in a high-κ matrix. Unlike bulk metallic nanoparticles, mNPs behave like molecules, offering a source of polarizable electron density without the low percolation thresholds and tunneling issues of traditional metallic structures. 

Using Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) and the Modern Theory of Polarization within the Quantum Espresso code, the research models several inclusion types, including rod-like and disk-like structures of varying sizes. The methodology includes structural relaxation and polarization calculations under a static field (0.001 a.u.). Key findings demonstrate that dielectric permittivity enhancements are not merely a function of inclusion volume but are significantly influenced by shape and orientation. For instance, while an Ag8 inclusion provides a ~30% increase in dielectric constant (εr), multi-layer disk-like inclusions (e.g., disks 332, 432, and 442) can achieve over 70% enhancement. The study identifies that the 'reach' of the induced polarization field is strongest when inclusions are oriented parallel to the applied field and identifies the matrix-nanoparticle interface as the critical site of dielectric enhancement. Furthermore, the study highlights that 2D disk-like nanoparticles show a decrease in polarization because electrons cannot move in the z-direction. The results provide a foundational understanding of quantum polarization effects in nanoscale composites, suggesting that precise control over nanoparticle geometry can be used to engineer next-generation high-κ dielectrics.

Research Context
The demand for high-κ dielectric materials is rising for advanced energy storage and processing power. Traditional Si/SiO2 gate materials face significant current leakage and tunneling at the few-nanometer scale. Nanocomposite materials combine a standard matrix with inclusions to provide tunable dielectric and mechanical properties. Molecular nanoparticles (mNPs) serve as a source of highly polarizable electron density while avoiding bulk metallic issues. Theoretical models for mixed materials must move beyond macroscale approximations to capture quantum response and local field effects. Previous work established that significant interfacial effects between inclusions and the matrix produce greater than expected polarization.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study investigates how the size, shape, and orientation of mNP inclusions affect the dielectric capacity of metal-oxide materials. The research hypothesizes that at mNP scales of <30 atoms, these morphological factors greatly alter electron behavior and atomic-scale polarization. The study aims to unravel how inclusion geometry impacts the dielectric response beyond simple volume-ratio predictions.

Methodological Details
The researchers used a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix as a high-κ gate dielectric. MgO was chosen for its cubic crystal structure, isotropic polarization, and low number of polarizable d-electrons. Silver (Ag) molecular nanoparticles (mNPs) were used as the inclusions within the MgO matrix. The study modeled three rod-like inclusions and five disk-like inclusions. Inclusions were built on an ideal Ag fcc lattice and allowed to optimize in the CPMD simulation. The matrix extended 2 Mg-O layers beyond the edge of the inclusion to prevent conduction into periodic images. The inclusion loading ratio was kept between 3-5% to separate periodic images. Calculations were performed using the Quantum Espresso code with a plane wave-basis set and LDA functional. Pseudopotentials were sourced from MaterialsCloud for Mg, O, and Ag atoms. The total energy convergence criteria were set to 10⁻⁸ and a force threshold of 10⁻⁴.

Procedures And Architectures
Initial electron minimization was calculated using Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization. A series of damped dynamics steps were used to allow ions and electrons to minimize fully. Lattice vectors were relaxed to remove stress from the inclusion within the matrix. Dielectric constant (εr) was calculated according to Equation 1 using a static field of 0.001 a.u. along the z-axis. The reference polarization is defined as that of the cell without an applied field. Electronic and ionic polarization were calculated using damped dynamics and fully relaxed electronic structure steps. The study accounted for quantum of polarization jumps by applying mathematical corrections during post-processing. Born effective charge (BEC) tensors were calculated to map the local charge density and induced fields. Forces were normalized to the bulk matrix to highlight the effect of the nanoparticle.

Key Results
An Ag8 inclusion in the MgO matrix resulted in an ≈ 30% increase in εr. Multi-layer disk inclusions (332, 432, and 442) exhibit more than 70% enhancement in εr over the matrix. The dielectric enhancement for disk-like inclusions is larger than expected based on volume ratios. Disk442 shows a polarization increase of more than twice compared to Rod223. Disk332 shows a similar εr value to Rod224 despite having fewer atoms. The 2D nanoparticles (421 and 441) show a decrease in polarization in both directions. Polarization along the z-axis for rods results in a greater increase than the perpendicular εr. BEC plots show that forces at the matrix-nanoparticle interface contribute primarily to increased εr. The reach of the induced field is further physically and stronger for parallel orientations.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The primary mechanism for dielectric enhancement is the induced field at the matrix-inclusion interface. The shape of the nanoparticle determines the spatial distribution and reach of the induced polarization field. Parallel orientation allows for stronger and more extended induced fields compared to perpendicular orientation. 2D disk nanoparticles exhibit decreased polarization because electrons are not free to move in the z-direction. The results suggest that mNPs behave as molecules, allowing for precise control over local polarization effects.

Contradictions And Limitations
DFT calculations using the LDA functional generally underestimate the bandgap of the material. Simulated results are volume averages and do not account for surface charge or edge effects. Computational constraints prevent the modeling of nanoparticles larger than a specific size threshold. The study does not include the effects of aggregation or separation of inclusions.

Claims
Nanoparticle morphology (shape and orientation) significantly enhances dielectric response beyond simple volume-ratio expectations. Disk442 shows a polarization increase of more than twice compared to Rod223. Multi-layer disks exhibit more than 70% enhancement in εr. 2D nanoparticles show a decrease in polarization in both directions. Precise control over inclusion geometry allows for engineering high-κ dielectrics.
The dielectric enhancement is primarily driven by induced fields at the matrix-inclusion interface. Forces are mainly due to forces felt by atoms at the matrix-nanoparticle interface. The shape of the nanoparticle influences the shape and reach of the induced polarization.  Isolating and manipulating interfacial effects is key to optimizing nanocomposite performance.

Data And Code Availability
The study utilizes the Quantum Espresso code version 6.0 and 6.6.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Test runs with thermostats between 200 and 600K showed that temperature effects on geometry were negligible.

Ethical Considerations
No specific ethical considerations are reported in the text.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents the εr values for various rod-like and disk-like inclusions. Figure 9 displays smeared BEC plots showing the reach of induced fields. Figure 1 provides an example of the local structure distortion caused by a silver inclusion.

Three Takeaways
1. Morphology (shape and orientation) is a critical determinant of dielectric enhancement in mNP nanocomposites. 2. Disk-like inclusions can provide >70% enhancement due to stronger local field reaches compared to rods. 3. Future research should explore different matrix materials like SiO2 and HfO2 and other transition metals.

summary.title: Low density interior in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expels ions to the subsurface
summary.authors: Shahrazad M A Malek (Memorial University of Newfoundland); Ivan Saika-Voivod (Memorial University of Newfoundland); Styliani Consta (The University of Western Ontario)
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the spatial distribution of sodium ions (Na+) within supercooled aqueous nanodroplets, specifically focusing on the structural influence of the solvent on ion localization. Utilizing molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, the researchers examined nanodroplets of varying sizes (N = 100 to 1100 water molecules) at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. A central finding is that at supercooled temperatures (200 K), larger nanodroplets (N $\ge$ 200) develop a heterogeneous internal structure characterized by an anomalous, low-density core with tetrahedral ordering surrounded by a higher-density, more disordered subsurface. In contrast, at room temperature (300 K), the ion distribution is nearly uniform in the droplet interior, largely governed by 'electrostatic confinement'—a harmonic potential effect where ions are drawn toward the droplet's center of mass by electrostatic and surface energy balances. However, at supercooling, the formation of the low-density tetrahedral core actively expels both single and multiple Na+ ions from the center. The ions preferentially reside in the high-density subsurface because it provides a better solvation environment than the ordered core. The researchers also developed an analytical 'electrostatic confinement' model to describe the forces on a single ion in a fluctuating droplet, noting that while the model accurately predicts room-temperature behavior, it fails to account for the structural transitions at supercooling. For smaller clusters (N = 100), the presence of the ion itself disrupts the formation of a tetrahedral core due to immediate solvation and significant shape fluctuations. The study concludes that the solvent's heterogeneous organization at low temperatures significantly alters ion distribution compared to room-temperature predictions, which has profound implications for atmospheric chemistry and the interpretation of mass spectrometry data for macromolecule conformations.

The spatial distribution of ions in droplets plays a decisive role in chemical reactivity in atmospheric and man-made aerosols. The structure and stability of supercooled clusters composed of ionic species and up to a few tens of water molecules has fascinated scientists over several decades. Most of the computational studies are for clusters at room or elevated temperature, while there are relatively a few computational studies of the supercooled clusters due to fact that they are notoriously challenging to be equilibrated. Our recent computer simulations for pristine supercooled water clusters have revealed an anomalous, inverted radial density profile emerging for N $\ge$ 200 molecules at low temperature, in which a lowdensity core with relatively good tetrahedral ordering is surrounded by a high density subsurface.

Research Question And Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the low density water core in supercooled droplets will differentiate the ion distribution from that at room temperature. In order to obtain insight into the forces that determine a single ion's location in a fluctuating droplet, we introduce a reference analytical model. We analyze the spatial distribution of a single ion in terms of a reference electrostatic model.

Methodological Details
We simulate Na+ ions in aqueous nanodroplets at T = 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. The system sizes vary from 100 H2O molecules to 1100 molecules. The simulations are performed by molecular dynamics (MD) as implemented in GROMACS v4.6.1. The water molecules are modeled with the TIP4P/2005 model. For Na+ the OPLS-AA parameters are taken from Ref. 48. The equations of motion are integrated with the leap-frog algorithm with a time step of 2 fs.

Procedures And Architectures
The energy of the charged droplet is written as the sum of the electrostatic energy and surface energy. The model predicts that the ion is subject to a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass. We name this effect 'electrostatic confinement' (EC). The simulations are carried out in the canonical ensemble -constant number of molecules N, volume V, and T. The temperature is controlled by using the Nosé-Hoover thermostat with time constant 0.1 ps.

Key Results
At high T, the radial distribution of a single Na+ ion in the droplet core is nearly uniform. At low T, there is significant layering for all nanodroplet sizes. The Voronoi-based density $\rho_v(r)$ monotonically decreases (or flat) with r for all nanodroplet sizes at high T. At low T, $\rho_v(r)$ shows a monotonic increase towards a subsurface peak. Rather than being centered at r = 0, the peak of $\rho_{Na}(r)$ is located within 0.1 nm of the peak in $\rho_v(r)$ (for N $\ge$ 200). Multiple ions are expelled from the drop's core and they show a maximum at the same location as the single ion.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Ions prefer the relatively disordered high density subsurface to the relatively ordered low density tetrahedral network of the core. The electrostatic confinement is more pronounced for an ion with a charge of at least $\pm$3e. The distribution of multiple ions cannot be explained by the predictions of the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation.

Contradictions And Limitations
For N = 100, the cluster does not show a tetrahedrally organized core. This smaller cluster is subject to larger relative shape fluctuations than the larger droplets. Sampling proves to be a challenge in such systems.

Claims
Supercooled aqueous nanodroplets develop a low-density tetrahedral core that expels Na+ ions to the high-density subsurface. The Voronoi-based density $\rho_v(r)$ shows a monotonic increase towards a subsurface peak at 200 K. The single Na+ ion peak $\rho_{Na}(r)$ aligns with the subsurface peak within 0.1 nm. In the N = 100 cluster, the ion does not show a tetrahedrally organized core. The distribution of multiple ions cannot be explained by the predictions of the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 3 shows $\rho(r)$ and $\rho_v(r)$ for pure water nanodroplets, illustrating high-temperature uniformity and low-temperature layering. Figure 4 confirms that ions prefer the disordered high density subsurface at 200 K.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that supercooled water nanodroplets form a tetrahedral interior that expels ions. 2. The strongest evidence is the spatial alignment of the Na+ ion peak with the high-density subsurface peak in the Voronoi density. 3. The future path involves investigating the conformations of macromolecules and peptides within these supercooled droplets.

summary.title: Learning design rules for selective oxidation catalysts from highthroughput experimentation and artificial intelligence
summary.authors: Lucas Foppa, Christopher Sutton, Luca M Ghiringhelli, Sandip De, Patricia Löser, Stephan A Schunk, Ansgar Schäfer, Matthias Scheffler
summary.executive_summary:
The design of heterogeneous catalysts is hindered by the vast complexity of materials and the rarity of high-performing candidates. This study proposes a novel methodology combining high-throughput experimentation (HTE) and subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial intelligence to identify 'SG rules'—specific physicochemical constraints that define outstanding catalytic performance. The research focuses on the selective oxidation of propylene into value-added oxygenates (acrolein and acrylic acid) using SiO2-supported catalysts composed of ruthenium (Ru), tungsten (W), and phosphorus (P). The researchers synthesized 120 distinct three-component catalyst compositions and tested them across a temperature range of 200–400 °C, generating an experimental dataset of product yields. These results were integrated with theoretical descriptive parameters calculated via density-functional-theory (DFT-PBEsol) using the FHI-aims code.

Unlike global models that aim to minimize average prediction error across all samples, the SGD approach identifies local behaviors by maximizing a quality function based on coverage and the cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence. This identifies subgroups with 'unusual' target values, effectively isolating the conditions that lead to exceptional reactivity. The study identified three key parameters: reaction temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity. A specific subgroup of 15 data points (representing 1.2% of the dataset) showed an average oxygenate yield of 24.15%, which is five times higher than the overall dataset average of 4.83%.

Crucially, the authors demonstrated that these SG rules are generalizable. By applying the rules derived from the three-component catalysts to the design of more complex systems, they synthesized four- and five-component catalysts. These advanced materials achieved oxygenate yields of 60.19% and 59.60%, respectively—nearly double the highest yield observed in the training set. While certain rules, such as temperature, were not directly transferable to the more complex systems, the study validates that local AI modeling can successfully guide the discovery of high-performing catalysts where explicit atomistic modeling is impractical.

claims.description: The SGD-HTE-&theory approach can identify local reactivity rules that are generalizable to more complex catalyst systems.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The design of heterogeneous catalysts is hindered by the vast complexity of materials and the rarity of high-performing candidates. This study proposes a novel methodology combining high-throughput experimentation (HTE) and subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial intelligence to identify 'SG rules'—specific physicochemical constraints that define outstanding catalytic performance. The research focuses on the selective oxidation of propylene into value-added oxygenates (acrolein and acrylic acid) using SiO2-supported catalysts composed of ruthenium (Ru), tungsten (W), and phosphorus (P). The researchers synthesized 120 distinct three-component catalyst compositions and tested them across a temperature range of 200–400 °C, generating an experimental dataset of product yields. These results were integrated with theoretical descriptive parameters calculated via density-functional-theory (DFT-PBEsol) using the FHI-aims code.

Unlike global models that aim to minimize average prediction error across all samples, the SGD approach identifies local behaviors by maximizing a quality function based on coverage and the cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence. This identifies subgroups with 'unusual' target values, effectively isolating the conditions that lead to exceptional reactivity. The study identified three key parameters: reaction temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity. A specific subgroup of 15 data points (representing 1.2% of the dataset) showed an average oxygenate yield of 24.15%, which is five times higher than the overall dataset average of 4.83%.

Crucially, the authors demonstrated that these SG rules are generalizable. By applying the rules derived from the three-component catalysts to the design of more complex systems, they synthesized four- and five-component catalysts. These advanced materials achieved oxygenate yields of 60.19% and 59.60%, respectively—nearly double the highest yield observed in the training set. While certain rules, such as temperature, were not directly transferable to the more complex systems, the study validates that local AI modeling can successfully guide the discovery of high-performing catalysts where explicit atomistic modeling is impractical.

Research Context
Heterogeneous catalysis involves an intricate interplay of surface reaction networks and dynamic restructuring of the catalyst material. Explicit atomistic modeling of the full catalytic progression by first-principles methods is often impractical. High-throughput experimentation (HTE) allows for testing large amounts of materials but identifying the next promising candidates is not straightforward. The number of possible materials is practically infinite, while the number of good catalysts is very small. Global models trained to minimize average prediction error may fail to focus on the most interesting materials and mechanisms. Alternative approaches are required to identify rules associated with high performance.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study seeks to identify key physicochemical descriptive parameters and constraints (rules) associated with high catalytic performance. The authors hypothesize that a local artificial intelligence approach (SGD) can identify these rules from a hybrid dataset of experimental and theoretical data. It is expected that these rules will not only reflect underlying processes but also guide the design of more complex catalysts. The target for discovery is the yield of oxygenate products (acrolein and acrylic acid) from propylene.

Methodological Details
The study investigated 120 different three-component catalyst compositions containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus. Catalysts were prepared on a SiO2 pseudo-liquid support, potentially exhibiting disordered or amorphous structures. Reaction temperatures were examined in the range between 200°C and 400°C. The reactions were carried out in tubular, fixed-bed reactors using a specific molar feed of Ar, H2O, N2, O2, and propylene. The target variable was the yield of oxygenates, defined as the molar rate of oxygenates divided by the molar rate of propylene. Candidate descriptive parameters were calculated for isolated atoms using DFT-PBEsol. The FHI-aims code was used to calculate these elemental properties. System-specific properties were derived by taking the composition-weighted average of per-element free-atom properties. In total, 11 descriptive parameters were used in the SGD analysis.

Procedures And Architectures
The study utilized a subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial intelligence approach to find local behaviors. SGD begins with the generation of a pool of propositions (π) representing inequalities of candidate parameters. The algorithm identifies selectors (σ) formed by propositions joined with 'AND' connectors. The selection process maximizes a quality function that measures how outstanding specific subselections are compared to the whole dataset. The quality function includes a coverage term to ensure statistical significance of the subgroups. The second term in the quality function is the cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence (m/no). m/no measures the dissimilarity between distributions, favoring SGs with target values that are as unusual as possible.

Key Results
The average oxygenates yield over the whole data set is equal to 4.83%. Only 41 measurements in the dataset were associated with yields above 20%. The maximum yield of oxygenates recorded in the dataset was 26.85%. SGD identified a subgroup with an average yield of 24.15%, which is five times higher than the overall average. This subgroup was described by three rules: 280 ≤ T ≤ 300°C, J_K > 0.55, and 3.910 ≤ V_Y < 4.002 eV. A designed four-component catalyst containing tellurium achieved the highest oxygenate yield of 60.19% at 400°C. A designed five-component catalyst containing tantalum achieved a yield of 59.60% at 400°C. The highest yields for the four- and five-component materials were approximately twice as large as the highest training yield.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The identified rules reflect specific underlying processes rather than global averages. The phosphorus content rule likely relates to the dilution of active metal sites on a phosphate matrix. The electronegativity rule effectively limits the range of ruthenium content to prevent undesired combustion. The SGD approach successfully identified interpretable, chemically meaningful, and complex patterns. The rules successfully guided the design of complex catalysts significantly more performant than any training observations.

Contradictions And Limitations
The oxygen content was not included in the material characterization as its proportion was unknown. The SG rule on temperature was not transferable to the four-component materials. It is unclear if the SG rules can identify exceptional materials for arbitrary ruthenium content or elements with significantly different radii. Different mechanisms may operate on materials with significantly different radii compared to tungsten. Future SGD analyses may need new data points covering unexplored portions of the materials space.

Claims
The SGD-HTE-&theory approach can identify local reactivity rules that are generalizable to more complex catalyst systems. The four-component catalyst reached 60.19% yield, satisfying the VY rule. The five-component catalyst reached 59.60% yield, satisfying the VY rule. Yields for complex catalysts were twice as large as the training set max. The temperature rule was not transferable to the four-component catalysts. This local modeling approach is suitable for finding exceptional materials that are hard to model explicitly.

Data And Code Availability
Further calculation details and values for the elemental properties are available in the electronic supporting information (ESI).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
SG rules were shown to be robust when using 90% of the data points for training. Rules were also robust when excluding data points with yields lower than 3%. The thresholds for the VY parameter remained similar despite variations in the training data.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A illustrates how SGD identifies selectors through propositions. Figure 2A and B show the distribution of yields and demonstrate the rarity of high performance. Figure 2C shows the specific rules for the three-component catalyst subgroup. Figure 3B shows the ternary diagram illustrating the limit on Ru content. Figure 4A shows the catalyst map for four-component materials and their VY values. Figure 5A and B show the SGD analysis of the four- and five-component data.

Three Takeaways
1. The study uses SGD to identify local rules (e.g., temperature, phosphorus content, electronegativity) for high-performance catalysts. 2. The methodology successfully guided the design of complex catalysts achieving oxygenate yields over 60%, doubling the training maximum. 3. SGD is a powerful tool for discovering exceptional materials where explicit atomistic modeling is impractical.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study proposes an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method for producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) intended for soil conditioning through a solvent-free mechanochemical process. By utilizing reverse logistics, the researchers repurpose eggshell waste (calcite) and react it with potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4) using high-energy ball milling. The process successfully synthesizes new phosphate phases, specifically K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4. These materials act as 'smart release' fertilizers; they provide a controlled delay in the bioavailability of phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) compared to the highly soluble KH2PO4 precursor, while simultaneously increasing the bioavailability of calcium (Ca) relative to the raw eggshell material. Experimental data from both citric acid solubility tests and soil release assays confirm these behaviors. In soil environments, the material promotes the formation of hydroxyapatite, a stable long-term reservoir for calcium and phosphorus that becomes available as soil pH acidifies. The mechanochemical approach is highlighted for its ecological advantages, as it operates in a solvent-free environment, produces no liquid or solid waste, and ensures significant savings during production. Ultimately, the research provides a viable pathway for sustainable agricultural nutrient management by transforming food industry waste into high-value, eco-friendly fertilizer components.

Research Context
Reverse logistics is a key instrument of economic and social development characterized by a set of actions, procedures and means to enable the collection and restitution of solid waste. This concept is perfectly applied in the agriculture context to provide novel processes for the synthesis of different calcium and / or potassium phosphates. Eggshells are important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources, specifically calcite. The production of these materials is traditionally processed by solid state mechanochemical activation to promote a chemical reaction from solid reagents. This process uses mainly friction and impact forces to break reagent bonds and promote solid phase ion migration. The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, providing a delay of the bioavailability of P and K. These materials also improve the bioavailability of Ca, turning them into an excellent alternative for nutrient management. The solid-state mechanochemical activation allows the reactions to occur in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste. As far as the authors know, no mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of calcium and potassium hydrogen phosphate from calcite and KH2PO4. New technologies of ecological fertilizer production have been prioritizing environmental care using industrial and other potential wastes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to provide novel processes for the synthesis of different calcium and / or potassium phosphates from any source of calcium carbonate. The primary goal is to evaluate acid-basic reactions between these precursors to form potassium calcium phosphates. It is hypothesized that the applied energy must be large enough to be able to break the reagent bonds and promote solid phase ion migration. The authors expected to form a new structure, specifically producing K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4. The researchers predicted that these phosphates would exhibit very different solubility according to the different bonds between different metal cations. They hypothesized that the produced potassium calcium phosphates would provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K. It was predicted that these materials would also improve the bioavailability of Ca turning these materials an excellent alternative. The study seeks to establish a solvent-free method ensuring huge savings during the production process. The ultimate objective is to develop an eco-friendly fertilizer that guarantees a better nutrient management by playing on the solubility of calcium, potassium and phosphorus.

Methodological Details
The eggshells were collected by the authors in their homes, washed with water and dried at room temperature. The KH2PO4 PA was supplied from Vetec. The milling process was performed with high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7. The system utilized a 250 ml zirconia bowl and 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4 was used for the essays. Trials were performed for 15 min and 30 min. The milling continued for 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h. Rotational speeds tested were 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm. The mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. Samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) MAS. The authors also employed thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Nutrient content was obtained by dissolving the samples by using acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture. Digestion was performed by 24 h at 250 °C. Analysis was determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. The material was pelletized in a steel pelletizer applying the pressure of 5 bar. Pellet weight was standardized to 100 mg/L of P. Release assays were conducted in 2% citric acid solution. One single pellet were used in each essay in triplicate. The beaker was immersed into 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution in a 600 mL beaker. The system was kept closed with polyvinyl chloride (PVC) film at 25 °C. Aliquots of 1.2 mL were collected from 15 min to 30 days. Phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes containing moist soil. Pre-treated paper was used to mark the P diffusion in soil. In each Petri dish, 78 g of dry and sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil were added. The desired density of 1.2 g.cm -3 was achieved. To achieve 70% of the maximum soil water retention capacity, 15 mL deionized water were added. The papers are scanned and analyzed using GNU Image Manipulation Program. Scanned images were converted to black-with binary images. The area of the high P-zone is quantified using the histogram command. Soil release essays were carried out under aerobic conditions in plastic container containing 50 g of sandy soil. Experiments were performed with 75% water saturation. Trials occurred at 3, 7, 15 and 30 days. Pellet weight was standardized to 300 mg of P per kg of soil. Potassium and calcium were extracted from the soil by HCl (0.05 Mol/L) and KCl (1 Mol/L) methods. Phosphorus was extracted from soil using Mehlich 1 method. Molybdenum blue was used to quantify phosphorus released content. Potassium and calcium were quantified by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy (FAAS).

Procedures And Architectures
The milling process utilized a high-energy ball mill. The specific hardware used was a Fritsch Pulverisette 7. The setup included a 250 ml zirconia bowl. The process employed 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. Weight ratios of 1:1 (w/w) were applied to the eggshell and KH2PO4. Milling durations were varied from 15 min to 24 h. Rotational speeds were adjusted to 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm. The reaction stoichiometry was set to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was used for phase identification. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) MAS was utilized for chemical environment analysis. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) tracked mass loss events. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) was also performed. Samples were subjected to acid digestion in an H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture. Digestion occurred at 250 °C for 24 h. Atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods determined the nutrient content. Pelletization was performed at a pressure of 5 bar. The pellets were standardized to 100 mg/L of P. The release study used a 2% citric acid solution. Soil experiments were conducted in Petri dishes with moist soil. Soil was prepared with a density of 1.2 g.cm -3. Water retention was maintained at 70% of the maximum capacity. Data analysis involved GNU Image Manipulation Program. Images were processed into black-with binary images. The high P-zone area was quantified via histogram command. Soil release was tested under aerobic conditions with 75% water saturation. Experiments were conducted at 3, 7, 15 and 30 days. Pellets were standardized to 300 mg of P per kg of soil. Potassium and calcium were extracted using HCl (0.05 Mol/L) and KCl (1 Mol/L). Phosphorus was extracted using the Mehlich 1 method. Molybdenum blue was used for phosphorus quantification. Flame atomic absorption spectroscopy quantified potassium and calcium.

Key Results
The XRD patterns show that milling at 2 h and 400 rpm produces a mixture of phosphates. The primary phase formed is mainly K3CaH(PO4)2. The secondary phase is possibly CaKPO4. Below these specific milling parameters, only the reactants diffraction patterns are found. It was noticed that only a minimal energy is required to initiate the mechanochemical reaction. Consequently, the diffraction patterns have huge changes attributed to the formation of different polymorphic potassium calcium phosphate phases. When milling time increases, secondary reactions begin such as mechanochemical dehydroxylation. The non-stoichiometric reaction of the main products is evident after 24 h of milling. TGA curves show that the residual mass (89%) is consistent to the theoretical (87%). The thermal degradation of eggshell showed an experimental residue (56%) close to the theoretical (59%). Three mass loss events were observed in milled samples, with the first step centered at 280°C. The second step at 420°C is associated to partial structural water loss and structure dimerization. The final step at 710°C corresponds to final structural water loss reaction and structure polycondensation. Samples processed at 600 rpm present a similar thermal decomposition. However, they show different residuals masses according to the milling time. The 31 P NMR MAS spectra of KH2PO4 shows a single intense signal at δ = 3.74 ppm. Shifts at δ = 3.28 ppm and δ = 2.82 ppm are reported to calcium phosphates compounds. These include hydroxyapatite and octocalcium phosphate. A signal at δ = 0.74 ppm suggests H(PO4)2 5-species agreeing with the KCaPO4 formation. A shift at δ = -5 ppm in sample milled by 2 h at 600 rpm is attributed to pyrophosphate. Phosphorus and potassium release behavior were slower for milled samples. This shows that the phosphates obtained by milling improve the nutrients management. Calcium release was different, as the new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available. Phosphorus and potassium showed better correlation with pseudo-second order model. A substantial decrease of the kinetic constant was observed, attesting the delay in nutrient supply. The temporal profile for KH2PO4 indicates a P increase from 0 mg/kg to 107 mg/kg after 3 days. This represents 40% of total P from precursor (KH2PO4). For sample 2 h/600 rpm, the phosphorus release is more progressive. It reached 25 mg/kg at 3 days and 45 mg/kg at 30 days. This corresponds to 15% of total P content recovered from the milled sample. The P radial diffusion profile from sample milled for 2h/600 rpm is intermediate. It was 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than precursor at the end of 30 days. The kinetic study of K release in soil shows a slight decrease at 3 days. After that, both materials reach around 100% release. There is no increase in the bioavailable calcium when eggshell precursor (CaCO3) is applied in soil. However, this concentration increases to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for 2 h/600 rpm sample. This corresponds to around 8% of calcium recovery from sample. The slower release for calcium and phosphorus are probably related to hydroxyapatite formation. Hydroxyapatite was identified from 3 until 30 days in soil conditions.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The applied energy must be large enough to break the reagent bonds and promote solid phase ion migration. The phosphates obtained by milling improve the nutrients management maintaining their bioavailability. The new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available. Hydroxyapatite is an important long-term calcium and phosphorus slow release fertilizer. The mechanochemical process is solvent-free, ensuring huge savings during the production process. The method provides an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method of producing calcium phosphate bioceramics. This study proposes the use of eggshell to design an eco-friendly fertilizer. The results indicate new phosphate phases like K3CaH(PO4)2 and KCaPO4 present a slower release character.

Contradictions And Limitations
The process mechanism involved is still quite complex to evaluate. Below these milling parameters, no evidence of chemical reaction is observed. It suggests that in low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade the total amount of calcite. Solubility is influenced by the size of the metal cation and its charge. Potassium dihydrogen phosphate exhibits much faster solubilization behavior than calcium or calcium and potassium phosphates. There is no increase in the bioavailable calcium when eggshell precursor (CaCO3) is applied in soil.

Claims
Mechanochemical synthesis provides an eco-friendly method to produce calcium phosphate bioceramics from eggshell waste. The present article provides an environmentally beneficial method of producing calcium phosphate bioceramics. The mechanochemical process was used, free of solvent, and presenting no unwanted subproduct. Below these milling parameters, no evidence of chemical reaction is observed. The method ensures huge savings during the production process.
The synthesized potassium calcium phosphates function as smart release fertilizers by delaying P and K bioavailability while increasing Ca availability. The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers. Phosphates obtained by milling improve the nutrients management maintaining their bioavailability. The new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available. Potassium dihydrogen phosphate exhibits much faster solubilization behavior. These materials provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K.
Soil application of the 2h/600rpm sample results in the formation of hydroxyapatite, ensuring long-term nutrient release. Hydroxyapatite is an important long-term calcium and phosphorus slow release fertilizer. The slower release for calcium and phosphorus are probably related to hydroxyapatite formation. There is no increase in the bioavailable calcium when eggshell precursor (CaCO3) is applied. It is a source of bioavailable calcium compared to the precursor eggshell.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the XRD patterns of the powders obtained after milling. Figure 2 displays the TGA curve of KH2PO4 and the milled samples. Figure 5 illustrates the Phosphorus and potassium release behavior in citric acid. Figure 6 presents the kinetic study of the nutrient release in soil. Figure 7 shows the hydroxyapatite formation identified from 3 until 30 days.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the solvent-free mechanochemical synthesis of calcium phosphates from eggshell waste. 2. The strongest evidence is the observed delay in P and K release and improved Ca availability in soil. 3. The future path involves exploring these materials as nanocomposites to promote better solubilization.

In order to investigate the release behavior closer to real conditions, soil release essays were carried out under aerobic conditions in plastic container containing 50 g of sandy soil (Table S2) with 75% water saturation. The experiments were performed at 3, 7, 15 and 30 days, using a single pellet for each container, the pellet weight was standardized to 300 mg of P per kg of soil. After each release period the solid residues samples were removed from the soil and characterized by XRD; potassium and calcium were extracted from the soil by HCl (0.05 Mol/L) and KCl (1 Mol/L) methods, respectively; and phosphorus was extracted from soil using Mehlich 1 method (Embrapa, 1979). summary.executive_summary: This research addresses the 'lab-to-fab gap' in organic solar cell (OSC) technology, where high efficiencies achieved in laboratory settings using spin-coating are difficult to replicate in industrial-scale manufacturing. To overcome this, the authors demonstrate the feasibility of using slot-die coating, a technique highly compatible with roll-to-roll manufacturing, to produce flexible organic solar cells. The study focuses on the high-performing PM6:Y6 active layer system, which exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA). To maintain material integrity during the coating process, the authors employ a 'hot' slot-die coating technique, heating the substrate, syringe, tube, and slot-die head simultaneously. This process was conducted in open-air using o-xylene, a non-hazardous 'green' solvent, and without the use of additives. The researchers optimized the coating parameters, specifically finding that a coating temperature of 100°C provided the best balance between drying kinetics and morphology, preventing the material aggregation that occurs at temperatures above 100°C, which otherwise degrades the fill factor. Furthermore, they investigated active layer thickness, identifying an optimal range around 200 nm that balances light absorption with charge transport. A significant improvement in performance was achieved by introducing a small amount of the fullerene acceptor PC61BM to create a ternary PM6:Y6:PC61BM system. This ternary blend yielded a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 7.2% and demonstrated enhanced charge dissociation and collection probabilities. Finally, the devices exhibited excellent stability, retaining over 99% of their initial efficiency after more than 1000 hours of dark storage under ISOS-D-1 protocols. These results provide a clear pathway for the industrialization of high-efficiency, flexible, and environmentally friendly organic solar cells using scalable manufacturing processes.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This research addresses the 'lab-to-fab gap' in organic solar cell (OSC) technology, where high efficiencies achieved in laboratory settings using spin-coating are difficult to replicate in industrial-scale manufacturing. To overcome this, the authors demonstrate the feasibility of using slot-die coating, a technique highly compatible with roll-to-roll manufacturing, to produce flexible organic solar cells. The study focuses on the high-performing PM6:Y6 active layer system, which exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA). To maintain material integrity during the coating process, the authors employ a 'hot' slot-die coating technique, heating the substrate, syringe, tube, and slot-die head simultaneously. This process was conducted in open-air using o-xylene, a non-hazardous 'green' solvent, and without the use of additives. The researchers optimized the coating parameters, specifically finding that a coating temperature of 100°C provided the best balance between drying kinetics and morphology, preventing the material aggregation that occurs at temperatures above 100°C, which otherwise degrades the fill factor. Furthermore, they investigated active layer thickness, identifying an optimal range around 200 nm that balances light absorption with charge transport. A significant improvement in performance was achieved by introducing a small amount of the fullerene acceptor PC61BM to create a ternary PM6:Y6:PC61BM system. This ternary blend yielded a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 7.2% and demonstrated enhanced charge dissociation and collection probabilities. Finally, the devices exhibited excellent stability, retaining over 99% of their initial efficiency after more than 1000 hours of dark storage under ISOS-D-1 protocols. These results provide a clear pathway for the industrialization of high-efficiency, flexible, and environmentally friendly organic solar cells using scalable manufacturing processes.

Research Context
The primary challenge in OSC commercialization is the lab-to-fab gap. Current spin-coating techniques have poor potential for upscaling. Slot-die coating is preferred for roll-to-roll manufacturing. Scalable techniques need to use non-hazardous solvent systems. PM6:Y6 is a promising candidate for high-efficiency systems. PM6 exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA) behavior.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to minimize the lab-to-fab gap. The goal is to manufacture OSCs using large-scale compatible processes. The research investigates slot-die coated flexible devices based on PM6:Y6. It is hypothesized that high efficiencies can be achieved using scalable techniques. The authors aim to bring the technology to the edge of commercialization.

Methodological Details
Materials were used directly without purification. Active layer materials include PM6 and Y6. The ternary component used is PB61BM. The flexible substrate is ITO-coated PET. The green solvent used is o-xylene. The device uses an inverted geometry: ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag. The study screens coating temperatures from 60°C to 120°C. Solution concentrations were tested between 12 and 28 mg/mL. Drum speed was kept at 1.5 m/min. Flow rate was set at 0.12 mL/min. The active area was approximately 0.8 cm^2.

Procedures And Architectures
A homemade roll-coater was used for coating. A syringe pump controls the ink flow rate. ZnO nanoparticle ink was coated at 75°C. ZnO was annealed at 100°C for 10 min. The head, syringe, drum, and tube were kept at the same temperature. MoO3 and Ag were thermally evaporated under vacuum. Activation involves a reverse bias current of -5 V. Encapsulation was done using epoxy-based glue. Curing occurred under UV light for 5 min.

Key Results
Binary PM6:Y6 devices achieved 6.3% efficiency. Ternary PM6:Y6:PCBM devices reached 7.2% efficiency. The optimal coating temperature was 100°C. Bimolecular recombination was reduced at 100°C with S = 0.978. PCE increases with thickness up to 217 nm. The highest average PCE for thick layers was 5.8%. Ternary blends showed 12% higher JSC. The ternary PCE reached 6.6% and 6.7% for different ratios. The ternary device retained 99.4% efficiency after 1050 hours. Binary devices retained over 97% efficiency after 1500 hours.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Higher coating temperatures induce better carrier collection. Fast drying above 100°C induces material aggregation. Aggregation on edges impacts the fill factor. The slope values suggest dominant trap-assisted recombination. PC61BM generates an energy cascade effect. Ternary blends enhance dissociation and collection probabilities.

Contradictions And Limitations
Open-air processing leads to high trap-assisted recombination. Higher temperatures decrease the average fill factor. Aggregation at high temperatures creates stripe inhomogeneities.

Claims
Slot-die coating at 100°C is the optimal method for high-efficiency flexible PM6:Y6 solar cells. PCE showed a clear improvement trend towards 100°C. S value closest to unity was at 100°C. FF drops significantly at 120°C. This facilitates scalable roll-to-roll manufacturing.
Adding a small amount of PC61BM as a ternary component significantly enhances device performance. Ternary devices reached 7.2% PCE. Dissociation probability increased to 96.3%. PCBM shows weak and broad absorption. The ternary blend improves charge extraction and stability.

Data And Code Availability
The paper does not specify a data or code repository.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study screened temperatures from 60°C to 120°C. Concentrations were screened from 12 to 28 mg/mL. Thicknesses were varied to investigate absorption and transport.

Ethical Considerations
No specific ethical considerations are reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the absorption of PM6 and Y6. Figure 2 shows J-V curves and EQEs. Figure 3 displays PCE and FF evolution box plots. Figure 4 shows the dried active layer stripe. Table 1 lists PV parameters for different temperatures. Figure 6 shows ternary blend J-V curves. Figure 7 compares binary and ternary parameters. Figure 10 shows stability under dark storage.

Three Takeaways
1. The study demonstrates high-efficiency PM6:Y6 devices (7.2% PCE) using scalable slot-die coating. 2. Hot coating at 100°C is critical to optimize morphology and minimize bimolecular recombination. 3. Ternary blends with PC61BM significantly improve charge dissociation and collection on flexible substrates.

summary.authors: Zejun Wang (South China University of Technology); Jiawen Zhou (South China University of Technology); Yiheng Zhang (South China University of Technology); Weiya Zhu (South China University of Technology); Yuan Li (South China University of Technology)
summary.executive_summary: This study presents the design and synthesis of a novel class of stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) specifically developed for high-efficiency photothermal conversion. Unlike many organic radicals that are unstable in air, these ANARs exhibit significant thermal, electrochemical, and light stability due to their rich resonance structures, which include closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide configurations. The researchers synthesized four star-shaped ANAR materials—TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8—through a facile two-step process involving the demethylation and subsequent oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. A defining feature of these radicals is their extremely high spin concentration and highly enhanced nonradiative decay, which are critical for efficient light-to-heat conversion. Among the variants, TPA-TPA-O6 demonstrated superior performance, characterized by a remarkably wide absorption spectrum extending from 300 to 2000 nm in the powder state. This broad absorption allows for highly efficient sunlight harvesting, enabling TPA-TPA-O6 to achieve a water evaporation efficiency of 89.41% and an evaporation rate of 1.293 kg/m² h under 1 sun irradiation. The material also displayed outstanding photothermal stability over multiple laser cycles and showed significant potential in practical applications like solar-driven seawater desalination, where it successfully reduced concentrations of primary ions (Na+, Mg2+, Ca2+, and K+). The study establishes a novel strategy for designing stable organic-small-molecule photothermal materials by leveraging radical-promoted nonradiative decay and high spin concentration.
