judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents the design and synthesis of a novel class of stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) specifically developed for high-efficiency photothermal conversion. Unlike many organic radicals that are unstable in air, these ANARs exhibit significant thermal, electrochemical, and light stability due to their rich resonance structures, which include closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide configurations. The researchers synthesized four star-shaped ANAR materials—TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8—through a facile two-step process involving the demethylation and subsequent oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. A defining feature of these radicals is their extremely high spin concentration and highly enhanced nonradiative decay, which are critical for efficient light-to-heat conversion. Among the variants, TPA-TPA-O6 demonstrated superior performance, characterized by a remarkably wide absorption spectrum extending from 300 to 2000 nm in the powder state. This broad absorption allows for highly efficient sunlight harvesting, enabling TPA-TPA-O6 to achieve a water evaporation efficiency of 89.41% and an evaporation rate of 1.293 kg/m² h under 1 sun irradiation. The material also displayed outstanding photothermal stability over multiple laser cycles and showed significant potential in practical applications like solar-driven seawater desalination, where it successfully reduced concentrations of primary ions (Na+, Mg2+, Ca2+, and K+). The study establishes a novel strategy for designing stable organic-small-molecule photothermal materials by leveraging radical-promoted nonradiative decay and high spin concentration.

Research Context
Open-shell organic radicals are gaining attention for applications in optoelectronics and photothermal materials due to their unique properties. However, organic small molecules are relatively overlooked compared to inorganic or polymer materials. Inorganic materials pose safety issues, while polymers suffer from poor synthesis reproducibility. Existing organic small molecules face drawbacks such as cumbersome synthesis and poor stability. It is challenging to prepare airstable radicals because of their high reactivity with oxygen.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to design and synthesize a series of aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) without steric hindrance group protection. The researchers hypothesized that these neutral conjugated nitrogen oxide radicals would exhibit high thermal, electrochemical, and light stability. It was predicted that these radicals would convert near-infrared (NIR) light into heat via nonradiative decay. The goal was to develop a stable organic-small-molecule photothermal material for solar-driven water evaporation.

Methodological Details
Four star-shaped ANAR materials were synthesized by introducing different cores like triphenylamine and triazine. The materials were prepared via facile demethylation and subsequent oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. The radical species were characterized using cyclic voltammetry, UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, and electron spin resonance. CV curves were measured for 15 cycles in dichloromethane with a 0.1 M nBu4NPF6 supporting electrolyte. The scan rate was 0.1 V/s with a saturated calomel electrode as reference. TPA-TPA-O6 was loaded inside white polyurethane (PU) foam by impregnation and drying at 80 °C. An interface heating evaporation system was established by floating the foam on water. Photothermal property was evaluated under an 808 nm laser with 0.8 W cm⁻² power. Solar-driven water evaporation was measured under 1 sun illumination (1 kW m⁻²).

Procedures And Architectures
The ANAR materials were designed by introducing different cores like triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, and spiro fluorene. The materials were prepared via facile demethylation and consequent oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. The radical species were characterized using cyclic voltammetry, UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, and electron spin resonance. CV curves were measured for 15 cycles in dichloromethane with a 0.1 M nBu4NPF6 supporting electrolyte. The scan rate was 0.1 V/s with a saturated calomel electrode as reference. TPA-TPA-O6 was loaded inside white polyurethane (PU) foam by impregnation and drying at 80 °C. An interface heating evaporation system was established by floating the foam on water. Photothermal property was evaluated under an 808 nm laser with 0.8 W cm⁻² power. Solar-driven water evaporation was measured under 1 sun illumination (1 kW m⁻²).

Key Results
TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited a wide absorption spectrum from 300 to 2000 nm in the powder state. The PLQY of all radical products was significantly reduced to lower than 1%. Demethylated counterparts exhibited highly reversible CV curves and negligible changes after 15 cycles. HOMO levels were recorded as -4.90, -4.81, -4.97, and -4.84 eV. The ESR signal intensity of TPA-TPA-O6 and Spiro-O8 were significantly enhanced. Under 808 nm laser irradiation, TPA-TPA-O6 temperature increased from 25 °C to about 210 °C within 60 s. TPA-TPA-O6 achieved a water evaporation efficiency of 89.41%. The water evaporation rate was recorded as 1.293 kg/m² h. The equilibrium temperature of the foam reached 81.2 °C under 600 s continuous irradiation.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
High spin concentration leads to highly nonradiative decay, which enhances photothermal conversion. Radical character in the solid state is indicated by a long absorption tail from 400-825 nm. Strong donor-acceptor conjugation effect reduces the optical bandgap and determines paramagnetic properties. Rich resonance structures including nitro-like and nitroxide structures contribute to stability. This study provides a novel strategy for designing stable high spin radical materials.

Contradictions And Limitations
TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 show lower performance due to low concentration of radical spin. These materials might be partially protonated to form hydroxyl groups. Lower HOMO energy levels make it difficult for these radicals to be oxidized by O2.

Claims
TPA-TPA-O6 is a high-performance photothermal material with extremely wide absorption and high efficiency. It exhibits a wide absorption from 300 to 2000 nm. It achieves a solar-driven water evaporation efficiency of 89.41%. It achieves a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg/m² h. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 show lower conversion efficiency. It shows excellent potential for solar-driven desalination.
ANARs are structurally stable due to their rich resonance. They exhibit high thermal and electrochemical stability. They have rich resonance structures. It is challenging to prepare airstable radicals normally. This provides a novel strategy for stable organic materials.

Data And Code Availability
The Supporting Information is available free of charge.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study compares different cores like triphenylamine, triazine, and pyrene. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 show lower performance due to low radical spin concentration.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 6B shows TPA-TPA-O6 high broadband light absorption. Figure 5A shows temperature increased rapidly from 25 °C to 210 °C. Figure 6F shows an evaporation rate of 1.293 kg/m² h.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the synthesis of stable star-shaped ANAR materials for photothermal conversion. 2. The strongest evidence is the 89.41% efficiency and 1.293 kg/m² h evaporation rate of TPA-TPA-O6. 3. The future path involves developing ANAR materials with enhanced planarity for organic electronics and spintronics.

summary.title: Metal-Free Photocatalysis at Charged Aqueous Interface: Boosting the Photocatalytic Oxidative Coupling of Arylamines to Azoaromatics under Ambient Conditions
summary.authors: Shivendra Singh; Vidhi Agarwal; Tridib K Sarma; Tushar Kanti Mukherjee
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic methodology for the oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles. Azoaromatics are a significant class of functional organic molecules with wide-ranging applications in optical storage, molecular switches, and various industrial processes. Traditional synthesis methods, such as diazotization, are often hampered by the production of unstable diazonium intermediates and significant waste. Furthermore, metal-catalyzed methods frequently suffer from slow kinetics, poor selectivity, and the requirement of high temperatures or inert atmospheres. The authors developed an efficient protocol utilizing Eosin Y (EY) as a low-cost organic photocatalyst and K3PO4 as a base in an aqueous medium. By employing CTAB micelles, they created a unique microenvironment that hosts both the photocatalyst and the substrates within the micellar scaffold. This spatial proximity facilitates a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with an ultrafast time constant of 0.3 ps. The methodology achieves 100% conversion and 100% selectivity for the conversion of p-anisidine to 1,2-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene within 4 hours, using a minimal photocatalyst loading of only 0.6 mol% EY. This approach significantly outperforms previous catalytic methods, demonstrating an 8.3-fold reduction in catalyst dose. The study confirms a broad substrate scope, including both electron-rich and electron-deficient amines. Mechanisms were investigated through fluorescence quenching experiments, which yielded a linear Stern-Volmer plot with a quenching rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1, confirming the non-diffusive nature of the PET. Radical trap experiments using BHT verified the formation of amine radicals via the PET mechanism. Atmospheric oxygen acts as a sacrificial oxidant, regenerating the photocatalyst through the formation of hydrogen peroxide. This work represents the first report on the aqueous phase synthesis of azo compounds using these specific micellar interfaces, providing a highly efficient and green pathway for azoaromatic synthesis.

claims.description: Micellar CAIs provide a scaffold for non-diffusive PET.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic methodology for the oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles. Azoaromatics are a significant class of functional organic molecules with wide-ranging applications in optical storage, molecular switches, and various industrial processes. Traditional synthesis methods, such as diazotization, are often hampered by the production of unstable diazonium intermediates and significant waste. Furthermore, metal-catalyzed methods frequently suffer from slow kinetics, poor selectivity, and the requirement of high temperatures or inert atmospheres. The authors developed an efficient protocol utilizing Eosin Y (EY) as a low-cost organic photocatalyst and K3PO4 as a base in an aqueous medium. By employing CTAB micelles, they created a unique microenvironment that hosts both the photocatalyst and the substrates within the micellar scaffold. This spatial proximity facilitates a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with an ultrafast time constant of 0.3 ps. The methodology achieves 100% conversion and 100% selectivity for the conversion of p-anisidine to 1,2-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene within 4 hours, using a minimal photocatalyst loading of only 0.6 mol% EY. This approach significantly outperforms previous catalytic methods, demonstrating an 8.3-fold reduction in catalyst dose. The study confirms a broad substrate scope, including both electron-rich and electron-deficient amines. Mechanisms were investigated through fluorescence quenching experiments, which yielded a linear Stern-Volmer plot with a quenching rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1, confirming the non-diffusive nature of the PET. Radical trap experiments using BHT verified the formation of amine radicals via the PET mechanism. Atmospheric oxygen acts as a sacrificial oxidant, regenerating the photocatalyst through the formation of hydrogen peroxide. This work represents the first report on the aqueous phase synthesis of azo compounds using these specific micellar interfaces, providing a highly efficient and green pathway for azoaromatic synthesis.

Research Context
Azoaromatics are an important class of organic molecules. Traditional diazotization produces unstable diazonium intermediates. Metal-catalyzed methods suffer from slow kinetics. Photocatalytic reductive coupling suffers from poor product selectivity. Designing an aqueous green catalytic route is still of great importance.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a micellar CAI facilitate efficient azoaromatic synthesis? The study hypothesizes that CAIs modulate redox potentials. Micelles are expected to host both PC and substrates. The study aims to achieve high selectivity and yields.

Methodological Details
The study examined the photophysical behavior of Eosin Y. Three surfactants were tested: CTAB, SDS, and TX-100. EY showed a bathochromic shift in CTAB and TX-100. EY exhibited fluorescence quenching in premicellar concentrations. Enhanced fluorescence (2.4-fold) occurred near the CMC. EY@CTAB was found to be stable with K3PO4. Micelles were characterized using HR-TEM measurements. Radical traps were used to validate the PET mechanism. BHT was added to the reaction mixture. GC-MS and NMR were used for characterization.

Procedures And Architectures
The conversion of p-anisidine was triggered by green light. Reaction used 0.6 mol% EY and 40 mM CTAB. K3PO4 was employed as the base. Spherical micelles formed at 40 mM CTAB. Atmospheric O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant. O2 transforms into hydrogen peroxide as a byproduct. Up-conversion measurements were used to determine time constants. The PET precedes the proton abstraction step.

Key Results
The reaction achieved 100% conversion of the substrate p-anisidine. The conversion occurred within a fast 4 h timeframe. The photocatalyst loading was limited to 0.6 mol% EY. The PET process occurred with a 0.3 ps time constant. The reaction showed an 8.3-fold reduction in catalyst dose. Conversion yields for p-chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline reached 98 and 95%. The quenching rate constant was 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CAIs provide unique electric fields to facilitate selectivity. The micellar scaffold brings PC and substrates into close proximity. The non-diffusive PET is instantaneous in nature. The PET occurs at the micellar surface. Redox potentials are modulated at the interface.

Contradictions And Limitations
SDS showed a lack of any interaction. DABCO resulted in slightly less conversion yields. p-nitroaniline showed a lack of electron transfer.

Claims
Micellar CAIs provide a scaffold for non-diffusive PET. The mechanism involves non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer. The process is ultrafast with a 0.3 ps time constant. p-nitroaniline does not show electron transfer. This opens newer opportunities for azoaromatic synthesis.

Data And Code Availability
Data is available via the ChemRxiv identifier.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Control experiments used H2O2 sensing strips. BHT was used to trap radicals.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows a bathochromic shift of 9 and 16 nm. Table 1 lists optimized reaction conditions. Figure 2b shows a linear Stern-Volmer plot. Figure 2d shows fluorescence up-conversion measurements. Figure S15 shows a characteristic HR-MS peak.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a metal-free, aqueous-phase synthesis of azoaromatics at micellar interfaces. 2. The strongest evidence is the 100% conversion achieved with 0.3 ps PET kinetics and minimal catalyst loading. 3. The future path lies in expanding the scope of azoaromatic synthesis under green, ambient conditions.

summary.title: Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS 2 , MoSe 2 , WS 2 , and WSe 2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement
summary.authors: Takahiro Nakahara (Osaka Metropolitan University); Takashi Kobayashi (Chuo University); Tetsuji Dohi (Chuo University); Takeshi Yoshimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Norifumi Fujimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Daisuke Kiriya (Osaka Metropolitan University)
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a universal postpreparation strategy to significantly enhance the photoluminescence (PL) intensity of monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), specifically addressing both sulfur-based (MoS2, WS2) and selenium-based (MoSe2, WSe2) compounds. While existing chemical treatments like p-type doping and superacids are effective for sulfur-based materials, selenium-based compounds have lacked similar universal improvements. The authors developed a method utilizing paraffin, a simple hydrocarbon with a high thermal coefficient, to remove substrate effects—a major limitation of monolayer TMDC optical properties. By melting paraffin at 80 °C and applying it to monolayers via spin coating assisted by a heat blower, the researchers induced spontaneous crystal fluctuations and gradual desorption of the monolayers from their substrates. This mechanism, driven by the large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin and the resulting mechanical stress at the interface, leads to significant PL improvements: 215-fold for MoS2, 55-fold for WS2, 50-fold for MoSe2, and 9-fold for WSe2. Raman spectroscopy confirmed the physical changes, showing a negative shift in the E' peak (indicating strain) and a positive shift in the A' peak (indicating reduced carrier concentration). Furthermore, the paraffin-coated monolayers maintain transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility, making them highly suitable for applications in flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells. The study demonstrates that the spontaneous deformation, which can range from plane fluctuations to bundled structures, effectively decouples the TMDC from the substrate, thereby enhancing the exciton-dominant emission.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a universal postpreparation strategy to significantly enhance the photoluminescence (PL) intensity of monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), specifically addressing both sulfur-based (MoS2, WS2) and selenium-based (MoSe2, WSe2) compounds. While existing chemical treatments like p-type doping and superacids are effective for sulfur-based materials, selenium-based compounds have lacked similar universal improvements. The authors developed a method utilizing paraffin, a simple hydrocarbon with a high thermal coefficient, to remove substrate effects—a major limitation of monolayer TMDC optical properties. By melting paraffin at 80 °C and applying it to monolayers via spin coating assisted by a heat blower, the researchers induced spontaneous crystal fluctuations and gradual desorption of the monolayers from their substrates. This mechanism, driven by the large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin and the resulting mechanical stress at the interface, leads to significant PL improvements: 215-fold for MoS2, 55-fold for WS2, 50-fold for MoSe2, and 9-fold for WSe2. Raman spectroscopy confirmed the physical changes, showing a negative shift in the E' peak (indicating strain) and a positive shift in the A' peak (indicating reduced carrier concentration). Furthermore, the paraffin-coated monolayers maintain transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility, making them highly suitable for applications in flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells. The study demonstrates that the spontaneous deformation, which can range from plane fluctuations to bundled structures, effectively decouples the TMDC from the substrate, thereby enhancing the exciton-dominant emission.

Research Context
Monolayer TMDCs are attracting attention due to their thin crystal structure. They are expected to have applications in optical transistors, light-emitting diodes, and solar cells. However, a drawback of the optical behavior is their poor photoluminescence (PL) intensity. This is caused by factors such as over-carrier concentrations, strains, and defects. In the case of n-type materials of MoS2 and WS2, p-type doping successfully enhances PL intensity. The p-dopant enhances exciton dominant emission by decreasing trion generation. Another reported chemical treatment method is the treatment of a superacid molecule. This can produce PL enhancement of hundreds of times. However, the above methods are not effective for the selenium-based TMDCs of MoSe2 and WSe2. In terms of applying for selenium-based compounds, oleic acid treatments succeeded. Hydrohalic acid treatment on MoSe2 also showed PL enhancement. Defect repairing in the crystalline lattice has been suggested for enhancement. The process has succeeded in MoSe2 but has not been reported for WSe2. In the case of WSe2, reported methods separate a monolayer from substrates by floating. This removes the substrate effect. There are different strategies for different TMDCs, and no universal strategy has been found.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study developed a method that enhances PL intensity in both sulfur-based and selenium-based TMDCs. The factor of PL enhancement is remarkable for all compounds. MoS2, WS2, WSe2, and MoSe2 show significant factors of enhancement. The paraffin coating was revealed to induce gradual spontaneous fluctuation and eventual desorption. The spontaneous fluctuation and desorption remove the substrate effect. This is the key factor in enhancing PL intensity in the monolayers. The method is due to applying the strain by the large thermal expansion coefficient in paraffin. The underlining science is applicable to other 2D layered materials. Paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent, making it suitable for packaging flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells.

Methodological Details
The paraffin used in this research has a melting point of 42-45 °C. For paraffin coating, the paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C in advance. Paraffin was dropped onto a sample placed on a spin coater. A heat blower was applied to keep the paraffin in a melted state. The paraffin coating process was applied to monolayer WS2, MoS2, WSe2, and MoSe2. These monolayer TMDCs showed different band gaps and emission wavelengths. The study used as-exfoliated (original) flakes for the comparison. PL enhancement was observed on the Si/SiO2 substrate. It was also observed on the monolayer WS2 on a quartz substrate. The prepared film is transparent, enabling observation under an optical microscope. PL spectra were measured through the paraffin film. A thick film of paraffin achieved by simple casting was not transparent.

Procedures And Architectures
The paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C. The paraffin was dropped onto a sample on a spin coater. A heat blower was applied during the spin coating to prevent immediate solidification. The paraffin coating was revealed to induce gradual spontaneous fluctuation and desorption. Desorption is due to stress at the interface with paraffin. Deformation to a shrunk bundled structure occurs if not surrounded by bulk flakes. The spontaneous fluctuation and desorption remove the substrate effect. The method is due to applying the strain by the large thermal expansion coefficient. The underlining science is applicable to other 2D layered materials. Paraffin coating involves the penetration of paraffin underneath each monolayer TMDC.

Key Results
MoS2 showed a remarkable increase in PL by a factor of 215. WS2 showed PL enhancement of about 36 times in Figure 1b. WS2 showed a factor of enhancement of 55-fold in Figure 2b. WSe2 showed a factor of enhancement of 9-fold. MoSe2 showed a factor of enhancement of 50-fold. The factor of enhancement is dependent on each sample. The E' peak shifted in the negative direction by about -0.72 cm-1 on average. The A' peak shifted in the positive direction by 1.03 cm-1. PL mapping confirmed PL enhancement in the whole plane. The intensity is about 2.3 times greater in the center. The peak position around the center shifts slightly by 5-10 meV.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The deformation removes the substrate effect from the TMDCs. The removal of the substrate effect is a factor for PL enhancement in selenium-based TMDCs. Paraffin induces strain via the large thermal expansion coefficient. The mechanical stress induces the fluctuation of monolayer TMDCs. Partial area desorbs from the substrate and forms a wrinkle. The area of the strain decreases the band gap, known as the funnel effect. PL enhancement is due to a combination of two effects: strain and desorption. Paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent for optoelectronic devices.

Contradictions And Limitations
A thick film of paraffin resulted in a glassy appearance. This thick film was not transparent. The factor of enhancement is dependent on each sample. Large deformation is prevented if the monolayer is surrounded by bulk flakes.

Claims
Paraffin coating is a universal strategy for PL enhancement across both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs. The method is applicable for both sulfur-based and selenium-based TMDCs. MoS2, WS2, WSe2, and MoSe2 show factors of enhancement. The factor of enhancement is dependent on each sample. The underlining science is applicable to other 2D layered materials.
The primary mechanism of PL enhancement is the removal of the substrate effect through spontaneous fluctuation and desorption. Spontaneous fluctuation and desorption remove the substrate effect. This is the key factor in enhancing PL intensity. PL enhancement is due to a combination of two effects. This engineering method is useful for straining thin 2D materials.
Paraffin-coated TMDCs are suitable for flexible and transparent optoelectronics. Paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent. Suitable for packaging flexible light-emitting displays. A thick film of paraffin... was not transparent. It extends the design of applying TMDCs as optoelectronics material.

Data And Code Availability
Data and code availability is not specified.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Bulk flakes prevent deformation of the monolayer. Thick paraffin films affect transparency.

Ethical Considerations
Ethical considerations are not reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the paraffin coating process. Figure 1b shows PL spectra for monolayer WS2. Figures 1c and 1d show optical microscopy and PL mapping. Figure 2a shows different band gaps for as-exfoliated flakes. Figure 2b shows the factors of enhancement. Figures 3a to 3d show optical microscope images of MoS2. Figure 3e shows the PL spectra for the deformed sample. Figure 3f shows the removal of the substrate effect. Figure 4 shows Raman shifts of E' and A' peaks. Figure 5 shows a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes. Figures 5c and 5d show the plausible PL enhancement mechanism.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a universal paraffin coating method for PL enhancement. 2. The strongest evidence is a 215-fold enhancement for MoS2. 3. The future path involves transparent and flexible optoelectronics.

summary.title: Atmospheric pressure continuous flow methane oxidation to methanol and acetic acid using H 2 O 2 over Au-Fe catalyst
summary.authors: Anuradha V Jagtap A †$ (CSIR-National Chemical Laboratory); Pawan Kumar A †$ (CSIR-National Chemical Laboratory); Sharad Gupta (CSIR-National Chemical Laboratory); N Abharana (Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)); S N Jha (Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)); D Bhattacharyya (Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)); T G Ajithkumar (CSIR-National Chemical Laboratory); C P Vinod (CSIR-National Chemical Laboratory)
summary.executive_summary:
This study addresses the "holy grail" challenge of the direct partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol and acetic acid under mild, atmospheric conditions. Methane, a primary constituent of natural gas and a significant contributor to global warming, is highly desirable as a feedstock for high-value chemicals. However, the activation of non-polar methane molecules is hindered by their stable tetrahedral structure, requiring harsh conditions that often lead to complete oxidation into carbon dioxide. Current catalytic technologies suffer from low product yields and a lack of commercial scalability due to high pressure and temperature requirements.

To overcome these obstacles, the authors developed a bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst supported on hydrophobic silica (HS). The catalyst was synthesized using a modified deposition precipitation method to ensure the fine dispersion of metal species. Characterization via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) revealed the presence of low-valent Fe 3-δ+ species, which are identified as critical sites for methane activation. The study highlights the synergistic effect between gold and iron, where Au nanoparticles help stabilize the active Fe sites. Furthermore, the hydrophobic nature of the silica support is crucial; it prevents the active sites from being blocked by moisture and facilitates the easy desorption of methanol, thereby preventing over-oxidation.

Experimental results demonstrate the high efficiency of the AuFeHS catalyst. In batch reactions at 20 bar pressure, the catalyst achieved a remarkable methanol yield of 1666 mmol/g(Fe+Au) with 95% selectivity. Crucially, the researchers demonstrated successful production in a continuous flow process at atmospheric pressure, achieving a methanol yield of 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au). Additionally, by co-feeding carbon monoxide (CO), the system exhibited a "selectivity switch," producing acetic acid as the primary product with an excellent yield. Isotope labeling experiments using CD4 confirmed that the oxygenates originated directly from the methane feed rather than the catalyst support. These findings suggest that bimetallic modulation and support engineering offer a viable pathway for the commercialization of methane-to-oxygenate technologies at ambient pressures.

Co-feeding CO enables a selectivity switch to acetic acid.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the "holy grail" challenge of the direct partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol and acetic acid under mild, atmospheric conditions. Methane, a primary constituent of natural gas and a significant contributor to global warming, is highly desirable as a feedstock for high-value chemicals. However, the activation of non-polar methane molecules is hindered by their stable tetrahedral structure, requiring harsh conditions that often lead to complete oxidation into carbon dioxide. Current catalytic technologies suffer from low product yields and a lack of commercial scalability due to high pressure and temperature requirements.

To overcome these obstacles, the authors developed a bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst supported on hydrophobic silica (HS). The catalyst was synthesized using a modified deposition precipitation method to ensure the fine dispersion of metal species. Characterization via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) revealed the presence of low-valent Fe 3-δ+ species, which are identified as critical sites for methane activation. The study highlights the synergistic effect between gold and iron, where Au nanoparticles help stabilize the active Fe sites. Furthermore, the hydrophobic nature of the silica support is crucial; it prevents the active sites from being blocked by moisture and facilitates the easy desorption of methanol, thereby preventing over-oxidation.

Experimental results demonstrate the high efficiency of the AuFeHS catalyst. In batch reactions at 20 bar pressure, the catalyst achieved a remarkable methanol yield of 1666 mmol/g(Fe+Au) with 95% selectivity. Crucially, the researchers demonstrated successful production in a continuous flow process at atmospheric pressure, achieving a methanol yield of 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au). Additionally, by co-feeding carbon monoxide (CO), the system exhibited a "selectivity switch," producing acetic acid as the primary product with an excellent yield. Isotope labeling experiments using CD4 confirmed that the oxygenates originated directly from the methane feed rather than the catalyst support. These findings suggest that bimetallic modulation and support engineering offer a viable pathway for the commercialization of methane-to-oxygenate technologies at ambient pressures.

Research Context
Methane is one of the constituents of natural gas. Its presence in waste landfills and manure contributes to global warming. Methane's storage and transportation are impractical as it needs high pressure. Conversion into chemicals can occur using an indirect route. Activation of non-polar methane is a major obstacle. The regular tetrahedron structure requires harsh conditions. Thermodynamics suggests activated C-H bonds readily undergo complete oxidation to CO2. Direct conversion to chemicals like methanol is an important research topic. Direct partial oxidation of methane to methanol is a holy grail problem. Current reports suffer from low product yield and harsh conditions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
It is highly desirable to construct a catalyst material that can activate methane at mild conditions. The goal is to selectively produce desired oxygenates. The researchers aim to disclose an Au-Fe catalyst supported over hydrophobic silica. The study explores oxidation of methane to methanol using H2O2 as an oxidant. They also examine how co-feeding CO produces acetic acid. The hypothesis is that this process can surpass the high-pressure batch process. It is expected that the catalyst can work at atmospheric pressure. The research aims to show an overall yield for these products.

Methodological Details
A modified deposition precipitation method was used to disperse Fe onto hydrophobic silica. The optimum Fe concentration was 0.46 wt % for the AuFeHS catalyst. The optimum Au concentration was 0.23 wt % for the AuFeHS catalyst. These concentrations were confirmed by ICP-OES. Hydrophobic silica was used to help peroxide close to the active sites. The hydrophobicity was confirmed by contact angle analysis with an angle of 118. Initial screening was performed in a batch reactor at 10 bar methane pressure. The catalysts were tested with H2O2 (15% w/v) as the oxidant. Continuous flow was conducted at atmospheric pressure for up to 7 h. The reaction temperature was optimized to 80 C. Isotope labeling with CD4 was used to confirm the alcohol source.

Procedures And Architectures
The catalyst was prepared via a modified deposition precipitation method. Metal loadings were confirmed using ICP-OES. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed the oxidation states of the elements. Fe 2p spectra identified Fe 3+ and low-valent Fe 3-δ+ species. XANES spectra revealed the single atomic nature of the Fe species. EXAFS spectra confirmed that Au is mostly in an elemental state. In-situ IR spectroscopy was employed to probe isolated metal atoms. Hydrophobicity was confirmed by contact angle analysis. The continuous flow process was executed in a fixed-bed reactor. Gas chromatography and NMR were used to quantify the products.

Key Results
In the batch process at 20 bar, the AuFeHS catalyst achieved a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au. The methanol selectivity reached 95%. In the continuous flow process at atmospheric pressure, the AuFeHS catalyst produced a methanol yield of 224 mmol/gFe+Au. Co-feeding CO resulted in a selectivity switch to acetic acid. In the batch process with CO, the acetic acid yield was 3403 µmol/gcat. The methanol yield in the continuous flow reactor reached 0.42 molmethanol kgcatalyst-1 h-1. Temperature optimization confirmed that 80 C is the best condition. Isotope labeling with CD4 confirmed the alcohol originated from the methane feed.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The unprecedented activity is attributed to the synergy between the Fe and Au. Low-valent Fe 3-δ+ species are identified as important Fe sites. Au nanoparticles provide stabilization of the Fe species. The hydrophobic support helps peroxide close to the active sites. A hydrophobic environment also facilitates easy desorption of the methanol. Acidic sites on the bimetallic catalysts are crucial for the C-H sigma complex. Au nanoparticles provide low-energy activation sites for the adsorption of CO. Bimetallic modulation is a clever way to achieve catalytic conversion of lower alkanes.

Contradictions And Limitations
Small nanoparticles of Au were observed even at low loadings. The role of Na and Lewis acid sites is beyond the scope. Current yields with molecular oxygen are so poor. The authors note that the yields with molecular oxygen are far in sight.

Claims
The AuFeHS catalyst achieves high methanol yield and selectivity at atmospheric pressure. Yield of 224 mmol/gFe+Au in continuous flow. Selectivity reached 95% in batch. Yields with molecular oxygen are so poor. Opens the doors for the activation of methane at atmospheric conditions.
Co-feeding CO enables a selectivity switch to acetic acid. Selectivity switch occurred with CO. Acetic acid yield was 3403 µmol/gcat. No contradicting evidence reported. Provides a pathway for acetic acid production.

Data And Code Availability
Data and code availability not reported.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
HS catalyst produced no product. FeHS catalyst produced 24.2 mmol/gFe of methanol. AuHS catalyst produced 12 mmol/gAu.

Ethical Considerations

Due to the massive combinatorial space of Li atoms across multiple sites (120 sites for 56 Li atoms), traditional brute-force searches are computationally impossible. The authors present a novel workflow to systematically identify and energetically rank all crystallographically predicted configurations. The methodology begins by applying a strict geometric constraint, eliminating structures with Li-Li distances below 1.7 Å. This significantly narrows the search space and defines feasible occupancy ratios. Symmetry-equivalent structures are then removed using Local Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to efficiently process millions of potential configurations. To avoid the high cost of performing DFT on every configuration, the study utilizes a Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) model. This model was trained on a representative subset of 1,235 single-point DFT calculations using the ONETEP code with PBE GGA functionals. The descriptors for the MLR model are based on the frequency occurrence of specific Li-Li interactions. The workflow successfully predicted energies with a high correlation of 0.9996 and identified that the lowest energy structures favor an 8:48 occupancy ratio. The study highlights that many previously reported structures in literature may be physically unfeasible due to overlapping atoms. Executive Summary
This study addresses a critical gap in the understanding of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), a promising solid electrolyte for Li-ion batteries, where there is currently no consensus on its ground state Li occupancy. Due to the massive combinatorial space of Li atoms across multiple sites (120 sites for 56 Li atoms), traditional brute-force searches are computationally impossible. The authors present a novel workflow to systematically identify and energetically rank all crystallographically predicted configurations. The methodology begins by applying a strict geometric constraint, eliminating structures with Li-Li distances below 1.7 Å. This significantly narrows the search space and defines feasible occupancy ratios. Symmetry-equivalent structures are then removed using Local Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to efficiently process millions of potential configurations. To avoid the high cost of performing DFT on every configuration, the study utilizes a Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) model. This model was trained on a representative subset of 1,235 single-point DFT calculations using the ONETEP code with PBE GGA functionals. The descriptors for the MLR model are based on the frequency occurrence of specific Li-Li interactions. The workflow successfully predicted energies with a high correlation of 0.9996 and identified that the lowest energy structures favor an 8:48 occupancy ratio. The study highlights that many previously reported structures in literature may be physically unfeasible due to overlapping atoms. By providing an open-access database of all generated structures, the work aims to enhance the accuracy, reproducibility, and consistency of future computational research on c-LLZO and other partially occupied crystals.

Research Context
Solid electrolytes for Li-ion batteries promise improved safety. These materials offer reduced production costs. C-LLZO is a prominent solid electrolyte candidate. However, there is no consensus of c-LLZO's Li occupancy. There is disagreement about the ground state.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to find and rank all possible Li site occupancies. The authors intend to ascertain the presence of a significant energy difference. They hope to elicit whether structural properties are indicative of a structure's energy.

Methodological Details
The search space involves 120 sites with 56 Li. A brute-force combinatorial method is unviable. The study begins by eliminating all overlapping Li atoms. A minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å was imposed. Local sensitive hashing (LSH) was used for symmetry reduction. This allowed symmetry checks on over 100 million structures. The study performed 1235 single point DFT calculations.

Procedures And Architectures
All DFT calculations were performed with the ONETEP code. Calculations used the PBE GGA exchange correlation functional. A kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV was applied. Energies were fit using a multiple linear regression (MLR) model. Structures were represented by a frequency occurrence list. Data were split into test and training sets with a 1:3 ratio.

Key Results
The model achieved a correlation of 0.9996. All structures occur within a range of 5.8 eV. 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48. Four structures were within 0.026 eV of the lowest.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The method identifies energetically favourable configurations. It highlights that many reported structures are not reflective of a real system. The workflow aims to improve accuracy and reproducibility.

Contradictions And Limitations
The ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions. It assumes a reasonable retention of ordering. Large-scale energy prediction falls outside the scope.

Claims
The workflow can accurately predict the energetic ordering of partially occupied crystal structures. The MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996. Structures occur within a range of 5.8 eV. The model does not include entropic contributions. This allows for fast evaluation of possible structures.
A large portion of previously reported c-LLZO structures are physically unfeasible. Structures involve overlapping Li atoms. These cannot exist without a Li-Li interaction.  This highlights a lack of consensus in previous literature.

Data And Code Availability
Structures are provided in a freely accessible database.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The method was validated for both 13:43 and 12:44 ratios. Geometry relaxation was tested on a small dataset of 20 structures.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the Li-Li interaction constraints. Figure 2b shows the 8:48 ratio for lowest energy structures. Figure 3 outlines the workflow for finding the 4 final structures.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a fast evaluation procedure to order all crystallographically predicted structures. 2. The strongest evidence is the 0.9996 correlation of the MLR model. 3. The future path involves improving accuracy and reproducibility in computational LLZO research.

summary.title: Self-assembling materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities
summary.authors: Noriyuki Uchida (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology); Takahiro Muraoka (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology)
summary.executive_summary: This article provides a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in the development of bioinspired supramolecular materials designed to mimic the dynamic interactions occurring at bio-interfaces, such as the extracellular matrix (ECM) and phospholipid bilayers. These bio-interfaces are fundamental to various cellular activities, including adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation. The authors emphasize that mimicking the dynamic actions of biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies—such as membrane proteins and phospholipid bilayers—is a highly effective strategy for developing biomaterials in regenerative medicine and drug delivery systems. The paper highlights several key technological breakthroughs in supramolecular chemistry and nanotechnology. First, it discusses self-assembling peptide hydrogels, specifically using RADA16 variants like A16G, which exhibit lower stiffness and thixotropic properties. These hydrogels, particularly when conjugated with N-cadherin (A16G-Ncad), were shown to significantly enhance the migration of neuroblasts in injured neonatal neocortex models, offering a novel approach for neuro-regenerative therapy. Second, the study explores the JigSAP peptide, which features a jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surface. This unique architecture allows for the efficient incorporation (93 mol%) and sustained release of growth factors like VEGF, which was demonstrated to promote angiogenesis in ischaemic stroke models. Third, the article describes the use of redox-responsive peptides, such as JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII, where point mutations of methionine residues allow for stimulus-controlled gel-sol transitions to manage cargo release kinetics. Finally, the paper addresses the stabilization of phospholipid nanosheets (bicelles) using metal-binding peptides (Chol-MBP) and Cu2+ ions. These stabilized nanosheets exhibit prolonged blood circulation compared to conventional spherical vesicles. Furthermore, the authors introduce a photo-responsive molecular machine, AzoMEx, which triggers endocytosis-like membrane fission in giant unilamellar vesicles. This technology enables the efficient encapsulation and delivery of large biomacromolecules, such as M13 phages, into multiple organs while maintaining their infectivity. Collectively, these supramolecular materials represent a powerful platform for reconstructing dynamic biomimetic interfaces to achieve unprecedented breakthroughs in biomedical applications.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This article provides a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in the development of bioinspired supramolecular materials designed to mimic the dynamic interactions occurring at bio-interfaces, such as the extracellular matrix (ECM) and phospholipid bilayers. These bio-interfaces are fundamental to various cellular activities, including adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation. The authors emphasize that mimicking the dynamic actions of biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies—such as membrane proteins and phospholipid bilayers—is a highly effective strategy for developing biomaterials in regenerative medicine and drug delivery systems. The paper highlights several key technological breakthroughs in supramolecular chemistry and nanotechnology. First, it discusses self-assembling peptide hydrogels, specifically using RADA16 variants like A16G, which exhibit lower stiffness and thixotropic properties. These hydrogels, particularly when conjugated with N-cadherin (A16G-Ncad), were shown to significantly enhance the migration of neuroblasts in injured neonatal neocortex models, offering a novel approach for neuro-regenerative therapy. Second, the study explores the JigSAP peptide, which features a jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surface. This unique architecture allows for the efficient incorporation (93 mol%) and sustained release of growth factors like VEGF, which was demonstrated to promote angiogenesis in ischaemic stroke models. Third, the article describes the use of redox-responsive peptides, such as JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII, where point mutations of methionine residues allow for stimulus-controlled gel-sol transitions to manage cargo release kinetics. Finally, the paper addresses the stabilization of phospholipid nanosheets (bicelles) using metal-binding peptides (Chol-MBP) and Cu2+ ions. These stabilized nanosheets exhibit prolonged blood circulation compared to conventional spherical vesicles. Furthermore, the authors introduce a photo-responsive molecular machine, AzoMEx, which triggers endocytosis-like membrane fission in giant unilamellar vesicles. This technology enables the efficient encapsulation and delivery of large biomacromolecules, such as M13 phages, into multiple organs while maintaining their infectivity. Collectively, these supramolecular materials represent a powerful platform for reconstructing dynamic biomimetic interfaces to achieve unprecedented breakthroughs in biomedical applications.

Research Context
Cellular activities occur through dynamic actions of biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies located at bio-interfaces. The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a complex network of proteins that regulates migration and differentiation. Phospholipid bilayers are the major component of membranes and contribute to substance transportation and signal transduction. Stimuli-responsive transformation is a notable characteristic for functionalizing phospholipid bilayers for transportation. Membrane-embedded proteins are the central molecules performing membrane-mediated signal transduction. Current research seeks to develop artificial materials that mimic these dynamic actions for regenerative medicine.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to construct artificial bio-interfaces that mimic the dynamic actions seen at bio-interfaces. The authors hypothesize that supramolecular chemistry and nanotechnology can be used to construct and functionalize bio-interfaces with dynamic natures. It is predicted that self-assembling molecules, like fibre-forming amphiphilic peptides, can create artificial extracellular matrices. The study also explores whether membrane-deforming supramolecular materials can be used for in vivo cargo delivery. The hypothesis suggests that stiffness-controlled hydrogels can promote the migration of neurons in injured brains. Additionally, it is hypothesized that jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces can improve the incorporation and release of growth factors.

Methodological Details
The study utilizes self-assembling peptide fibres as versatile supramolecular scaffolds. Peptide amphiphiles bearing fatty acid chains construct nanofibres by forming cylindrical micelles. Diphenylalanine was extensively studied as a backbone to afford supramolecular fibres. RADA16 peptides are composed of naturally occurring amino acids and form nanofibres in aqueous media. Mutants such as A8G and A16G were designed by replacing alanine with glycine. A16G-tagged N-cadherin (A16G-Ncad) was incorporated into hydrogels to facilitate neuroblast migration. Time-lapse imaging was used to observe neuroblast migration on hydrogel coatings. The study investigated neuroblasts in an injured neonatal neocortex model. JigSAP peptides (Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2) were synthesized for protein incorporation. Circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopic analysis and MD simulations were used to characterize morphology. Rheological analysis was performed to evaluate the storage and loss moduli of hydrogels. JigSAP-tagged VEGF was tested in an ischaemic stroke model produced by distal middle cerebral artery occlusion. Phospholipid nanosheets were prepared by mixing DPPC with Chol-MBP at a 5/1 ratio. Cu2+ ions were used to crosslink the Chol-MBP peptides. Blood circulation was observed via confocal laser scanning microscopy of the earlobe. AzoMEx, a diazocine-core molecular machine, was embedded in DOPC-based giant unilamellar vesicles. M13 phages were encapsulated into GUVDOPC/AzoMEx and administered via tail vein injection.

Procedures And Architectures
Peptide fibres are constructed through β-sheet-type hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interaction. The A16G mutant forms bundled nanofibres and a more robust hydrogel than RADA16. The A16G hydrogel exhibits thixotropic properties and decreased stiffness compared to RADA16. JigSAP features a jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surface from AXXXA and GXXXG motifs. The AXXXA motif prompts nanofibre formation through dovetail packing. JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII incorporate methionine residues to allow redox-responsiveness. Methionine is oxidised by reactive oxygen species to methionine sulfoxide. Chol-MBP binds two Cu2+ ions to inhibit the dissociation of phospholipid nanosheets. AzoMEx undergoes a light-triggered opening-closing motion by photoisomerization. The molecular machine changes the distance between two cationic NMe3+ moieties. Photoisomerization triggers outside-in fission of the liposomal membrane.

Key Results
A16G hydrogel demonstrated significantly lower stiffness and thixotropic properties. A16G-Ncad hydrogels significantly increased the migration rate of neuroblasts. A16G-Ncad hydrogels facilitated the migration of neuroblasts into the injured neocortex in vivo. JigSAP showed an incorporation efficiency of 93 mol% for EGFP-JigSAP. Non-tagged EGFP showed a significantly lower incorporation efficiency of only 3 mol%. EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 showed incorporation efficiencies of 66 mol% and 55 mol%, respectively. JigSAP released 21 mol% of EGFP-JigSAP after a 24-hour incubation period. The percentage of released protein from JigSAP increased to 39 mol% after 168 hours. The release of EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 stagnated after 48 hours. VEGF-JigSAP promoted angiogenesis in the injured cortex of the stroke model. DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed in the blood vessels. M13 phages retained infectivity in the spleen at [25.6 ± 13.2] × 10^9 virions/mg. M13 phages retained infectivity in the liver at [18.3 ± 3.2] × 10^9 virions/mg. M13 phages retained infectivity in the kidney at [1.3 ± 0.6] × 10^9 virions/mg. M13 phages retained infectivity in the heart at [1.1 ± 0.5] × 10^9 virions/mg. M13 phages retained infectivity in the lung at [0.5 ± 0.3] × 10^9 virions/mg. M13 phages retained infectivity in the brain at [0.2 ± 0.1] × 10^9 virions/mg.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The fibrous self-assembly of A16G and A16G-Ncad mimics the structure and dynamic function of intrinsic scaffold cells. JigSAP demonstrates wide applicability for the controlled sustained release of full-length growth factors. Stabilized bicelles serve as suitable carriers for whole-body delivery via blood administration. The AzoMEx technology enables the protection and delivery of large biomacromolecules like viruses. These supramolecular materials provide a powerful strategy for unprecedented regenerative medicines and drug delivery.

Contradictions And Limitations
Bicelles composed of mixtures of surfactants and phospholipids are essentially unstable without stabilization. summary.title: GUIDEMOL: a Python graphical user interface for molecular descriptors based on RDKit
summary.authors: Joao Aires
summary.executive_summary: GUIDEMOL is a specialized Python computer program designed to facilitate the calculation of molecular descriptors and 3D grid representations using the RDKit software. Built using the tkinter package, the application provides a comprehensive graphical user interface (GUI) aimed at scientists and students who may lack formal programming skills. The tool allows for the calculation of descriptors already implemented in RDKit, as well as more complex representations such as 3D grid voxels and electrostatic potentials (EP). The application offers a suite of user-friendly widgets, including buttons, checkbuttons, and radiobuttons, which manage calculations for descriptors like RDF, MORSE, WHIM, and AUTOCORR3D. Furthermore, it provides functionality for generating 3D molecular models through MMFF94 optimization, including preprocessing steps like metal removal and hydrogen addition. A significant feature of GUIDEMOL is its ability to compute electrostatic potentials based on Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges, as well as voxel representations based on atomic numbers or Wildman-Crippen contributions. To accommodate different workflows, the software also includes a command-line interface (CLI) specifically for grid representations. The tool's output is saved in CSV format, including molecule names and IDs. By providing an open-source solution under the BSD license, the authors offer a template that can be easily extended for other chemoinformatics procedures or different descriptor types. The project addresses a clear need in the QSPR/QSAR methodology for accessible, high-quality software that can be integrated into educational curricula and professional research pipelines alike.

Executive Summary

Built using the tkinter package, the application provides a comprehensive graphical user interface (GUI) aimed at scientists and students who may lack formal programming skills. The tool allows for the calculation of descriptors already implemented in RDKit, as well as more complex representations such as 3D grid voxels and electrostatic potentials (EP). The application offers a suite of user-friendly widgets, including buttons, checkbuttons, and radiobuttons, which manage calculations for descriptors like RDF, MORSE, WHIM, and AUTOCORR3D. Furthermore, it provides functionality for generating 3D molecular models through MMFF94 optimization, including preprocessing steps like metal removal and hydrogen addition. A significant feature of GUIDEMOL is its ability to compute electrostatic potentials based on Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges, as well as voxel representations based on atomic numbers or Wildman-Crippen contributions. To accommodate different workflows, the software also includes a command-line interface (CLI) specifically for grid representations. The tool's output is saved in CSV format, including molecule names and IDs. By providing an open-source solution under the BSD license, the authors offer a template that can be easily extended for other chemoinformatics procedures or different descriptor types. The project addresses a clear need in the QSPR/QSAR methodology for accessible, high-quality software that can be integrated into educational curricula and professional research pipelines alike.

Research Context
Molecular descriptors are fundamental to the QSPR/QSAR methodology. This methodology is widely used by scientists across diverse fields. Chemoinformatics is becoming standard in chemistry, biology, and material science curricula. There is a demand for educational software to support these subjects. Existing tools include CDK-based platforms like PaDEL and the BlueDesc calculator. Other resources include the OCHEM web service and ChemDes. RDKit is widely used in machine learning but requires programming skills. Python's tkinter enables the development of user-friendly interfaces for such tools.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to develop a minimalist interface for routine chemoinformatics tasks. It seeks to provide easy access to RDKit descriptors for non-programmers. The tool is designed to calculate well-established descriptors efficiently. It also aims to enable direct 3D representation processing for AI algorithms. The hypothesis is that a GUI/CLI hybrid will facilitate user accessibility and extensibility.

Methodological Details
The software is built using the Python programming language. The tkinter package provides the graphical user interface components. RDKit is the underlying engine for molecular processing. Users can select input and output files via dialog windows. The application logs successful processes and failures in a directory. 3D structures are optimized using the MMFF94 variant. Maximum iterations for optimization are set to 5000. Hydrogen atoms are added to the 3D models. Metal removal and fragment selection options are provided.

The GUI uses a grid geometry manager for widgets. Interactive elements include buttons, checkbuttons, radiobuttons, and entries. Users can select specific 3D descriptors like RDF and WHIM. summary.authors: Jing Fang (Peking University); Tianzuo Li (Peking University); Jiyeon Lee (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Dahye Lim (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Lianjie Xu (Peking University); Yajie Liu (Peking University); Jongcheol Seo (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Wen-Bin Zhang (Peking University)
summary.executive_summary: This study reports the first synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR). The authors achieved this by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, effectively using the protein's original fold as the entangling template. This method circumvents the need for exogenous entangling motifs typically required for topological proteins. The cat-DHFR was synthesized in E. coli using a streamlined process involving two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-inteins and circular permutation to manage steric hindrance. Comprehensive characterization using SDS-PAGE, LC-MS, and SEC confirmed the compact, concatenated structure. Far-UV and Near-UV CD spectra demonstrated that the protein retains its overall fold, though with minor secondary structure disturbances. Functional assays revealed that cat-DHFR retains significant enzymatic activity (~5 U/mg), despite a lower turnover rate (kcat) and higher substrate affinity (Km) compared to the linear control (~14 U/mg). Binding affinity tests via ITC showed that mechanical interlocking significantly influences substrate and cofactor interactions. Additionally, cat-DHFR exhibited enhanced stability against thermal and solvent stress, suggesting that topological restriction improves protein robustness. This work establishes a new framework for designing single-domain topological proteins with identical chemical compositions to their linear counterparts, preserving function while enhancing stability.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the first synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR). The authors achieved this by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, effectively using the protein's original fold as the entangling template. This method circumvents the need for exogenous entangling motifs typically required for topological proteins. The cat-DHFR was synthesized in E. coli using a streamlined process involving two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-inteins and circular permutation to manage steric hindrance. Comprehensive characterization using SDS-PAGE, LC-MS, and SEC confirmed the compact, concatenated structure. Far-UV and Near-UV CD spectra demonstrated that the protein retains its overall fold, though with minor secondary structure disturbances. Functional assays revealed that cat-DHFR retains significant enzymatic activity (~5 U/mg), despite a lower turnover rate (kcat) and higher substrate affinity (Km) compared to the linear control (~14 U/mg). Binding affinity tests via ITC showed that mechanical interlocking significantly influences substrate and cofactor interactions. Additionally, cat-DHFR exhibited enhanced stability against thermal and solvent stress, suggesting that topological restriction improves protein robustness. This work establishes a new framework for designing single-domain topological proteins with identical chemical compositions to their linear counterparts, preserving function while enhancing stability.

Research Context
Nature uses protein domains as modules to tailor existing functions. Natural protein domains are based on linear polypeptide chains. However, their backbone has quite limited topological diversity. Although scarce, topological proteins could potentially lead to enhanced protein stability. In recent years, topology has been recognized as a unique dimension for protein engineering. Current artificial topological proteins usually contain multiple domains. This complicates the study of topological effects on structure-property relationships. Ideally, a single-domain topological protein shall exhibit the most profound impact of chemical topology.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to convert a model enzyme into its single-domain catenane counterpart. The researchers investigate if rewiring the loop region can introduce artificial entanglement. They hypothesize that using the original fold as the entangling template can create a single-domain catenane. The goal is to change chemical topology without collapsing the fold.

Methodological Details
The study uses DHFR from Escherichia coli. Synthesis involves two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs. Protein expression was carried out at 16 °C for 20 h. Proteins were purified using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography. The identities of cat-DHFR and l-DHFR were confirmed by their accurate molecular weights. Far-UV CD spectra were used to evaluate secondary structure. Both IMS-MS and CID were applied for topology characterization.

Procedures And Architectures
Gaussian linking number (GLN) was used to identify splitting positions. Cleavage between residues 88 and 89 provided the split points. Ring I was circularly permutated for cyclization. The gene cassette included two DHFR segments and split-inteins. A linear DHFR control (the linear control) was designed for comparison.

Key Results
SDS-PAGE shows a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. The SEC overlay shows a larger retention volume for cat-DHFR. Far-UV CD spectra show cat-DHFR remains folded. cat-DHFR shows lower activity (~5 U/mg) than the linear control. The Km of cat-DHFR is Km approximately 5-fold higher. The KD for DHF is 173-fold for DHF higher. The KD for NADPH is 14-fold for NADPH higher. The KD for THF is increased by ~3.6-fold. The catalytic efficiency was reduced by an order.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The catenane topology reinforced by the catenane the fold. Mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal resilience. Topology has the most profound impact of chemical topology. Concatenated forms are much more compact than linear chains.

Contradictions And Limitations
No crystal structure was obtained. cat-DHFR shows lower catalytic activity than the linear control. The Km of cat-DHFR is Km approximately 5-fold higher.

Claims
cat-DHFR retains enzymatic activity and maintains its fold despite its topology. cat-DHFR remains folded. cat-DHFR retains a significant portion of the activity. cat-DHFR shows lower activity than the linear control. The Km of cat-DHFR is 5-fold higher. Reduced activity may be further restored.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Steric hindrance of split-inteins required circular permutation. Linker length impacts the yield of catenane.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a illustrates the molecular design and retrosynthetic analysis. Figure 2 displays SDS-PAGE and LC-MS characterization. Figure 4c provides the kinetic curves for enzymatic activity. Table 1 lists the Km and kcat values.

Three Takeaways
1. Synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of DHFR. 2. Topology is confirmed by LC-MS and CD spectra. 3. Activity could be improved through directed evolution.

summary.title: Non-idealities in CO2 electroreduction mechanisms revealed by automation-assisted kinetic analysis
summary.authors: Joy S Zeng (Massachusetts Institute of Technology); Vineet Padia (Massachusetts Institute of Technology); Joseph H Maalouf (Massachusetts Institute of Technology); Aditya M Limaye (Massachusetts Institute of Technology); Alexander H Liu (Massachusetts Institute of Technology); Michael A Yusov (California Institute of Technology); Ian W Hunter (Massachusetts Institute of Technology); Karthish Manthiram (California Institute of Technology)
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses a fundamental challenge in electrocatalysis: the difficulty of performing "cohesive kinetic analysis" due to the heavy data requirements of manual experimentation. While linearization methods like Tafel analysis are common, they often fail to capture complex phenomena such as surface coverage effects, mixed rate control, and electrolyte poisoning. To overcome this, the researchers developed a robotic platform capable of automating sequential electrochemical experiments. This system can accommodate up to ten cells, each featuring distinct electrodes, electrolytes, gas compositions, and voltages, facilitating the collection of high-quality kinetic data over wide reaction conditions. The researchers utilized this platform to investigate the carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) to carbon monoxide (CO) on three immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts: cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc). Their results revealed significant non-idealities that are often missed by traditional analyses. Specifically, they observed that bicarbonate and CO2 order dependencies are non-linear and fluctuate with applied potential. For CoPc and CoTPP, bicarbonate inhibition was attenuated at more reductive potentials, a behavior explained by a model involving bicarbonate poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control. In contrast, FePc exhibited amplified bicarbonate inhibition at reductive potentials, suggesting a mechanism where the most abundant reactive intermediate precedes the unoccupied site. The study also characterized CO2 order dependencies, ranging from nearly ideal first-order behavior at CoPc to surface saturation at CoTPP and complex intersecting behavior at FePc. By demonstrating that these non-idealities are prevalent across these catalysts, the work highlights the importance of accounting for poisoning and coverage effects. Furthermore, it suggests that discrepancies in existing literature may arise from measurements taken in limited ranges of operating conditions, where only a single facet of a complex kinetic landscape is observed. The automated workflow significantly improves labor efficiency and data consistency, providing a robust framework for future mechanistic inquiries in electrocatalysis. The robot also features an SQL database for data management and an online gas chromatograph for product quantification, ensuring that non-100% Faradaic efficiency reactions can be accurately monitored.

Linearization strategies yield incomplete results. These rely on highly simplifying assumptions. Cohesive kinetic analyses allow for consideration of complexities. Manual data collection is intensive yet menial.

Can a robotic platform automate electrochemical kinetic analysis? The study investigates CO2RR mechanisms at immobilized metal tetrapyrroles. It aims to reveal non-idealities like electrolyte poisoning, mixed control.

Methodological Details
The study used three catalysts: CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. CoPc was loaded at 5.98 x 10 -11 mol/cm 2. CoTPP was loaded at 5.11 x 10 -10 mol/cm 2. FePc was loaded at 8.04 x 10 -10 mol/cm 2. Electrolytes had an overall 1 mol/L ionic strength.

Trends are explained by bicarbonate poisoning and mixed control. CoPc/CoTPP poisoning is attenuated as the local equilibrium shifts. FePc trends involve a species prior to the unoccupied site. On-cycle poisoning can explain observed trends via divergent flux.

Average FE closure was only 60% due to oxygen reduction. CoPc rates were ten times lower than literature. Flow configuration can have unexpected influence.

Automation enables faster, more facile rate data collection. The workflow was more time-and labor-efficient. It enables faster and more facile rate data collection. Automated kinetic analysis would ideally be expensive. This could further standardize and accelerate the workflow.

CoPc rates were ten times lower than literature.

Figure 1A shows the robot design. Figure 2A-C shows bicarbonate dependence. Figure 3A-C shows CO2 dependence. Figure S5 shows FE closure. Figure S7 shows CoPc rates.

1. Robotic automation facilitates cohesive kinetic analysis. 2. Non-idealities like poisoning and coverage are prevalent. 3. Future work may include membranes and automated mechanism enumeration.

summary.authors: B Mallada (Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic); M Ondráček (Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic); M Lamanec (Czech Academy of Sciences); A Gallardo (Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic); A Jiménez-Martín (Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic); B De La Torre; P Hobza (Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic); P Jelínek (Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic)

summary.executive_summary: This study provides the first direct experimental visualization of a π-hole—a theoretically predicted π-electron-deficient cavity—in a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). While π-holes have been predicted via quantum calculations and inferred indirectly from experimental data, direct real-space observation had been lacking. The authors demonstrate that the presence of π-holes, specifically in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbons like 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An), significantly alters submolecular charge distribution and affects physical-chemical properties. By comparing FCl-An with anthracene (An), the study reveals that halogen substituents reverse the electron population of the π-bond system, creating an electron-deficient cavity. Using a CO-functionalized tip and a qPlus sensor on an Au(111) surface, the researchers mapped the local contact potential difference (LCPD) with atomic resolution, identifying a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the FCl-An molecule that matches theoretical electrostatic potential calculations. Furthermore, the study investigates the impact of π-holes on molecule-surface interactions. They found that the π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule, which suppresses the induction of electron density at the molecule/metal interface. This leads to weakened electrostatic interactions and a larger adsorption height for FCl-An (360 pm) compared to An (330 pm). The research validates KPFM as a powerful tool for observing internal charge distributions and demonstrates how these submolecular features dictate the stabilization of non-covalent interactions and adsorption behaviors.
