judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study provides the first direct experimental visualization of a π-hole—a theoretically predicted π-electron-deficient cavity—in a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). While π-holes have been predicted via quantum calculations and inferred indirectly from experimental data, direct real-space observation had been lacking. The authors demonstrate that the presence of π-holes, specifically in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbons like 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An), significantly alters submolecular charge distribution and affects physical-chemical properties. By comparing FCl-An with anthracene (An), the study reveals that halogen substituents reverse the electron population of the π-bond system, creating an electron-deficient cavity. Using a CO-functionalized tip and a qPlus sensor on an Au(111) surface, the researchers mapped the local contact potential difference (LCPD) with atomic resolution, identifying a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the FCl-An molecule that matches theoretical electrostatic potential calculations. Furthermore, the study investigates the impact of π-holes on molecule-surface interactions. They found that the π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule, which suppresses the induction of electron density at the molecule/metal interface. This leads to weakened electrostatic interactions and a larger adsorption height for FCl-An (360 pm) compared to An (330 pm). The research validates KPFM as a powerful tool for observing internal charge distributions and demonstrates how these submolecular features dictate the stabilization of non-covalent interactions and adsorption behaviors.

Research Context
Non-covalent interactions are crucial in chemical and biological processes. These interactions are determined by dispersion and electrostatic forces. Precise knowledge of charge distribution is a fundamental requirement. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) have electron-rich delocalized π-bonds. Substituting peripheral hydrogens with electronegative substituents reverses electron population. This creates an electron-deficient cavity called a π-hole. π-holes significantly affect noncovalent intermolecular interactions. Intermolecular stacking interactions can be strongly affected by π-holes. The existence of π-hole has only been proven indirectly. Direct experimental observation that would clearly prove existence has been lacking.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to resolve the π-hole on a single molecule. Kelvin probe force microscopy is presented as an ideal imaging tool. The goal is to confirm the theoretical prediction of its existence. The research also explores the importance of π-holes in adsorption processes.

Methodological Details
The study investigated FCl-An and An molecules. Molecules were grown on an atomically clean Au(111) surface. The surface was kept at room temperature in ultrahigh vacuum. Scanning tunnelling microscopy revealed large-scale ordered molecular islands. Noncontact atomic force microscopy used a functionalized carbon monoxide tip. Kelvin probe force microscopy was employed to map the charge distribution. KPFM was used to resolve submolecular contrast. Measurements were conducted at a temperature of 4.2 K. Data was collected on a 64 x 80 pixels grid. The grid size was 3 nm x 5 nm.

Procedures And Architectures
Molecules were sublimated with two Knudsen cells simultaneously. KPFM maps were obtained by fitting a parabolic expression. Frequency shift vs bias spectroscopies were collected at all points. The data did not exhibit significant distortion from parabolic behaviour. Tip-sample height was chosen near Δf minima to avoid tip relaxation. DFT calculations were performed using the FHI-AIMS code. The PBE version of the GGA was used for exchange-correlation. The Au(111) slab consisted of 4 atomic layers. Van der Waals corrections were applied using the Tkatchenko-Scheffler method. KPFM images were simulated using the Probe Particle (PP) model. Electrostatic potential and electrical polarizability were used to generate KPFM maps.

Key Results
The study confirms the existence of the π-hole in FCl-An. KPFM images reproduced the characteristic bow-tie pattern in FCl-An. The bow-tie pattern matches the electrostatic potential for free-standing molecules. Adsorption height of FCl-An was 360 pm. Adsorption height of An was 330 pm. The difference in adsorption height was 30 pm. An molecules show more significant induced electron density. Induction energy is larger for An than for FCl-An.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule. This inhibits the induction of charge density at the interface. Weakened induced electrostatic interactions result in larger adsorption heights. The study demonstrates the potential of scanning microscopy for internal charge distribution. Submolecular charge distribution fundamentally affects chemical and physical properties.

Contradictions And Limitations
Tip relaxations can noticeably influence the KPFM signal. Relaxation causes a deviation in the LCPD signal. AFM images do not provide direct evidence of the π-hole.

Claims
KPFM provides direct real-space visualization of the π-hole. The study confirms the existence of the π-hole. KPFM images reproduced the characteristic bow-tie pattern. AFM images do not provide direct evidence. The study shows the potential of scanning microscopy.
The π-hole influences the adsorption height on metallic surfaces. FCl-An had an adsorption height of 360 pm. An had an adsorption height of 330 pm. The difference in height was 30 pm.  π-hole influences the electrostatic interaction.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 2a shows molecular self-assembly on Au(111). Figure 3a displays the electrostatic potential for FCl-An. Figure 4a shows Δf-z spectroscopy for both molecules. Figure 4b and 4c show calculated induced electron density.

Three Takeaways
1. KPFM successfully visualized the π-hole in FCl-An. 2. The π-hole leads to a 30 pm increase in adsorption height. 3. Submolecular charge distribution dictates molecule-surface interactions.

summary.title: Machine learning force field ranking of candidate solid electrolyte interphase structures in Li-ion batteries
summary.authors: James M Stevenson; Garvit Agarwal; Leif D Jacobson
summary.field_subfield: Computational Materials Science; Machine Learning; Battery Materials
summary.executive_summary: The Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) is a critical yet poorly understood material layer formed in lithium-ion batteries, consisting of complex organic and inorganic components that protect electrodes from side reactions. Current computational methods, such as pure density functionals, often underestimate reaction barriers, while hybrid functionals struggle with metal systems and suffer from poor computational scaling for periodic systems. This work addresses these limitations by developing a Machine Learning Force Field (MLFF) based on a Quantized Recurrent Neural Network (QRNN) architecture. By employing multitask learning, the model is trained simultaneously on pure and hybrid DFT labels, allowing it to capture a broad range of chemical behaviors. The study utilizes a sophisticated sampling procedure, incorporating active learning, Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR), and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) methods to generate and refine geometries. The training set was further augmented with the SPICE dataset of general organic chemistry to shape the model's latent space. Using the Schrodinger "SEI Simulator," the authors generated initial candidate structures from a 1M LiPF6 in EC solution and performed NPT MD annealing at 400 K and 1000 atm. The study then ranks these candidates by mean potential energy. Validation was conducted against known surface reaction energy barriers, as experimental properties like density and diffusivity are currently unavailable for these specific compositions. The results provide the first set of ranked SEI candidate structures and reveal that P-F and Li-O bonds correlate with higher stability, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with lower stability. This research demonstrates that MLFFs can successfully model the most complex redox reactive systems, providing a foundation for future optimization of SEI chemistry through the comparison of diverse electrolyte formulations.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) is a critical yet poorly understood material layer formed in lithium-ion batteries, consisting of complex organic and inorganic components that protect electrodes from side reactions. Current computational methods, such as pure density functionals, often underestimate reaction barriers, while hybrid functionals struggle with metal systems and suffer from poor computational scaling for periodic systems. This work addresses these limitations by developing a Machine Learning Force Field (MLFF) based on a Quantized Recurrent Neural Network (QRNN) architecture. By employing multitask learning, the model is trained simultaneously on pure and hybrid DFT labels, allowing it to capture a broad range of chemical behaviors. The study utilizes a sophisticated sampling procedure, incorporating active learning, Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR), and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) methods to generate and refine geometries. The training set was further augmented with the SPICE dataset of general organic chemistry to shape the model's latent space. Using the Schrodinger "SEI Simulator," the authors generated initial candidate structures from a 1M LiPF6 in EC solution and performed NPT MD annealing at 400 K and 1000 atm. The study then ranks these candidates by mean potential energy. Validation was conducted against known surface reaction energy barriers, as experimental properties like density and diffusivity are currently unavailable for these specific compositions. The results provide the first set of ranked SEI candidate structures and reveal that P-F and Li-O bonds correlate with higher stability, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with lower stability. This research demonstrates that MLFFs can successfully model the most complex redox reactive systems, providing a foundation for future optimization of SEI chemistry through the comparison of diverse electrolyte formulations.

Research Context
The SEI is a vital but poorly-understood class of materials. It protects electrode materials from unwanted side reactions. Key questions about SEIs remain unanswered. Simulating such systems is difficult as no existing method is fully applicable to the task. Existing pure density functionals tend to badly underestimate reaction barriers. Even the fastest of the useful density functional theory (DFT) methods are much too slow. Hybrid functionals such as wB97X struggle with metals. They also have very poor computational scaling for periodic systems. MLFFs promise to allow atomistic simulation with wide applicability. They provide the fast sampling of classical force fields. Traditional force fields are very difficult to fit for complex systems. Multitask learning lets us train MLFFs to both labels.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The primary research question asks whether multitask training with a QRNN model can simulate complex reactions characteristic of an SEI. We hypothesized that training on both pure and hybrid DFT labels simultaneously would allow the model to learn a robust chemical representation. Specifically, we predicted that multitask learning would permit the ranking of candidate SEI structures. We hypothesized that using enhanced reaction sampling like AFIR and NEB on the QRNN potential energy surface would yield high-quality geometries. We aim to produce the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy. This work is hoped to be the start of a more quantitative understanding of battery interphases. We hypothesize that this will be an impetus to development of machine learning models for battery materials. We also predict that the multitask abilities of QRNN will allow the model to handle disparate data from general organic chemistry without significant loss in accuracy. We further hypothesize that using the best available model to sample new geometries will allow for the study of hypotheses related to SEI composition.

Methodological Details
We selected wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD as our reference level of theory for non-periodic systems. PBE-D3 in a plane wave basis was used for periodic systems. A random subset of non-periodic systems was labeled with PBE-D3 to improve information exchange. We tested reference atomic partial charges and found GFN1-xTB to be the most suitable for generating charge labels. We used multiple rounds of active learning for data generation to increase accuracy. Data generation included using enhanced reaction sampling using AFIR and NEB on the QRNN potential energy surface. We used the multitask abilities of QRNN to add the SPICE dataset. The SPICE subset consists of elements H, Li, C, O, F, and P. We added GFN1-xTB atomic partial charge labels to this data. To increase model capacity, we doubled the width of the hidden layers in our neural networks. We used a higher-priority dataset composed only of the periodic and cluster surface reaction subset. We applied decoupled weight norms with the norms not included in the optimizer. We used the Adamax optimizer with a learning rate of 2e-3. For our final model, we used a weight decay of 1e-3. Each system starts with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6-. This gives a 1 M solution with 7416 total atoms. We defined four sets of candidates with different levels of added Li. Levels were 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions per box. We used only 1% of the data as our validation set. Our batch size was 64.

Procedures And Architectures
We utilized a QRNN model for sampling and structure building. We used multiple rounds of active learning for data generation. We used enhanced reaction sampling using AFIR and NEB. Initial SEI candidate structures were generated using the SEI Simulator. The SEI Simulator uses OPLS4 molecular dynamics with reaction templates. We annealed the produced geometries using our reactive QRNN model with NPT MD at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each. We then ranked each set of candidates by calculating the mean potential energy. Ranking was performed over an MD trajectory of 20 ps at 300 K and 1 atm. For periodic systems, we performed DFT using Quantum Espresso. We also performed gas-phase wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD DFT using Psi4. The plane wave energy cutoff was 40 Ry. The Brillouin zone integration used a 3x3x3 k-point mesh for bulk supercells. We used lithium surfaces with 54 atoms for NEB periodic systems. For non-periodic systems, we extracted clusters within 3-6 Angstroms.

Key Results
We validated our model against the best available calculations for surface reaction energy barriers. We refer to the lowest-energy SEI candidate structure out of the most lithiated subgroup (33 added Li atoms) as our 'best' candidate. We performed statistical analysis of the bonding in SEI candidate structures. We recalculated the Lewis structure of the entire system. We tabulated the counts of various bond types versus the total system energy. The results show that P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures. Conversely, C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable ones. We observed no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE when adding SPICE data. We observed only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. This implies that the increased scope of data did not impose a heavy cost on model capacity.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Multitask training allows a machine learning force field to model the complex reactions characteristic of an SEI. This is the most complex redox reactive system simulated using an MLFF. The latent space of these MLFF models contains unused capacity. This capacity can be applied to broadening chemical applicability. We recommend using a supplemental dataset of general organic chemistry to shape the latent space.

Contradictions And Limitations
We cannot compare the density, diffusivity, viscosity, or elastic modulus against experimental values. Such experiments do not exist for any SEI composition. The scope is still small compared to what is required. There is no unique way to determine the boundaries of each cluster. We do not regard our current model as final.

Claims
Multitask training with a QRNN model allows an MLFF to model the complex reactions characteristic of an SEI. The model captured complex redox reactions. It is the most complex redox system simulated.  Allows for atomistic simulation with DFT accuracy.
The latent space of these MLFF models contains unused capacity that can be applied to broadening chemical applicability. Adding SPICE data showed no increase in PBE-head RMSE. There was only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE.  Allows for broadening chemical applicability.
P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable SEI structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable ones. P-F and Li-O bonds are more stable. C-O and Li-F bonds are less stable.  Provides a basis for SEI optimization.

Data And Code Availability
The candidate structures, energies, and scripts are available at https://figshare.com/s/e842ae88023902700e12.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The model showed no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE when adding SPICE data. The model showed only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. We found little effect of early stopping validation for this dataset. Higher weight decay was helpful but reduced reaction barriers, leading to a 1e-3 weight decay for the final model.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 4 shows bond counts with respect to total system energy for the most lithiated SEI candidate set. Table 1 validates the model against surface reaction energy barriers.

Three Takeaways
1. Multitask training with a QRNN model allows for the simulation of complex redox reactive SEI systems. 2. The model was validated against surface reaction energy barriers, showing its capability to rank candidate structures. 3. Future work will involve comparing multiple electrolyte formulations to optimize SEI chemistry.

summary.title: Biological activity of Ajuga iva extracts against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis
summary.authors: Leena Taha-Salaime (University of Haifa); Galina Lebedev (The Volcani Center); Jackline Abo-Nassar (Newe Ya'ar Research Center); Sally Marzouk (Newe Ya'ar Research Center); Moshe Inbar (University of Haifa); Murad Ghanim (The Volcani Center); Radi Aly (Newe Ya'ar Research Center)
summary.executive_summary: This study evaluates the efficacy of Ajuga iva plant extracts as a green alternative for controlling the African cotton leafworm (Spodoptera littoralis), a major pest affecting various crops including cotton, maize, and rice. The research focuses on the biological activity of phytoecdysteroids and clerodane diterpenes found in the Ajuga genus, which act as analogs to insect steroid hormones regulating molting and metamorphosis. The study demonstrates that crude extracts from Ajuga iva leaves significantly impair the development and survival of S. littoralis larvae in a dose-dependent manner. Specifically, first instar larvae showed mortality rates of 25%, 65%, and 85% when exposed to 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl concentrations of the extract, respectively. Third instar larvae experienced a significant reduction in Relative Growth Rate (RGR) and Larval Weight Gain (LWG), with high concentrations leading to zero survival within 8 to 10 days. The study also validated that a fractionated mixture of three purified phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) from the extract produced similar inhibitory effects on growth and survival. Histological examinations using DAPI and phalloidin staining revealed that the extract caused significant damage to the larval gut, including smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei and a reduction in actin filament organization. These morphological changes were associated with histolysis and apoptosis, suggesting that the extract's toxicity stems from disruptions in internal hormonal balances and direct tissue damage. The findings conclude that Ajuga iva components are promising candidates for Integrated Pest Management (IPM) programs, offering a potential way to reduce pesticide reliance while protecting human health and the environment.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study evaluates the efficacy of Ajuga iva plant extracts as a green alternative for controlling the African cotton leafworm (Spodoptera littoralis), a major pest affecting various crops including cotton, maize, and rice. The research focuses on the biological activity of phytoecdysteroids and clerodane diterpenes found in the Ajuga genus, which act as analogs to insect steroid hormones regulating molting and metamorphosis. The study demonstrates that crude extracts from Ajuga iva leaves significantly impair the development and survival of S. littoralis larvae in a dose-dependent manner. Specifically, first instar larvae showed mortality rates of 25%, 65%, and 85% when exposed to 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl concentrations of the extract, respectively. Third instar larvae experienced a significant reduction in Relative Growth Rate (RGR) and Larval Weight Gain (LWG), with high concentrations leading to zero survival within 8 to 10 days. The study also validated that a fractionated mixture of three purified phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) from the extract produced similar inhibitory effects on growth and survival. Histological examinations using DAPI and phalloidin staining revealed that the extract caused significant damage to the larval gut, including smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei and a reduction in actin filament organization. These morphological changes were associated with histolysis and apoptosis, suggesting that the extract's toxicity stems from disruptions in internal hormonal balances and direct tissue damage. The findings conclude that Ajuga iva components are promising candidates for Integrated Pest Management (IPM) programs, offering a potential way to reduce pesticide reliance while protecting human health and the environment.

Research Context
The African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis is a major agricultural pest. Current insect control relies heavily on synthetic insecticides. Synthetic pesticides pose risks to human health and the environment. Organic insecticides derived from plants like steroids show high toxicity. Phytoecdysteroids are plant-produced analogs of insect molting hormones. These compounds may cause abnormal development and death. Previous studies on Ajuga species showed inhibition of ecdysis and larval death. Ajuga iva contains three specific phytoecdysteroids and clerodane diterpenes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to determine if Ajuga iva crude extract affects S. littoralis larvae. It compares the effects of isolated phytoecdysteroids against commercial standards. It investigates if phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larval gut. The hypothesis is that A. iva crude extract containing three phytoecdysteroids will be a promising pest-control agent. The goal is to evaluate the efficiency of extracts at reducing larval damage.

Methodological Details
The study used leaf and stem powder from A. iva. Powder was homogenized and soaked in 100% MeOH. Concentrations of 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl were tested. Larvae were reared on castor bean leaves. First instar larvae were exposed for 3 days. Third instar larvae were exposed for 4 to 8 days. Data for 11 replicates (10 larvae each) were collected. Relative Growth Rate was calculated using weights at two time points. Larval survival was analyzed using a Friedman test. Gut morphology was examined using DAPI and phalloidin staining.

Procedures And Architectures
Crude extracts were prepared by homogenization and vacuum concentration. LC-TOF-MS was used to identify phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes. TLC was used to separate components into well-defined spots. Castor bean leaves were smeared with extract and Tween 20. Larvae were kept in a climate-controlled room at 25 °C. Gut tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the socioeconomic and geographic inequalities inherent in the 'Golden Open Access' (GOA) publishing model within the natural sciences. By analyzing metadata from 237 open-access journals, the author demonstrates a significant positive correlation between Article Processing Charges (APC) and journal metrics such as Impact Factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), and overall citability. Furthermore, the study finds that journals from developed countries tend to possess higher costs and higher impact metrics. The author argues that these trends create a structural barrier for researchers from developing countries and independent scholars who lack institutional funding. Because high-impact journals are often the primary outlets for career advancement and research exposure, the high cost of publication effectively gatekeeps scientific credibility and visibility. The paper highlights how current funding assistance models, like Research4Life, can be inadvertently restricted by the inclusion of international collaborators from developed nations. Ultimately, the research suggests that the current GOA framework may prioritize publisher profit and institutional privilege over the equitable distribution of scientific visibility, potentially sidelining critical research from the global south and independent researchers.

Research Context
Increased availability of journal articles has removed constraints for researchers. Many high-impact journals have transitioned to mandatory Golden Open Access. The cost associated with publishing in open-access journals makes this system problematic. Researchers from institutions in developing countries are still paying the full price. High-impact journals generate exposure through increased citations. Prices of high-impact journals become problematic for researchers without available funding.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study analyzes metadata of open-access journals. It determines links between publication costs, impact factor, eigen factor, and citability. The author discusses the implications of inequality in the open-access framework.

Methodological Details
Data was acquired from the Directory of Open Access Journals. The initial dataset contained n = 14275 records. R statistical software was used for all data analyses. The scholar package generated impact factors using journal name strings. The quantmod package converted all currencies to USD. A subset of journals (n = 1047) was queried using biological science keywords. Journals with an IF >40 were excluded from the analysis. The final analyses were performed on a vetted dataset of n = 237 journals. Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to analyze potential correlation.

Procedures And Architectures
Keywords like ecology and conservation were used to subset the data. APC was examined in relation to citability, IF, and Eigen Factor. The country of publisher was examined against cost and impact metrics. Data was cleaned using the dplyr and reshape2 packages. Visualizations were generated using the ggplot2 package. Correlation analyses were performed using functions from the ggpubr package.

Key Results
A linear trend was found between IF, EF, and citability in relation to APC. The mean APC for the 237 journals was $1344.27 USD. The mean IF was 2.855 and the mean EF was 0.017. The mean citability was 5925.92. APC was significantly positively correlated with IF (r(237) = 0.391, p < .001). APC showed a highly significant positive correlation with EF (r(237) = 0.303, p < .001). APC was highly significantly positively correlated with citability (r(237) = 0.323, p < .001).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Increasing publishing costs correlate with higher impact and citations. Publishers from developed countries are more likely to have higher metrics. Research from developing countries is less likely to gain exposure. Expensive APCs in prestigious journals are not linked to reliability. The system may prioritize publisher profit over scientific integrity. Higher ranking institutions have more access to expensive journals.

Contradictions And Limitations
Eligibility for financial assistance becomes void if a developed country collaborator is named. Researchers without institutional affiliation have even more narrow options. Personal experience shows rejection from funding assistance for important studies.

Claims
Higher APC correlates with higher journal metrics like Impact Factor and citability. APC was found to be significantly positively correlated with IF APC was highly significantly positively correlated with citability  research published in journals from developing countries is less likely to gain exposure
Journal prestige and cost are not measures of scientific reliability. Expensive APC in prestigious journals are not linked to reliability The impact factor of prestigious journals also creates a false perception of reliability  promoting the false ideology that prestige and costliness are the equivalent of reliable science

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows that journal publishers from developed countries were more likely to have higher APC, IF, EF, and citability.

Three Takeaways
1. Inequality in GOA publishing is linked to high APCs and geographic location. 2. APC correlates positively with IF, EF, and citability across 237 journals. 3. Address systemic issues to create a more inclusive environment for global research.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The study addresses the limitations of standard RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis, which often fails to detect 41-53% of positive cases due to low viral loads or RNA degradation. The authors developed a multiplex PCR-based detection method using two pools of 172 primer pairs (343 total) to target the entire viral genome. Mathematical modeling predicted a detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability using both pools. Experimental validation using spiked plasmids confirmed that the method could detect 1.1 copies of the virus with a 56% probability, suggesting higher efficiency than modeled. The assay was tested on 13 clinical nasopharyngeal specimens with viral loads ranging from 8 to 675,885 copies/uL, achieving 95-99% genome coverage at 100X depth. The study also highlights the identification of mutations like D614G and cautions against interpreting intra-host mutations in low-copy/low-depth samples. Furthermore, a multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method was developed using random hexamer-adapters and background removal, achieving >96% coverage of the S and N genes with a modest sequencing depth of approximately 0.6 million reads. This approach offers high specificity, showing 0% alignment to other human coronaviruses. The findings provide a robust tool for both sensitive diagnosis and evolutionary surveillance.

Research Context
RT-PCR is considered the gold standard for diagnosing SARS-CoV-2 infections. RT-PCR has been reported to detect 4-8 copies of virus. However, only about 47-59% of the true positive cases were identified by RT-PCR. 75% of RT-PCR negative results were actually later found to be positive. Heat inactivation of clinical samples causes loss of viral particles. Surveillance of SARS-CoV-2's evolution and for the containment of community spread requires NGS. The multiplex PCR strategy has significantly higher sensitivity than RT-PCR.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The primary research question investigates whether a multiplex PCR strategy targeting hundreds of regions can significantly improve detection sensitivity compared to standard RT-PCR. The authors established a mathematical model to estimate the limit of detection (LOD) for SARS-CoV-2 to identify opportunities for further improvement. They found that RT-PCR assays could only detect 4.8 copies of SARS-CoV-2 at 95% probability. The study also aimed to determine if the predicted probability of RT-PCR assays to detect one copy of SARS-CoV-2 is only 26%. The hypothesis is that by simultaneously amplifying multiple regions of the viral genome in a multiplex PCR reaction, they can increase the frequency of occurrence. They hypothesized that this multiplex PCR strategy could potentially detect nucleotide fragments resulting from degraded viral genomes. The authors assumed that an efficiency of 6% in amplifying the single-strand of a cDNA molecule would allow for a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. They also hypothesized that the SARS-CoV-2 panel can detect 1.15 copies of the virus at 95% probability. They predicted that using both pools of primers would provide full coverage of the entire viral genome. They predicted that using both pools in detection would lead to a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability.

Methodological Details
The workflow was designed so that the multiplex PCR products are further amplified in a secondary PCR. The PCR products were first analyzed by electrophoresis to visualize potential positives. Two plasmids, containing the full sequence of the S and N genes of SARS-CoV-2, respectively, were used to validate our multiplex PCR method. A total of 28 targets are expected to be amplified within our 172-amplicon panel. To simulate the use of real clinical samples, these two plasmids were spiked into cDNA generated from human total RNA. The copy number of each plasmid was precisely determined by droplet-based digital PCR (ddPCR) with a QX200 system from Bio-Rad. The two plasmids were diluted from approximately 9,000 copies to below one copy, and were amplified in multiplex PCR reactions. The library peaks of expected sizes were obtained from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids. The above two pools of primers were used to amplify the full SARS-CoV-2 genomes from a total of 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens. These specimens were previously diagnosed to be SARS-CoV-2 positive by using RT-PCR. The viral load was found to be from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL. These 13 viral genomes were successfully amplified and subsequently sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq. To confirm SARS-CoV-2 libraries could be sequenced at about 1,000 reads per amplicon, we sub-sampled the data of 5 genomes.

Procedures And Architectures
We designed a panel of 172 pairs of multiplex PCR primers in order to increase the sensitivity of detecting SARS-CoV-2. The average amplicon length is 99bp. The amplicons span across the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome with an average 76bp gap (76±10bp) between adjacent amplicons. We also designed a second pool of 171 multiplex PCR primer pairs. The target regions of these primer pairs overlap with the gaps between target regions of the previous pool of 172 primer pairs. Together, these two overlapping pools of primers provide full coverage of the entire viral genome. In this method, random hexamer-adapters were used to amplify DNA or cDNA targets in a multiplex PCR reaction. The large amounts of non-specific amplification products were removed by using Paragon Genomics' background removal reagent. For RNA samples, Paragon Genomics' reverse transcription reagents were used to convert RNA into cDNA. The results were analyzed by visualizing potential positives via electrophoresis and then interrogating the generated NGS sequencing library.

Key Results
The theoretical calculation gives a 66% probability to sample 1.1 copies. In practice, we experimentally observed a significantly higher 56% probability to detect 1.1 copies. While about 95% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus. 98-99% of the genomes were covered at 100X for 22 to 675,885 copies of virus at an average sequencing depth of 5,000 reads per amplicon. At least 93% of the genome was covered at 100X with 150,000 total reads. 86% of the genome was covered at 100X with 100,000 total reads. Even at 50,000 total reads per library, at least 58% of the genome was covered at 100X. 16% of the recovered bases, or 13% of the recovered reads, were within the viral N and S genes. 80% of SARS-CoV-2 and 78% of mitochondrial targets were covered. The depth of the recovered bases was within a 10-fold range on average. We further optimized this method so that 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome was recovered. 0% of the obtained sequencing reads from each of the 13 samples were aligned to the genome sequence of any of the above viral species.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
By amplifying hundreds of targets simultaneously, our multiplex PCR method is more sensitive than RT-PCR. Multiplex PCR... tolerates the presence of mutations in SARS-CoV-2. High-resolution electrophoresis is required to resolve the length of the amplification products in order to differentiate the target amplicons from the primer-dimers. For accurate sequencing and phylogenetic studies, a high-depth sequencing in the range of 300K reads per sample... [is] deemed necessary. The high specificity argues strongly that this panel could be further expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses. Metagenomic method is a powerful technology that can theoretically detect any sequences in the specimens. The coverage was superior given the recommended 50% threshold of coverage for drafting a genome.

Contradictions And Limitations
The predicted probability of RT-PCR assays to detect one copy of SARS-CoV-2 is only 26%. The yield of the libraries started to saturate when the copy number reached 1,700. The occurrence of such noise may be exacerbated by low viral copy inputs in the multiplex PCR, or low read depth per amplicon in sequencing. Some true intra-host mutations with %AF < 20% might be missed. Intra-host mutations might still be contaminated with noise originating from PCR amplification. Therefore, copy number and sequencing depth should be cautiously considered when a mutation is found to have low %AF.

Claims
The multiplex PCR method provides higher sensitivity and coverage than traditional RT-PCR. The multiplex PCR method provides a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies. RT-PCR has a reported detection limit of 4.8 copies. This allows for reliable identification even at very low viral loads.
A multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method achieves high coverage of SARS-CoV-2 with modest sequencing depth. The method achieved 96% coverage of the SARS-CoV-2 genome. Metagenomic methods usually require very high sequencing depth. This approach enables the economical discovery of novel pathogens.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the mathematical model for RT-PCR detection limits. Figure 1B illustrates the design of the 172-amplicon multiplex PCR panel. Figure 1C displays the estimated detection limit of the SARS-CoV-2 panel. Figure 1D outlines the workflow from multiplex PCR to secondary PCR. Figure 2A shows the library peaks obtained from spiked plasmids. Figure 2B demonstrates the quantification of peaks across a wide dynamic range. Figure 2C shows the experimental probability to detect 1.1 copies. Figure 2D displays the sequencing read depth and distribution of the plasmids. Figure 2E illustrates the percentage of amplicons recovered at different copy numbers. Figure 3A shows genome coverage at different viral copy numbers. Figure 3B demonstrates coverage at different total reads per library. Figure 3C shows the uniformity of the number of amplicons. Figure 3D displays the log10 distance of amplicons to the mean. Figure 3E shows the clustering of mutations across the 13 specimens. Figure 4A shows the percentage of recovered bases in the metagenomic method. Figure 4B displays the percentage of SARS-CoV-2 and mitochondrial targets covered. Figure 4C shows the base coverage of viral vs human targets. Figure 4D shows the preferential amplification of human exonic regions. Figure 4E shows the gaps in large repetitive human regions. Figure 4F shows the shorter gaps in SARS-CoV-2 and mitochondrial regions. Figure 4G shows the optimized recovery of the SARS-CoV-2 genome.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a multiplex PCR method with a predicted detection limit of 0.29 copies. 2. The strongest evidence is the 96% recovery of the SARS-CoV-2 genome using modest sequencing depth. 3. The future path involves expanding the panel for simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses.

summary.title: Translational accuracy of a tethered ribosome
summary.authors: Celine Fabret (CNRS); Olivier Namy (CNRS)
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the translational properties and accuracy of Ribo-T, a synthetic ribosome in Escherichia coli where the two subunits (30S and 50S) are covalently linked into a single entity. While Ribo-T has been previously shown to be functional and capable of sustaining cell growth, it exhibits a slow-growth phenotype with a protein synthesis rate of 50% compared to wild-type (WT) ribosomes. This research specifically evaluates how the tethered architecture affects three critical aspects of translation: programmed frameshifting, translation initiation, and stop codon termination. The authors used the pCL99 dual reporter system and various recoding signals to measure fidelity. Results indicate that Ribo-T ribosomes are largely insensitive to Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequences during -1 frameshifting, maintaining efficiencies nearly identical to WT ribosomes (e.g., 14% for IS911 vs. 13% for WT). However, Ribo-T ribosomes are severely impaired in +1 frameshifting, showing only 2% efficiency compared to 33% for WT, likely because they cannot sense the stimulatory SD sequence. Furthermore, Ribo-T ribosomes initiate translation much less efficiently when using an SD sequence, showing only a four-fold increase in activity compared to a no-SD control. Finally, the study identifies a slight but significant impairment in stop codon recognition, with Ribo-T ribosomes exhibiting higher readthrough rates across all three primary stop codons (UAG, UGA, and UAA). The authors suggest these defects may arise from the modified geometry of helix 44 (H44) and reduced conformational dynamics of the covalently linked subunits, which may hinder the binding of termination factors and the sensing of SD-ASD interactions. The study highlights the unexpected flexibility of the ribosome, demonstrating that while tethering allows for viability, it introduces specific constraints on certain translational recoding mechanisms.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the translational properties and accuracy of Ribo-T, a synthetic ribosome in Escherichia coli where the two subunits (30S and 50S) are covalently linked into a single entity. While Ribo-T has been previously shown to be functional and capable of sustaining cell growth, it exhibits a slow-growth phenotype with a protein synthesis rate of 50% compared to wild-type (WT) ribosomes. This research specifically evaluates how the tethered architecture affects three critical aspects of translation: programmed frameshifting, translation initiation, and stop codon termination. The authors used the pCL99 dual reporter system and various recoding signals to measure fidelity. Results indicate that Ribo-T ribosomes are largely insensitive to Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequences during -1 frameshifting, maintaining efficiencies nearly identical to WT ribosomes (e.g., 14% for IS911 vs. 13% for WT). However, Ribo-T ribosomes are severely impaired in +1 frameshifting, showing only 2% efficiency compared to 33% for WT, likely because they cannot sense the stimulatory SD sequence. Furthermore, Ribo-T ribosomes initiate translation much less efficiently when using an SD sequence, showing only a four-fold increase in activity compared to a no-SD control. Finally, the study identifies a slight but significant impairment in stop codon recognition, with Ribo-T ribosomes exhibiting higher readthrough rates across all three primary stop codons (UAG, UGA, and UAA). The authors suggest these defects may arise from the modified geometry of helix 44 (H44) and reduced conformational dynamics of the covalently linked subunits, which may hinder the binding of termination factors and the sensing of SD-ASD interactions. The study highlights the unexpected flexibility of the ribosome, demonstrating that while tethering allows for viability, it introduces specific constraints on certain translational recoding mechanisms.

Research Context
Ribosomes are evolutionary conserved complexes. A tethered ribosome, Ribo-T, was recently described. Ribo-T was shown to sustain cell growth. However, protein synthesis rate was 50% that with wild-type. Translational error rates remain low. Recoding events can occur during translation elongation. These sequences are powerful tools for investigation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
This study investigated the translational properties of Ribo-T. Do Ribo-T ribosomes maintain the correct reading frame? Do they terminate translation accurately at stop codons? Do they translate messenger RNA accurately?

Methodological Details
The experiments were performed with the E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain. The study used the poRibo-T2 vector. The ASD sequence of the Ribo-T 16S rRNA was altered. The bacterial pCL99 dual reporter system was used. This plasmid carries the lacZ-luc fusion gene. Translational efficiency was calculated as the ratio of luciferase activity to $\beta$-galactosidase activity. The median value was calculated for at least six independent experiments. The significance of differences was determined in Student's t-tests.

Procedures And Architectures
Target sequences were inserted into the MscI site. Double-stranded oligonucleotides were obtained by hybridization. In-frame controls were constructed for each sequence. Constructs were verified by sequencing. Ribo-T ribosomes were analyzed using orthogonal mRNA. Crosstalk was checked and found too low.

Key Results
Ribo-T ribosomes frameshift independently of the SD sequence. The efficiency for IS911 was 13% for wild-type. The efficiency for IS911 was 14% for Ribo-T. For IS3, the efficiency was 33% for either type. For dnaX, the efficiency was 43% for wild-type. For dnaX, the efficiency was 45% for Ribo-T. Replacing the SD sequence had no significant impact on Ribo-T ribosome frameshifting. Ribo-T ribosomes showed an efficiency of only 2% for +1 frameshifting. In contrast, wild-type ribosomes showed 33% efficiency for +1 frameshifting. Ribo-T ribosomes used the SD sequence much less efficiently. Luciferase induction was increased by a factor of four. summary.title: Efficient and Flexible Integration of Variant Characteristics in Rare Variant Association Studies Using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation
summary.authors: Hana Susak, Laura Serra-Saurina, Raquel Rabionet Janssen, Laura Domènech, Mattia Bosio, Francesc Muyas, Xavier Estivill, Georgia Escaramís, Stephan Ossowski
summary.executive_summary: Rare variants (RVs) are critical to understanding the etiology of complex diseases and may account for significant portions of missing heritability. While next-generation sequencing (NGS) allows for genome-wide analysis of RVs, traditional rare variant association studies (RVAS) often lack sufficient statistical power, particularly in small to medium-sized cohorts or when genetic variation explains a small fraction of phenotypic variance. To address these limitations, this study introduces BATI, a novel Bayesian rare variant Association Test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). Unlike current methods that may struggle with computational intensity or limited covariate integration, BATI efficiently incorporates individual and variant-specific features—such as functional annotations—as covariates within a full model estimation framework. By utilizing INLA, a non-sampling based numerical approximation, BATI provides a faster and more accurate inference process than traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, making it suitable for large-scale genomic scans. The researchers evaluated BATI within the 'rvGWAS' framework, a comprehensive suite for RVAS that includes quality control, data stratification, and multiple established tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, and MiST). Benchmarking was conducted using realistic 'semi-synthetic' whole-exome sequencing (WES) cohorts. These cohorts were designed to reflect real-world complexities by combining real WES background noise with known ClinVar risk variants. The results demonstrate that BATI substantially outperforms existing methods, especially in scenarios where risk variants explain very low variance (e.g., <0.5%). For example, BATI maintained high power (approaching 100% in some cases) where other methods failed to identify key genes like BRCA2 and BARD1. Furthermore, the study highlights how BATI handles complex population structures and benefits from prior information on protein function, particularly for loss-of-function (LoF) variants. Finally, the application of rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study successfully identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A, showcasing the practical utility of the framework.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Rare variants (RVs) are critical to understanding the etiology of complex diseases and may account for significant portions of missing heritability. While next-generation sequencing (NGS) allows for genome-wide analysis of RVs, traditional rare variant association studies (RVAS) often lack sufficient statistical power, particularly in small to medium-sized cohorts or when genetic variation explains a small fraction of phenotypic variance. To address these limitations, this study introduces BATI, a novel Bayesian rare variant Association Test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). Unlike current methods that may struggle with computational intensity or limited covariate integration, BATI efficiently incorporates individual and variant-specific features—such as functional annotations—as covariates within a full model estimation framework. By utilizing INLA, a non-sampling based numerical approximation, BATI provides a faster and more accurate inference process than traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, making it suitable for large-scale genomic scans. The researchers evaluated BATI within the 'rvGWAS' framework, a comprehensive suite for RVAS that includes quality control, data stratification, and multiple established tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, and MiST). Benchmarking was conducted using realistic 'semi-synthetic' whole-exome sequencing (WES) cohorts. These cohorts were designed to reflect real-world complexities by combining real WES background noise with known ClinVar risk variants. The results demonstrate that BATI substantially outperforms existing methods, especially in scenarios where risk variants explain very low variance (e.g., <0.5%). For example, BATI maintained high power (approaching 100% in some cases) where other methods failed to identify key genes like BRCA2 and BARD1. Furthermore, the study highlights how BATI handles complex population structures and benefits from prior information on protein function, particularly for loss-of-function (LoF) variants. Finally, the application of rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study successfully identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A, showcasing the practical utility of the framework.

Research Context
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) provides opportunities to study genetic variants at a genome-wide scale. Rare variants (RVs) play an important role in the etiology of complex genetic diseases. RVs are more likely to affect the structure, stability or function of proteins than common variants. Rare variant association studies (RVAS) identify disease loci based on the burden of rare and damaging variants. Traditional statistical methods like GWAS lack power because few individuals carry rare alternative alleles. To overcome this, studies consider multiple variable positions within functional biological units. Score-based methods pool minor alleles into a measure of burden for association tests. Advanced methods like SKAT and C-alpha consider heterogeneous effects among RVs. Recent methods like SKAT-O use a linear combination between burden and variance-component tests. Methods like MiST consider biological characteristics but are too computationally intensive for genome-wide scans because they avoid full model estimation. Calculating marginal likelihood for complex models in a fully Bayesian manner is often infeasible. Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods face concerns regarding convergence and extensive computation time. INLA is a non-sampling based numerical approximation procedure that is substantially faster than MCMC.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The researchers aimed to develop a Bayesian test that efficiently integrates variant characteristics. They proposed BATI to allow for full model estimation using the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). BATI is designed to flexibly integrate a large number of categorical and numeric characteristics of genetic variants as covariates. The primary hypothesis is that BATI will outperform existing RVAS methods on realistic, semi-synthetic whole-exome sequencing cohorts. This superiority is expected to be most pronounced when using meaningful biological context, such as functional annotation. The study hypothesizes that BATI will maintain high power in scenarios where risk variants explain a very small fraction of phenotypic variance. Specifically, the authors predict BATI will achieve power above 75% in cases where competing tests fail to identify risk genes.

Methodological Details
The study developed a new disease cohort simulator to allow for benchmarking using highly realistic disease cohorts. The simulator combines thousands of real WES datasets from various studies with known risk variants. It introduces predisposition variants found in ClinVar into the VCF files of cases. The study used two large datasets as basis for the simulation: 1000GP and the Iberian cohort. Samples were randomly assigned to cases or controls to create a breast cancer risk cohort. To ensure realism, variants with a MAF higher than 0.01 in any ancestry population were removed. The researchers performed RVAS tests on randomly split cohorts to establish significance thresholds. They obtained p-value thresholds for Burden, KBAC, SKAT-O, and MiST at 5%, 0.1%, and 0.01% TIER levels. For HBMR and BATI, they calculated thresholds for Bayes factor and resulting ΔDIC. The study used the median of 10 random splits as the significance thresholds. These thresholds were used to label a gene as significant for subsequent power analyses. The study integrated BATI into the 'rvGWAS' framework, which includes data quality control and filtering. rvGWAS also incorporates functional variant annotations and four commonly used RVAS tests.

Procedures And Architectures
BATI is implemented as a hierarchical Bayesian approach to the GLMM. The model assumes the observed phenotype Y_i belongs to an exponential family. The null hypothesis H_0 assumes no genetic effects where ε_i = X_t^α. The alternative hypothesis H_1 introduces genetic effects (G_ti Z)ω and G_ti δ. This approach is substantially faster than Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. BATI can flexibly integrate a large number of categorical and numeric characteristics of genetic variants as covariates. The rvGWAS framework integrates quality control, interactive filtering, and detection of data stratification. BATI achieves power close to 100% for three risk genes at 0.5% variance explained. At 0.1% TIER, BATI achieves over 80% power across all genes. BATI leverages both categorical and numerical variant characteristics to improve power. The method benefits significantly when risk genes contain mostly LoF variants. BATI performs at least as well as other methods when testing genes with missense variants. The use of semi-synthetic cohorts captures realistic background noise and variant distributions. Previous simulations lacked complexity, potentially leading to overly optimistic benchmark results. BATI provides a flexible testing approach that can be further extended and enhanced. The rvGWAS framework facilitates user-friendly and intuitive analysis of RVAS.

MiST performed poorly on realistic WES cohorts compared to artificial benchmark sets. This poor performance is likely due to zero-inflated p-values from inappropriate handling of low variant counts. Simulated variant data often lacks the noise-level and complexity of real data. Random 'causal' variants in simulations hamper benchmarking methods that leverage characteristics of disease variants.

At 0.1% TIER, BATI achieves over 80% power across all genes. BATI's performance is stable despite the smaller cohort size of the Iberian cohort. BATI represents a flexible testing approach that can be further extended.
Semi-synthetic cohorts provide a more rigorous and realistic benchmark than pure simulations. Combining real WES cohorts representing realistic background noise with real disease variants. Simulated variant data is well-known to lack the complexity and noise-level of real data. MiST performed poorly on realistic WES cohorts compared to artificial benchmark sets. Allows for more realistic expectations of the clinical researchers.

BATI is integrated within the rvGWAS framework for whole-exome or whole genome sequencing.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used 100 simulations of risk variants for each gene separately. They used the median of 10 random splits as the significance thresholds.

Table 2 shows gene-wise power plots for the 1000GP cohort. Figure 3 indicates the three TIER thresholds using red, green, and blue lines. Supplementary S6 Fig shows the similarity of estimated significance thresholds across 10 randomized splits.

1. The core contribution is BATI, a Bayesian RVAS test using INLA that efficiently integrates variant characteristics as covariates. 2. The strongest evidence is BATI's superior power (near 100%) at 0.5% variance explained where other methods fail. 3. The future path involves extending BATI as a flexible testing approach within the rvGWAS framework.

summary.title: A Combined Evidence Approach to Prioritize Nipah Virus Inhibitors
summary.authors: Nishi Kumari (Panjab University); Ayush Upadhyay (Delhi University); Kishan Kalia (D.A.V. College); Rakesh Kumar; Kanika Tuteja (Panjab University); Rani Paul (University of Lucknow); Eugenia Covernton; Tina Sharma; Vinod Scaria; Anshu Bhardwaj
summary.executive_summary: The Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly pathogenic zoonotic virus that has caused severe disease and mortality, with a case fatality rate exceeding 75%. Due to its potential to become a global pandemic and its inclusion on the WHO's 'R&D Blueprint list of priority diseases,' there is a critical and urgent need for the accelerated development of effective therapeutics. At present, there is no known specific treatment for NiV, and the effectiveness of broad-spectrum antivirals like ribavirin remains contradictory and limited. This study addresses this gap by establishing a systematic, evidence-based framework for the curation and prioritization of Nipah virus inhibitors (NVIs). The researchers conducted an extensive literature review of 838 papers to curate a structured knowledgebase (NVIK) containing 182 NVIs, of which 98 are unique small molecule inhibitors. A significant portion of these inhibitors reported IC50/EC50 values as low as 0.47 nM. To move beyond mere collation, the study implemented a "combined evidence strategy" for prioritization. This strategy involved two primary prongs: first, evaluating the robustness of the experimental assays used to identify the compounds; and second, performing a rigorous drug-likeness analysis. This analysis included diversity metrics, similarity to FDA-approved drugs for potential repurposing, similarity to existing antivirals, and screening via PAINS and DruLito filters. The resulting data revealed a chemically diverse library, where 93.3% of the inhibitors were found to be singletons in clustering analysis. Furthermore, the study identified 34 NVIs with structural similarities to 76 FDA-approved drugs, which could provide a path toward safer therapeutic profiles. The study successfully prioritized 11 NVIs, specifically highlighting NVIC0048 for its high overlap with FDA physicochemical ranges and NVIC0032 for its superior activity. Finally, the study developed a web-based platform using LAMP technology that provides community-driven search tools, including query-based and structure-based searches, to facilitate the continuous expansion of the NiV inhibitor landscape.

Executive Summary
The Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly pathogenic zoonotic virus that has caused severe disease and mortality, with a case fatality rate exceeding 75%. Due to its potential to become a global pandemic and its inclusion on the WHO's 'R&D Blueprint list of priority diseases,' there is a critical and urgent need for the accelerated development of effective therapeutics. At present, there is no known specific treatment for NiV, and the effectiveness of broad-spectrum antivirals like ribavirin remains contradictory and limited. This study addresses this gap by establishing a systematic, evidence-based framework for the curation and prioritization of Nipah virus inhibitors (NVIs). The researchers conducted an extensive literature review of 838 papers to curate a structured knowledgebase (NVIK) containing 182 NVIs, of which 98 are unique small molecule inhibitors. A significant portion of these inhibitors reported IC50/EC50 values as low as 0.47 nM. To move beyond mere collation, the study implemented a "combined evidence strategy" for prioritization. This strategy involved two primary prongs: first, evaluating the robustness of the experimental assays used to identify the compounds; and second, performing a rigorous drug-likeness analysis. This analysis included diversity metrics, similarity to FDA-approved drugs for potential repurposing, similarity to existing antivirals, and screening via PAINS and DruLito filters. The resulting data revealed a chemically diverse library, where 93.3% of the inhibitors were found to be singletons in clustering analysis. Furthermore, the study identified 34 NVIs with structural similarities to 76 FDA-approved drugs, which could provide a path toward safer therapeutic profiles. The study successfully prioritized 11 NVIs, specifically highlighting NVIC0048 for its high overlap with FDA physicochemical ranges and NVIC0032 for its superior activity. Finally, the study developed a web-based platform using LAMP technology that provides community-driven search tools, including query-based and structure-based searches, to facilitate the continuous expansion of the NiV inhibitor landscape.

Research Context
Nipah virus is a severe pathogen with a 50-100% mortality rate. It is a significant public health concern with pandemic potential. Current treatment options are severely lacking. Existing research on ribavirin has produced contradictory results. Nipah is listed on the WHO's priority diseases list. Existing databases for NVIs are currently scattered or lack evaluation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to develop a combined evidence-based strategy to systematically evaluate Nipah virus inhibitors. The objective is to curate the anti-Nipah compounds using a crowdsourcing model. A two-pronged strategy was devised for prioritization. The first prong prioritizes NVIs based on assay robustness. The second prong involves estimation of drug-likeness parameters.

Methodological Details
Inhibitors were collected from PubMed and Google sources. A total of 838 papers were considered for data-mining. A scoring system assigned a score of '10' for confirmed information. Papers with scores of 10, 5 and 4 were manually curated. The researchers created a knowledgebase of 182 NVIs. The library contains 98 unique small molecule inhibitors. Data quality was verified by a separate team of curators.

Procedures And Architectures
NVIK is developed using the open source LAMP server technology. The platform utilizes PHP, HTML, JavaScript, AJAX and CSS. Search options include Simple Search, Query Builder and Structure Search. Structure search supports SMILES, SDF and MOL formats. Near neighbours are identified using NNeib (version 5.12.0). Clusters are obtained using Jarp (version 6.0.2). A dissimilarity threshold of 0.15 is used. A total of 1875 descriptors were calculated using PaDel software.

Key Results
The NVIK database currently contains 182 entries. Of these, 98 are unique nipah inhibitors. EC50/IC50 values could be obtained for 70 compounds. Values range from 0.25 nM to 7562710 nM for all entries. The lowest reported value for small molecules is 0.47 nM. Clustering of 98 NVIs resulted in 90 clusters. The library is diverse, with 93.3% of NVIs being singletons. Thirty-four NVIs were found similar to 76 FDA approved drugs. DruLito screening showed that only two of 91 compounds passed all filters other than CMC.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The high percentage of singletons illustrates chemical diversity. NVIs show physicochemical distributions similar to FDA approved drugs. Similarity to FDA molecules can aid in prioritization of safe profiles. The combined strategy successfully prioritized 11 NVIs. NVIC0048 showed high overlap with FDA ranges. NVIC0032 exhibited better activity among the prioritized compounds.

Contradictions And Limitations
Data curation and quality check was done manually. Some entries in the knowledgebase lacked complete information. Existing focus on NVIs has limited or no evaluation.

Claims
NVIK provides a systematic map of the chemical space for NVIs. The researchers created a knowledgebase of 182 NVIs. The platform provides a structured knowledgebase. Previous datasets have limited evaluation. The platform facilitates further development.
A combined evidence approach allows for robust prioritization of NVIs. The study prioritised 11 NVIs. Prioritization used a combined evidence strategy. Only two of 91 compounds passed all but CMC filters. This aids in prioritizing candidates.
Identified NVIs show significant structural similarity to FDA-approved drugs. Thirty-four NVIs were similar to 76 FDA drugs. NVIs show similarity to FDA approved drugs.  Similarity aids in prioritizing safe profiles.

Data And Code Availability
Data is publicly available at the NVIK web platform.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A separate team of curators re-performed the curation.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the unique fields of the database. Figure 2 depicts the physicochemical property distribution. Figure 3 compares NVIs with FDA drugs and Enamine compounds. Figure 4 displays the DruLito filter results. Table 2 shows prioritized compounds and DruLito filter results.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a well-curated knowledgebase of 182 NVIs. 2. The strongest evidence of diversity is that 93.3% of NVIs are singletons. 3. The future path involves engaging the community for continuous curation.

summary.title: 3D Genome Analysis Identifies Enhancer Hijacking Mechanism for High-Risk Factors in Human T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
summary.authors: Lu Yang; Fengling Chen; Haichuan Zhu; Yang Chen; Bingjie Dong; Minglei Shi; Weitao Wang; Qian Jiang (Peking University Institute of Hematology); Leping Zhang (Peking University People's Hospital); Xiaojun Huang; Michael Q Zhang; Hong Wu
summary.executive_summary: This study provides an integrated analysis of 3D genome alterations and differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in 18 newly diagnosed T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) patients and 4 healthy T-cell controls. The researchers demonstrated that 3D genome organization—at the compartment, topologically associated domains (TAD), and loop levels—combined with gene expression profiles, can hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes based on T-cell differentiation trajectories. The analysis revealed that 3D genome alterations are associated with nearly 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL, with 56% directly related to structural changes. The study identified 34 previously unrecognized translocations in noncoding regions and 44 new translocation-mediated loops, revealing a mechanism of enhancer hijacking of the HOXA cluster. Specifically, the ectopic expression of the HOXA11-A13 genes was found to be associated with immature phenotypes and poor clinical outcomes, whereas other HOXA genes were not. The authors suggest that T-ALL chromosomal organizations represent 'frozen stages' of T-cell development. Mechanisms identified include 'cis' enhancer hijacking and 'trans' gene fusions, which epigenetically activate oncogenic transcription factors. Furthermore, HOXA13+ status was identified as an independent predictor for overall survival in pediatric and young adult T-ALLs. These findings suggest that 3D genome rewiring is a critical driver of T-ALL pathogenesis and identify potential therapeutic targets, such as anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors, for high-risk patients.

The authors suggest that T-ALL chromosomal organizations represent 'frozen stages' of T-cell development. Mechanisms identified include 'cis' enhancer hijacking and 'trans' gene fusions, which epigenetically activate oncogenic transcription factors. Furthermore, HOXA13+ status was identified as an independent predictor for overall survival in pediatric and young adult T-ALLs. Differential loop detection was split into two distance ranges (> or < 150 kb) to minimize potential bias.

summary.title: ProNetView-ccRCC: A web-based portal to interactively explore clear cell renal cell carcinoma proteogenomics networks
summary.authors: Selim Kalayci; Francesca Petralia; Pei Wang; Zeynep H Gümüş
summary.executive_summary: The study introduces ProNetView-ccRCC, an interactive, web-based exploration portal designed to visualize and navigate the complex phosphopeptide co-expression networks of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). As the Clinical Proteomics Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) produces increasingly large-scale and high-dimensional proteogenomic data, researchers face significant challenges in effectively communicating and interpreting the resulting high-order regulatory structures. Existing tools are often limited to static 2D images, which fail to capture the multi-layered interactions between gene/protein activities and biological pathways. To address this, ProNetView-ccRCC provides a 3D interactive interface that enables users to explore a network comprising 3,614 genes and 30 functional pathway-enriched modules. The platform was developed using the Three.js framework and WebGL, incorporating 3D layout algorithms from the iCAVE tool to ensure intuitive navigation through rotation and zooming. Users can query for specific proteins of interest, such as the oncogene ERG, to view its direct connections, mapping peptides, and associated clinical variables like tumor grade. For example, the portal can display ERG's connections to 11 genes and its specific statistical associations (p-value: 0.003, FDR: 0.118). Furthermore, the tool allows for filtered queries based on clinical phenotypes and FDR cut-offs, and provides links to the ProTrack tool for multi-omics heatmap analysis. By offering a free, open-access resource that operates on any modern web browser without requiring additional plugins, ProNetView-ccRCC empowers researchers across all computational skill levels to conduct interactive analyses, share results, and facilitate hypothesis generation in renal cancer research.

The platform was developed using the Three.js framework and WebGL, incorporating 3D layout algorithms from the iCAVE tool to ensure intuitive navigation through rotation and zooming. Users can query for specific proteins of interest, such as the oncogene ERG, to view its direct connections, mapping peptides, and associated clinical variables like tumor grade. For example, the portal can display ERG's connections to 11 genes and its specific statistical associations (p-value: 0.003, FDR: 0.118). Furthermore, the tool allows for filtered queries based on clinical phenotypes and FDR cut-offs, and provides links to the ProTrack tool for multi-omics heatmap analysis. By offering a free, open-access resource that operates on any modern web browser without requiring additional plugins, ProNetView-ccRCC empowers researchers across all computational skill levels to conduct interactive analyses, share results, and facilitate hypothesis generation in renal cancer research.

Research Context
CPTAC has performed comprehensive proteogenomic characterizations. Co-expression networks reveal regulatory relationships between proteins and PTMs. These networks are challenging to visually communicate due to large dimensions. Current tools are mainly used for static 2D images. A centralized platform is necessary.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The goal is to create an intuitive exploration environment for phosphopeptide networks. The portal aims to provide exploration of ccRCC study results. It seeks to enable quick and easy interactions with 30 functional network modules. It addresses the need for an open community resource tool.

Methodological Details
The portal explores the phosphopeptide coexpression network of ccRCC. It also explores 30 different network modules. The network characterizes 20,976 phosphopeptides in ccRCC. Network construction used a random-forest based algorithm. The data came from 103 ccRCC samples. Genes are connected if at least two phosphopeptides map to them are associated. Network modules were derived by using Glay clustering algorithm. Each module contains at least 20 genes. Pathway enrichment analysis used Fisher Exact test.

Procedures And Architectures
The portal enables interactive explorations in 3D. Implementation was built on the Three.js framework. Three.js provides an interface for WebGL. 3D layout algorithms were calculated within iCAVE. Client-side Javascript libraries include D3.js and dataTables.js. Styling used Bootstrap v3.3.7. The portal runs on all modern browsers. It does not require additional plug-ins.

Key Results
Users can interactively explore the large topology. Six modules were significantly associated with biological pathways. Searching for ERG highlights it in the network. ERG is a member of the Angiogenesis enriched module. The query returns the list of connections. ERG is directly connected to 11 genes. ERG maps to 5 different peptides. The portal shows association with tumor grade (p-value: 0.003, FDR: 0.118). Users can specify phenotype and FDR= 20%.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
ProNetView-ccRCC provides a free, open access environment. It helps understand the phosphopeptide network in the context of markers. It helps guide hypothesis generation for future studies. It facilitates researchers of wide-spectrum computational skill levels.

Contradictions And Limitations
The portal is specific to CPTAC ccRCC study. It runs on all modern browsers.

Claims
ProNetView-ccRCC allows intuitive exploration of complex 3D networks. The tool features a 3D network exploration interface. No contradicting evidence reported. It empowers researchers of wide-spectrum computational skill levels.
The portal enables precise queries for clinical metadata and gene associations. Users can easily query for proteins of interest. No contradicting evidence reported. This helps guide hypothesis generation for future studies.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the global ccRCC tumor phosphoproteomics co-expression network. Figure 1B links it to functional network modules. Figure 1C shows search results for the oncogene ERG. Figure 2A displays a snapshot of the Angiogenesis enriched module. Figure 2B shows node interaction and meta-data panel. Figure 2C shows a simple query for genes. Figure 2D shows genes highlighted in red. Figure 3A displays an interactive table of enriched pathways. Figure 3B shows highlights in the network for a pathway.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a web-based network exploration portal. 2. The strongest evidence is the visualization of ERG's 11 gene connections. 3. The future path is facilitating researchers of wide-spectrum computational skill levels.
