summary.title: Spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following primary tumor excision: a critical role for primary tumor secretome
summary.authors: Shaashua Lee, Anabel Eckerling, Boaz Israeli, Gali Yanovich, Ella Rosenne, Suzana Fichman-Horn, Ido Ben Zvi, Liat Sorski, Ronit Satchi-Fainaro, Tamar Geiger, Erica K Sloan, Shamgar Ben-Eliyahu
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the clinical phenomenon of spontaneous metastasis regression following primary tumor (PT) excision, a process where metastatic lesions disappear despite the absence of traditional treatment. Using an orthotopic model of MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells in nude mice, the authors demonstrate that surgical removal of the primary tumor leads to a significant reduction in early-stage micro-metastases. The study identifies a critical role for the primary tumor secretome, suggesting that the tumor secretes factors that support the survival and growth of distant metastatic foci. Specifically, the removal of the primary tumor eliminates these growth-promoting factors, thereby inducing regression in small metastases, while larger, potentially self-sufficient metastases remain stable. The researchers utilized a luciferase-mCherry reporter system to track metastasis development and identified four key secretome proteins—IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF—through a combination of human cytokine arrays and mass spectrometry-based proteomics. In vivo experiments confirmed that neutralizing these four factors arrested the development of micro-metastases even when the primary tumor was present. Furthermore, retrospective analysis of the TCGA provisional dataset showed that high levels of these four proteins correlated with poor survival in lung adenocarcinoma patients. These findings identify a vital 'perioperative window' where blocking tumor-secreted factors could potentially control minimal residual disease and influence long-term cancer outcomes. The study highlights how the primary tumor acts as a systemic source of pro-metastatic signals, and its excision can fundamentally alter the metastatic landscape by withdrawing these essential survival cues.

claims.description: Primary tumor excision induces regression of early-stage micro-metastases by removing essential secretome factors.
IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF are critical drivers of early metastatic survival.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the clinical phenomenon of spontaneous metastasis regression following primary tumor (PT) excision, a process where metastatic lesions disappear despite the absence of traditional treatment. Using an orthotopic model of MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells in nude mice, the authors demonstrate that surgical removal of the primary tumor leads to a significant reduction in early-stage micro-metastases. The study identifies a critical role for the primary tumor secretome, suggesting that the tumor secretes factors that support the survival and growth of distant metastatic foci. Specifically, the removal of the primary tumor eliminates these growth-promoting factors, thereby inducing regression in small metastases, while larger, potentially self-sufficient metastases remain stable. The researchers utilized a luciferase-mCherry reporter system to track metastasis development and identified four key secretome proteins—IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF—through a combination of human cytokine arrays and mass spectrometry-based proteomics. In vivo experiments confirmed that neutralizing these four factors arrested the development of micro-metastases even when the primary tumor was present. Furthermore, retrospective analysis of the TCGA provisional dataset showed that high levels of these four proteins correlated with poor survival in lung adenocarcinoma patients. These findings identify a vital 'perioperative window' where blocking tumor-secreted factors could potentially control minimal residual disease and influence long-term cancer outcomes. The study highlights how the primary tumor acts as a systemic source of pro-metastatic signals, and its excision can fundamentally alter the metastatic landscape by withdrawing these essential survival cues.

Research Context
Surgical removal of the primary tumor remains a cornerstone of cancer treatment. However, surgical procedures might accelerate postoperative progression of minimal residual disease. Alternatively, some reports show spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastasis. These regressions are documented in various cancers, particularly lung metastases. Proposed mechanisms include surgical trauma or the elimination of factors secreted by the primary tumor. Empirical testing has been limited because no animal model of spontaneous regression exists. Current knowledge emphasizes that the primary tumor exists as a systemic disease. There is continuous crosstalk between the primary tumor, its microenvironment, and distant organs.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The researchers sought to identify potential underlying mechanisms for spontaneous metastasis regression. They proposed that the primary tumor secretome supports the survival and growth of distant micro-metastases. The study hypothesized that removal of the primary tumor and its secreted factors induces regression of early-stage metastases. They predicted that specific factors identified in the secretome would mediate these pro-metastatic effects. The central question is whether early-stage metastatic foci are dependent on primary tumor signals.

Methodological Details
The study utilized a highly metastatic MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cell line. These cells were transduced with a firefly luciferase-mCherry vector to monitor metastasis. Cancer cells were maintained in DMEM supplemented with FBS and glutamax. Researchers used eight-week old female BALB/c nu/nu mice to form primary tumors. Cells were injected into the fourth mammary fat pad under anesthesia. Primary tumor volumes were calculated using a specific formula based on dimensions. Metastases were assessed using an IVIS spectrum apparatus for bioluminescence imaging. Primary tumors were excised once metastatic foci reached a total flux of 10^6 photons/s. Tumor cell-conditioned medium was prepared by incubating cells in serum-free medium. Tumor secretome supplementation was delivered via Alzet osmotic minipumps. Adhesion and tube formation studies were performed in vitro using HUVEC cells. A Human Cytokine Array compared expression levels of 102 soluble proteins. Mass spectrometry-based secretome analysis identified 2,600 proteins in the conditioned medium. Proteomics data were analyzed using MaxQuant and Perseus software. Patient outcomes were analyzed using the public TCGA provisional dataset. Survival curves were constructed using Kaplan Meier Analysis with hazard ratio calculations.

Procedures And Architectures
Primary tumor resection was performed under 2% isoflurane anesthesia. The sham surgery involved making an identical incision without touching the tumor. Conditioned medium was concentrated to a final volume of 100 μl/mouse. Conditioned medium (CM) and serum-free medium (SM) were used as controls. IncuCyte systems were used to image cell adhesion and tube formation over 24 hours. Cytokine analysis compared plasma from tumor-bearing, non-tumor-bearing, and post-excision mice. Proteins were digested overnight with LysC/Trypsin mix before LC-MS analysis. Peptides were separated by reverse-phase chromatography using a 140 min gradient. Neutralizing antibodies for IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF were injected daily. Lung sections were stained for Hematoxylin and Eosin for histological verification.

Key Results
Following primary tumor excision, a dramatic decrease in metastatic signal occurred. This regression was evident within the first 24 hours post-excision. Metastases were confirmed to have regressed into latent foci. H&E staining confirmed malignant foci were present 50 days post-excision. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastatic foci. Sham surgery did not induce regression, as metastatic signals continued to increase. Tumor-cell conditioned medium significantly enhanced cancer cell viability and adhesion. Conditioned medium also induced tube formation of human endothelial cells. Mice treated with conditioned medium showed 10-fold less regression than controls. The cytokine array identified 28 cytokines highly expressed in cancer cell medium. Proteomics identified 359 proteins as extracellular factors via GO analysis. Neutralization of four key factors completely blocked metastatic progression. High protein levels of these factors correlated with poor survival in lung adenocarcinoma. Survival analysis showed a hazard ratio of 2.05 for high protein expression.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The primary tumor secretome provides essential survival factors for early metastatic niches. Tumor-secreted factors like IL-8 and MIF promote angiogenesis and suppress apoptosis. The findings suggest that early-stage micro-metastases are dependent on PT-derived signals. Large metastatic foci may be self-sufficient and less dependent on the primary tumor. The perioperative period offers a window of opportunity to block pro-metastatic factors. Tailored combinations of neutralizing antibodies may control minimal residual disease.

Contradictions And Limitations
Regression was notably less prominent in larger metastatic foci. The study focused on MDA-MB-231 HM, limiting generalizability to other tumor types. Other secreted factors are likely involved but were not all blocked. The prevalence of post-operative regression in humans remains unknown.

Claims
Primary tumor excision induces regression of early-stage micro-metastases by removing essential secretome factors. Signal decreased up to 100-fold. Metastases regressed into latent foci. Sham surgery did not cause regression. Larger metastases showed less regression. Suggests a perioperative window for intervention.
IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF are critical drivers of early metastatic survival. Neutralization completely blocked progression. High levels correlate with poor survival. Proteomics identified these as extracellular factors. Other factors are likely involved. Enables tailored perioperative antibody therapy.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-B shows a 100-fold decrease in metastatic signal post-excision. Figure 1E shows regression is less prominent in larger metastases. Figure 2D shows 10-fold less regression with conditioned medium. Figure 3B shows antibody neutralization completely blocks metastatic progression. Figure 3D shows the hazard ratio of 2.05 for poor survival.

Three Takeaways
1. The primary tumor secretome is essential for the survival of early-stage micro-metastases. 2. Removal of the primary tumor induces regression of these early foci by withdrawing growth factors. 3. Targetting IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF during the perioperative window may arrest metastatic progression.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study explores the molecular dynamics of macrophage activation using Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy. The researchers utilized murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells as a model to observe the innate immune response triggered by CpG DNA and lipopolysaccharide (LPS). By employing Principal Component Analysis (PCA), the authors identified significant spectral variations in macromolecules, including nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids. Key findings demonstrate that CpG DNA stimulation leads to a rapid increase in RNA synthesis within the first two hours, followed by a shift toward DNA synthesis after six hours. Protein concentration was observed to increase significantly during the initial two hours of activation before declining. Furthermore, both CpG DNA and LPS treatment triggered substantial de novo lipogenesis, evidenced by increased concentrations of fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol from the earliest stages of treatment. The study concludes that ATR-FTIR spectroscopy is a viable, non-destructive, and rapid independent modality for monitoring the activation kinetics of macrophages in real-time, providing a broad view of metabolite changes that might be inaccessible through complex 'omics' techniques.

Research Context
FTIR spectroscopy has developed into a powerful biomedical tool for high-throughput analysis of biological systems. From a single spectrum, all delicate alterations in macromolecules can be revealed. The infrared spectrum serves as a fingerprint for metabolites. Macrophages are the front line of the immune system defending the organism. CpG DNA triggers the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines. LPS stimulates the monocytes and macrophages, releasing biological response mediators. However, how CpG ODN-mediated immune activation impacts relative amounts of metabolites has not been studied. While 'omics' techniques yield precise data, they require complex sample preparation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question addresses whether CpG ODN-mediated immune activation leads to global molecular changes detectable by FTIR spectroscopy. This is currently unknown in the field of spectroscopic analysis. The study aims to monitor the molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells. Furthermore, it investigates if FTIR spectroscopy can serve as an independent modality to monitor activation dynamics. The study hypothesizes that the spectroscopic fingerprints will reveal the kinetics of RNA synthesis and lipid metabolism. By comparing CpG DNA and LPS treatments, the study aims to identify shared and unique metabolic pathways.

Methodological Details
The study utilized murine macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells. These cells were cultured at 37 °C with 5% CO2. The culture medium was supplemented with 10% FBS and 2 mM L-glutamine. Cells were resuspended at a concentration of 2x10^6 /mL for treatment. The CpG DNA stimulated group was treated with 1 µM K3 ODN. The LPS stimulated group was treated with 0.5 µg/ml LPS. The control group was treated with 0.9% PBS; Sigma. Four different time points were used for measurements. Measurements included 10 min and 30 min. Measurements also included 2 h and 6 h. Samples were washed with 15 mL of sterile PBS. Replicates of n=5 were used in the data analysis.

Procedures And Architectures
Interferograms were collected using a Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One FTIR spectrometer. The spectrometer was equipped with an ATR unit and a Diamond-ZnSe crystal. To manage atmospheric interference, the air background was subtracted automatically. The spectrum of PBS was subtracted manually. Cell samples of 1 µl were dried with mild N2 flux. The best signal-to-noise ratio was achieved with a 128 scan number. The analysis used a 2 cm-1 spectral resolution. Post-processing involved 13-point Savitzky-Golay smoothing and baseline correction. PCA was performed on the 3000-650 cm-1 region.

Key Results
PCA analysis showed PC-1 gave a variability of 83%. CpG DNA induced significant changes in nucleic acid content starting from 10 min to 6 h (p < 0.1*). The RNA-specific peak (915 cm-1) increased significantly from the first minutes (p < 0.001***). The RNA synthesis increase was maintained until 2 h after stimulation (p < 0.1*). Total protein content increased significantly in CpG-treated cells from 10 min until 2 h (p < 0.001***). There was a very significant increase in triglycerides and cholesterol during activation. A significant increase is observed in fatty acid concentration.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The RNA-specific peak (915 cm-1) can define the activation state at the first minutes. CpG DNA induces RNA synthesis first, followed by DNA synthesis starting from 6 h. LPS was shown to inhibit DNA synthesis and elicit cell cycle arrest. De novo lipogenesis is triggered by pro-inflammatory reactions in macrophages. FTIR spectroscopy provides a broad view of the relative amounts of metabolites.

Contradictions And Limitations
The absorbance of IR light by water molecules is a limitation of infrared spectroscopy. Complex sample preparation in 'omics' techniques can result in alterations of chemical ratios. The mechanism of CpG DNA induced protein loss is not fully understood. The study notes that water superimposes other signals.

Claims
ATR-FTIR spectroscopy is a viable independent modality for monitoring macrophage activation kinetics. The study demonstrates the use of FTIR as an independent modality. It allows for a broad view of metabolite changes.  This can foster the design of ODNs for therapeutic uses. It provides a broad view of relative amounts of metabolites.
CpG DNA triggers rapid early RNA synthesis followed by a transition to DNA synthesis. The RNA-specific peak increased significantly from first minutes. DNA synthesis starts from 6 h after stimulation.  This helps define the activation state at the very first minutes.

Key Figures Tables
Figure A1 shows the spectrum of resting RAW 264.7 cells. Figure 2.C shows CpG DNA significantly increased the RNA-specific peak. Figure 3.C shows the significant increase in amide I band integration. Figure 4.D and 4.E show the significant increase in triglycerides and cholesterol.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is using FTIR to monitor macrophage activation dynamics. 2. The strongest evidence is that CpG DNA triggers RNA synthesis first, then DNA synthesis starts from 6 h. 3. The future path involves investigating the mechanisms of CpG DNA induced protein loss.

summary.title: The Foster method: Rapid and non-invasive detection of clinically significant American Foulbrood disease levels using eDNA sampling and a dual-target qPCR assay, with its potential for other hive pathogens
summary.authors: John F Mackay, Rebecca E Hewett, Noa T Smith, Tammy L Waters, John S Scandrett
summary.executive_summary:
American Foulbrood (AFB) is a devastating and destructive disease in honeybees, caused by the Gram-positive bacteria Paenibacillus larvae. Diagnosis currently relies heavily on the subjective and time-consuming task of visual inspection by beekeepers, which often requires dismantling hives and can result in missed infections. Furthermore, traditional sampling methods like collecting debris from hive baseboards are invasive and require multiple hive visits. This study introduces the "Foster method," a novel environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling technique that utilizes colony entrance swabs combined with a dual-target qPCR assay for P. larvae. This approach is designed to detect clinically significant infections rapidly and non-invasively, potentially even before visual symptoms are apparent.

The researchers evaluated the method across five quarantine apiaries in New Zealand, comparing samples from nurse bees, whole baseboard swabs, and entrance swabs. The dual-target assay was engineered to use the multi-copy 16S gene for high sensitivity and the single-copy ftsZ gene for precise quantification. Results demonstrated high analytical sensitivity, with the assay reliably detecting down to 4 copies per 10 µL. While the 16S marker typically amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than the ftsZ marker, the latter provided a reliable basis for spore quantification.

The study tested the method across three distinct cohorts. In a first cohort of 45 quarantine hives, the method successfully identified clinical signs and predicted progression in several colonies. A second cohort of 23 hives further validated that hives with clinical AFB showed significantly higher spore levels in both bees and entrance swabs. A third cohort demonstrated that even when eluates were pooled into groups of eight or twelve, individual hives with high levels of AFB could be clearly detected. Statistical analysis revealed a strong correlation between increasing spore levels and clinical signs, establishing that a spore quantity of 565,000 or more indicates a 95% probability of clinical infection.

The Foster method eliminates the need to dismantle hives, making it highly suitable for rapid screening and biosecurity surveillance. While new hiveware can lead to lower entrance spore counts initially, the method remains highly effective at identifying infected hives. Additionally, the authors suggest the method's versatility for detecting other pathogens and pests, such as Nosema ceranae or invasive mites, providing a scalable tool for honeybee health management.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
American Foulbrood (AFB) is a devastating and destructive disease in honeybees, caused by the Gram-positive bacteria Paenibacillus larvae. Diagnosis currently relies heavily on the subjective and time-consuming task of visual inspection by beekeepers, which often requires dismantling hives and can result in missed infections. Furthermore, traditional sampling methods like collecting debris from hive baseboards are invasive and require multiple hive visits. This study introduces the "Foster method," a novel environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling technique that utilizes colony entrance swabs combined with a dual-target qPCR assay for P. larvae. This approach is designed to detect clinically significant infections rapidly and non-invasively, potentially even before visual symptoms are apparent.

The researchers evaluated the method across five quarantine apiaries in New Zealand, comparing samples from nurse bees, whole baseboard swabs, and entrance swabs. The dual-target assay was engineered to use the multi-copy 16S gene for high sensitivity and the single-copy ftsZ gene for precise quantification. Results demonstrated high analytical sensitivity, with the assay reliably detecting down to 4 copies per 10 µL. While the 16S marker typically amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than the ftsZ marker, the latter provided a reliable basis for spore quantification.

The study tested the method across three distinct cohorts. In a first cohort of 45 quarantine hives, the method successfully identified clinical signs and predicted progression in several colonies. A second cohort of 23 hives further validated that hives with clinical AFB showed significantly higher spore levels in both bees and entrance swabs. A third cohort demonstrated that even when eluates were pooled into groups of eight or twelve, individual hives with high levels of AFB could be clearly detected. Statistical analysis revealed a strong correlation between increasing spore levels and clinical signs, establishing that a spore quantity of 565,000 or more indicates a 95% probability of clinical infection.

The Foster method eliminates the need to dismantle hives, making it highly suitable for rapid screening and biosecurity surveillance. While new hiveware can lead to lower entrance spore counts initially, the method remains highly effective at identifying infected hives. Additionally, the authors suggest the method's versatility for detecting other pathogens and pests, such as Nosema ceranae or invasive mites, providing a scalable tool for honeybee health management.

Research Context
American Foulbrood (AFB) is a destructive disease in honeybees caused by Paenibacillus larvae. The spores are extremely hardy and can remain infectious for over 30 years. A single infected larva can generate millions of spores, leading to rapid spread. Infection can be spread unknowingly by the beekeeper through contaminated honey or hive frames. In New Zealand, the rise in hive density and less skilled beekeepers has increased reported infections. Diagnosis is currently based on visual symptoms, which is laborious and prone to missing disease. Hives must be dismantled and disrupted to inspect for clinical signs of AFB. Traditional confirmation by culture is a variable process and can take up to a week. While qPCR is a faster diagnostic tool, most applications have not used the quantitative data. Quantification is important because low levels of AFB are often not clinically relevant. Previous publications used the 16S gene due to high sensitivity but at the expense of specificity. Sensitivity for bacterial targets can be compromised by deletions or sequence polymorphisms. Many microbiological qPCR tests now utilize two independent targets to enhance both sensitivity and specificity. Internal controls may improve sensitivity by preventing inhibitors from preventing the amplification of targets. Previous methods required installing collection sheets, necessitating dismantling the hive twice and repeat visits. The ability to detect relevant levels from a single entrance sample would permit far more rapid sampling.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aimed to develop a novel eDNA sampling method for the detection of hives with clinically significant AFB infections. It sought to determine if entrance swabs could remove the need to dismantle the hive. The goal was to utilize quantification data to detect infections before visual symptoms are apparent. The hypothesis was that quantification of P. larvae could provide predictive information regarding clinical signs. The study aimed to evaluate if entrance swabs could provide predictive information for other bee pathogens.

Methodological Details
The study sampled hives from five quarantine apiaries across multiple regions in New Zealand. Sampling occurred two-monthly from late 2018 to early 2020. Samples included nurse bees, whole baseboard swabs, and hive entrance swabs. Bees were collected from brood frames in 50 mL sterile containers. Swabs were moistened in sterile water and swiped for three to five seconds. Swabs were rotated during collection to ensure all surfaces could collect hive material. Swabs were sent to the laboratory at ambient temperature. Bee samples were frozen at -20°C while swabs were stored at ambient temperature. Genomic DNA extraction was performed from each sample containing 10 bees. Extraction utilized a column-based Bee Pathogen DNA/RNA Extraction Kit. Homogenization involved 3 mL DXL buffer, zirconia silica beads, and a Mini Beadbeater 16. Samples were homogenized for 3 minutes and incubated at 65°C for 10 minutes. Homogenate was centrifuged at 15,000 x g for 5 minutes. Supernatant was processed through a nucleic acid binding column. Swabs were processed with 800 µL DXL buffer and zirconia silica beads. Pooled applications involved vortexing individual swabs for 10 seconds before pooling. A synthetic DNA standard incorporating both amplicon sequences was used for quantification. The 153 bp standard was quantified on a DS-11 FX microvolume spectrophotometer. Quantification standards were generated from 10^6 copies per µL down to 2 copies per µL. Cq's were converted to spore levels using the amplification efficiency of the single copy ftsZ gene. Statistical analysis included a binary logistic regression model in Minitab. Analysis of variance was calculated to confirm the correlation between spores and clinical signs.

Procedures And Architectures
The study used a commercially available multiplex qPCR assay for P. larvae. The assay utilized the multi-copy 16S gene for sensitivity and the single copy ftsZ gene for quantification. Bees were euthanized by freezing and then homogenized with zirconia silica beads. The Mini Beadbeater 16 was used for 3 minutes of homogenization. Incubation occurred at 65°C with manual inversion every 3 minutes. DNA was extracted using a column-based kit with beadbeating. For swabs, 800 µL DXL buffer was added to the beads. Swab eluates were pooled into groups of eight and twelve. A synthetic DNA standard was used to create a standard curve. Quantification was based on a formula using the y-intercept and ftsZ efficiency. Binary logistic regression identified the relationship between spore levels and clinical disease likelihood. A p-value of <0.05 was considered significant for all analyses.

Key Results
The AFBduo assay showed high analytical sensitivity down to 4 copies per 10 µL. The assay demonstrated excellent linearity over 7 orders of magnitude. The 16S target typically amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than the ftsZ target. Bee DNA extraction yielded high purity with OD260/280 between 1.8 and 1.9. Extracted DNA samples indicated no inhibitors were present in the samples. In the first cohort of 45 hives, 8 showed clinical signs. Table 1 shows the progression of P. larvae levels in three colonies. In a second cohort of 23 hives, 4 showed clinical signs. Hives with clinical AFB demonstrated much higher spore levels in bees and entrance swabs (Table 2). Even in pools of twelve, single hives with higher levels of AFB could be clearly detected. Statistical analysis indicated a strong relationship (p = 0.00) between spore levels and clinical signs. A spore quantity of 565,000 or more revealed a 95% probability of clinical signs.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 16S marker provided high sensitivity but could not be relied on for quantification due to variability. The single copy ftsZ gene was preferred for quantification purposes. Entrance swabbing removes the need to dismantle and disrupt the hive. Dismantling the hive to swab the whole baseboard was not required. Entrance swabs could clearly be differentiated from levels in non-infected hives. The method can identify infected hives with pre-clinical infections or missed symptoms. New hiveware may result in lower entrance spore levels initially. The Foster method provides a fast, one-time sampling and quantification method. The method could be adapted for biosecurity surveillance of unwanted hive pests. Quantification provides an important risk element regarding the likelihood of clinical signs.

Contradictions And Limitations
One hive without visual signs (Hive 11) showed levels similar to clinically affected hives. In two cases, bees showed high spore levels while hiveware showed low levels. These hives were new and the colonies were newly established from an infected parent. There had not been enough time for spores to deposit on entrance surfaces. Further research is required to assess the accumulation rate of spores. Refining the clinical spore threshold levels requires more hives to be tested.

Claims
The Foster method enables rapid, non-invasive screening of honeybee hives for clinically significant American Foulbrood (AFB). The method allows for sampling via colony entrance swabs. It removes the requirement to dismantle the hive. The dual-target qPCR assay provides high confidence in results. New hiveware can lead to lower entrance spore counts. The method allows for faster sampling of hives than dismantling. It could be used for biosecurity surveillance of other pests.

Data And Code Availability
Data availability is not specified in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Robustness was tested with synthetic DNA standards.

Ethical Considerations
Ethical considerations are not specified in the text.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 shows the progression of P. larvae levels in three colonies. Table 2 displays P. larvae levels in nurse bees and entrance swabs. Table 3 presents results for pooled swab eluates. Table 4 compares sample types including bees, baseboard, and entrance swabs. Supplementary figure 4 shows the analysis of variance results.

Three Takeaways
1. The Foster method provides a rapid, non-invasive way to detect clinically significant AFB levels using entrance swabs and dual-target qPCR. 2. A spore quantity of 565,000 or more provides a 95% probability of clinical signs being present. 3. The method can be adapted for biosecurity surveillance of other pathogens and pests, providing a scalable risk assessment tool.

    *Expanding Executive Summary*:
    American Foulbrood (AFB) is a devastating and destructive disease in honeybees, caused by the Gram-positive bacteria *Paenibacillus larvae*. Diagnosis currently relies heavily on the subjective and time-consuming task of visual inspection by beekeepers, which often requires dismantling hives and can result in missed infections. Furthermore, traditional sampling methods like collecting debris from hive baseboards are invasive and require multiple hive visits. This study introduces the "Foster method," a novel environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling technique that utilizes colony entrance swabs combined with a dual-target qPCR assay for *P. larvae*. This approach is designed to detect clinically significant infections rapidly and non-invasively, potentially even before visual symptoms are apparent.

    The researchers evaluated the method across five quarantine apiaries in New Zealand, comparing samples from nurse bees, whole baseboard swabs, and entrance swabs. The dual-target assay was engineered to use the multi-copy 16S gene for high sensitivity and the single-copy *ftsZ* gene for precise quantification. Results demonstrated high analytical sensitivity, with the assay reliably detecting down to 4 copies per 10 µL. While the 16S marker typically amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than the *ftsZ* marker, the latter provided a reliable basis for spore quantification.

    The study tested the method across three distinct cohorts. In a first cohort of 45 quarantine hives, the method successfully identified clinical signs and predicted progression in several colonies. A second cohort of 23 hives further validated that hives with clinical AFB showed significantly higher spore levels in both bees and entrance swabs. A third cohort demonstrated that even when eluates were pooled into groups of eight or twelve, individual hives with high levels of AFB could be clearly detected. Statistical analysis revealed a strong correlation between increasing spore levels and clinical signs, establishing that a spore quantity of 565,000 or more indicates a 95% probability of clinical infection.

    The Foster method eliminates the need to dismantle hives, making it highly suitable for rapid screening and biosecurity surveillance. While new hiveware can lead to lower entrance spore counts initially, the method remains highly effective at identifying infected hives. Additionally, the authors suggest the method's versatility for detecting other pathogens and pests, such as *Nosema ceranae* or invasive mites, providing a scalable tool for honeybee health management.

summary.title: SPOT-Contact-Single: Improving Single-Sequence-Based Prediction of Protein Contact Map using a Transformer Language Model
summary.authors: Jaspreet Singh (Griffith University); Thomas Litfin (Griffith University); Jaswinder Singh; Kuldip Paliwal (Griffith University); Yaoqi Zhou (Griffith University)
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses a major bottleneck in protein structure prediction: the reliance on multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) and evolutionary profiles, which are often unavailable for proteins lacking natural homologs. While MSAs provide high-quality information for known families, they are computationally expensive to generate and non-existent for many sequences. The authors propose SPOT-Contact-Single, a novel contact-map predictor that bypasses the need for evolutionary profiles by utilizing features extracted from a pre-trained Transformer language model, ESM-1b. Specifically, the model incorporates attention maps from ESM-1b, concatenated with one-hot amino acid encodings and structural features from the SPOT-1D-Single predictor. The architecture utilizes an ensemble of six ResNet-12 models trained on a large-scale dataset of 34,691 proteins. Evaluation across multiple independent benchmarks, including CASP14-FM and the SPOT-2018 set, demonstrates that SPOT-Contact-Single significantly outperforms existing single-sequence-based methods like SSCpred (achieving a 15% improvement in F1-score). More notably, it drastically outperforms evolution-based methods such as TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact on proteins with very low homology (Neff=1), yielding improvements of 48.7% and 48.5% in F1-score, respectively. Beyond accuracy, the method offers massive gains in computational efficiency, performing inference 22 times faster than TrRosetta on CPUs. These results position SPOT-Contact-Single as a highly effective, high-speed screening tool for large-scale genomic protein contact prediction where evolutionary data is sparse or absent.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses a major bottleneck in protein structure prediction: the reliance on multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) and evolutionary profiles, which are often unavailable for proteins lacking natural homologs. While MSAs provide high-quality information for known families, they are computationally expensive to generate and non-existent for many sequences. The authors propose SPOT-Contact-Single, a novel contact-map predictor that bypasses the need for evolutionary profiles by utilizing features extracted from a pre-trained Transformer language model, ESM-1b. Specifically, the model incorporates attention maps from ESM-1b, concatenated with one-hot amino acid encodings and structural features from the SPOT-1D-Single predictor. The architecture utilizes an ensemble of six ResNet-12 models trained on a large-scale dataset of 34,691 proteins. Evaluation across multiple independent benchmarks, including CASP14-FM and the SPOT-2018 set, demonstrates that SPOT-Contact-Single significantly outperforms existing single-sequence-based methods like SSCpred (achieving a 15% improvement in F1-score). More notably, it drastically outperforms evolution-based methods such as TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact on proteins with very low homology (Neff=1), yielding improvements of 48.7% and 48.5% in F1-score, respectively. Beyond accuracy, the method offers massive gains in computational efficiency, performing inference 22 times faster than TrRosetta on CPUs. These results position SPOT-Contact-Single as a highly effective, high-speed screening tool for large-scale genomic protein contact prediction where evolutionary data is sparse or absent.

Research Context
Most current protein contact-map prediction methods rely on evolutionary information derived from MSAs. However, many proteins lack homologs, causing performance to drop significantly for these targets. Generating these evolutionary profiles is also computationally intensive for large-scale tasks. Single-sequence-based methods like SSCpred exist but provide less information for neural networks to learn. There is a need to explore features beyond simple one-hot encoding. Unsupervised deep learning methods can extract features inspired by NLP language models.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study examines if ESM-1b's attention maps can improve single-sequence-based contact-map prediction. The authors hypothesize that unsupervised learning features concatenated with one-hot encoding will outperform existing methods. They specifically predict better performance for proteins with a low effective number of homologs. The study also tests whether an ensemble of models trained with different features and strategies improves results.

Methodological Details
The researchers utilized a benchmark dataset from ProteinNet containing 50,914 proteins. Proteins were clustered at a 95% sequence identity cut-off. To minimize overfitting, they removed proteins with hits to 100 validation proteins at an e-value < 0.1. The final training set contained 34,691 proteins after filtering for lengths under 500. The validation set consisted of 88 proteins. A stringent test set named SPOT-2018 contained 669 proteins. A subset of 46 proteins with Neff=1 formed the Neff1-2018 set. An additional independent test set included 15 free modeling targets from CASP14-FM.

Procedures And Architectures
The model uses a 12-block ResNet architecture based on an improved version. The network employs convolutional layers with a channel size of 64 and kernel size of 3. Input features include one-hot encoding, SPOT-1D-Single outputs, and ESM-1b attention maps. Attention maps were gathered from all twenty attention heads across all layers. Six models were trained with different feature combinations and training strategies. The models were trained using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001. A batch size of 1 was used with early stopping of 3. The final result is an ensemble taking the mean of all six models.

Key Results
SPOT-Contact-Single achieved a 15% improvement in F1-score over SSCpred on CASP14-FM. On Neff=1 proteins in SPOT-2018, it outperformed TrRosetta by 48.7% in F1-score. It outperformed SPOT-Contact by 48.5% in F1-score on proteins without homologs. The F1-score of SPOT-Contact-Single was 0.32, which is 45% higher than evolution-based methods. In terms of precision, the model showed a ~100% improvement over SSCpred for long-range contacts. On CPU, SPOT-Contact-Single completed inference in 116 seconds. This is 22 times faster than TrRosetta.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Attention maps from pre-trained Transformers capture essential structural patterns that compensate for missing evolutionary data. The ensemble approach provided a 4% improvement over the second-best individual model. The method is suitable for large-scale genomic prediction due to its speed. The architecture can be applied to proteins by processing them as smaller domains.

Contradictions And Limitations
Single-sequence methods are not yet as competitive as evolution-based methods when homologs are plentiful. MSAs provide co-mutation information more effectively than unsupervised learning features. The use of ESM-1b attention maps limits predictions to proteins under 1024 amino acids.

Claims
SPOT-Contact-Single significantly outperforms evolution-based methods on proteins with no known homologs. It showed 48.7% improvement over TrRosetta. It showed 48.5% improvement over SPOT-Contact. It achieved an F1-score of 0.32 vs 0.22. MSA-based methods remain more effective when homologs exist. The model is an ideal tool for de-novo proteins.
The proposed method is much faster than current profile-based predictors. It is 22 times faster on CPU. It is 42 times faster on GPU.  It is suitable for genomic scale prediction.

Data And Code Availability
The authors provided links to TrRosetta, SPOT-Contact, and ESM-1b.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Adding SPOT-1D-Single features to one-hot encoding improved F1-score by 22.90%. Using all layers of ESM-1b attention maps provided further precision improvements. Concatenating all features together showed an additional 2.92% F1-score increase.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 describes the feature combinations for the six trained models. Table 2 shows the effect of different features on validation performance. Table 3 compares direct contact-map and distogram-based prediction strategies. Table 4 presents the results of the six individual models and the ensemble. Table 5 compares the performance of all methods on low-homology proteins. Table 6 compares SPOT-Contact-Single against SSCpred and ESM-1b on CASP14-FM. Figure 2 shows precision for top predictions at different ranges. Figure 3 plots F1-score as a function of Neff values. Figure 4 displays native and predicted contact-maps for a low Neff protein.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a contact-map predictor using ESM-1b attention maps and an ensemble ResNet architecture. 2. The strongest evidence is the 48.7% F1-score improvement over TrRosetta on proteins without homologs. 3. The future path involves using more advanced architectures like Transformers or Performers.

    Current protein structure prediction relies on identifying inter-residue contacts. Most existing predictors, such as TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact, utilize evolutionary profiles derived from MSAs. However, many proteins lack homologous sequences, causing performance to drop significantly for these targets. While single-sequence-based methods like SSCpred exist, they provide limited information for neural networks to learn. There is a critical need to explore features beyond one-hot encoding, specifically leveraging unsupervised deep learning models like ESM-1b that can extract high-dimensional embeddings from protein sequences.

    *Research Question/Hypothesis:*
    The central research question explores whether ESM-1b's attention maps can serve as a viable input feature to improve contact-map prediction for proteins with few homologs. The study hypothesizes that concatenating unsupervised learning features with one-hot encoding and structural properties will outperform existing single-sequence and MSA-based predictors. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that an ensemble of models trained with different feature combinations and training strategies (direct vs. distogram prediction) will yield a more robust and accurate prediction than any individual model.

    *Methodological Details:*
    The study utilized a benchmark dataset from ProteinNet, containing 50,914 proteins with high-resolution crystal structures. To minimize overfitting, the authors removed any proteins with hits to a 100-protein validation set at an e-value of less than 0.1. This resulted in a training set of 34,691 proteins and a validation set of 88 proteins, after filtering for lengths under 500. For independent testing, the authors curated the SPOT-2018 set, removing any homologs from the training set using HHblits at an e-value of less than 0.1. A specific subset of 46 proteins with Neff=1 was used for the Neff1-2018 benchmark. Additionally, 15 free-modeling targets from CASP14-FM were used for evaluation.

    *Procedures/Architectures:*
    The architecture is based on a 12-block ResNet using an improved version of the ResNet model. The network uses convolutional layers with a channel size of 64 and a kernel size of 3. Six models were trained using different input features, including one-hot encoding, SPOT-1D-Single outputs (SS3, SS8, ASA, HSE, and torsion angles), and ESM-1b attention maps from all layers and heads. The models were trained using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 1, with early stopping of 3. The final prediction was an ensemble of these six models, taking the mean of individual predictions.

    *Key Results:*
    SPOT-Contact-Single achieved a 15% improvement in F1-score over SSCpred on the CASP14-FM test set. On proteins with no homologs (Neff=1) in the SPOT-2018 set, it outperformed TrRosetta by 48.7% and SPOT-Contact by 48.5% in F1-score. On the Neff1-2018 set, it achieved an F1-score of 0.32, which is 45% higher than the 0.22 achieved by evolution-based methods. In terms of efficiency, it completed inference for the CASP14-FM set in 116 seconds on CPU, which is 22 times faster than TrRosetta.

    *Interpretation:*
    The results suggest that attention maps from pre-trained Transformer models capture essential structural information that compensates for the lack of evolutionary data. The ensemble approach proved superior, providing a 4% improvement over the second-best individual model. This indicates that combining multi-source features (unsupervised embeddings, 1D structural properties, and sequence identity) provides a more comprehensive signal for the ResNet architecture to learn contact geometries.

    *Contradictions/Limitations:*
    The study notes that single-sequence-based methods are not yet as competitive as evolution-based methods when many homologs are available, as MSAs provide co-mutation info more effectively. Additionally, using ESM-1b attention maps limits the model to proteins with less than 1024 amino acids, which may require domain-based processing for larger proteins.

    *Claims:*
    - Claim 1: Superiority on low-homology proteins.
    - Claim 2: Significant computational efficiency.
    - Claim 3: Outperformance of current single-sequence baselines.

The project addresses a significant pedagogical barrier: while the synthesis of data and mathematical models is fundamental for generalizing biological insights and informing policy, the "foreign" language of equations can alienate researchers and students from empirical backgrounds. The apps are designed to be accessible, with nine available in multiple languages including English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. A key distinguishing factor of EcoEvoApps is its open-source nature, allowing for community contributions in translation, new apps, and teaching plans. The project aims to democratize access to theoretical insights, providing a scalable, customizable resource for both individual learners and educators seeking to improve quantitative literacy in the life sciences.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
EcoEvoApps is an open-source R package and website developed to facilitate the integration of theoretical mathematical models with empirical research in ecology and evolutionary biology (EEB). The project addresses a significant pedagogical barrier: while the synthesis of data and mathematical models is fundamental for generalizing biological insights and informing policy, the "foreign" language of equations can alienate researchers and students from empirical backgrounds. This alienation often leads to lower citation rates for equation-heavy papers and poorer student evaluations for quantitative courses. To counter this, the authors created the ecoevoapps package, which provides 11 interactive Shiny apps simulating fundamental EEB models, including competition (e.g., abiotic resource competition) and predator-prey dynamics (e.g., Lotka-Volterra, MacArthur-Rosenzweig). The apps are designed to be accessible, with nine available in multiple languages including English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. Beyond the interactive interface, the package includes run_ functions for simulation and plot_ functions for generating ggplot2 visualizations, serving as a gateway for users to learn command-line coding and implementation of mathematical models. The researchers validated the tool’s effectiveness in two classroom settings. In an upper-division Ecology course at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), a survey of 51 students revealed that 40 out of 51 students (approximately 78%) found the apps moderately to very helpful for understanding the models as a whole, with specific improvements noted in understanding "carrying capacity" and "coexistence." Similarly, a survey at the University of Missouri (MU) demonstrated that using the interactive apps led to substantial gains in student confidence, particularly among those with higher interest in the topics. A key distinguishing factor of EcoEvoApps is its open-source nature, allowing for community contributions in translation, new apps, and teaching plans. The project aims to democratize access to theoretical insights, providing a scalable, customizable resource for both individual learners and educators seeking to improve quantitative literacy in the life sciences.

Research Context
Integrating theory with observations is a fundamental driver of progress in the life sciences. Mathematical models can promote a deeper conceptual understanding of biological systems and help disentangle complex interactions. Integration can also have important applications in biological forecasts and in informing actions and policies. However, numerous barriers limit such integration between empirical and theoretical approaches. The language of mathematical models may seem foreign to those with empirical backgrounds. Consequently, equation-heavy papers tend to be cited less often. While there are calls for quantitative training, there are few advances in the pedagogy of theoretical models. Interactive tools that allow users to explore model structure can help increase student interest and understanding.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asks if interactive tools can facilitate communication and collaboration between theoretical and empirical researchers. The authors hypothesize that interactive simulations can help students gain more familiarity with a model. The research questions focus on whether these apps can help communicate and learn insights from theoretical models in undergraduate settings.

Methodological Details
The authors surveyed syllabi for undergraduate ecology courses and commonly-used textbooks to select models. The first release of the ecoevoapps package includes 11 interactive apps. A core set of nine apps are available in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The researchers evaluated the apps in an upper-division Ecology course at the University of California, Los Angeles. A survey was conducted with 51 students at UCLA. Similar surveys were conducted with students in a General Ecology course at the University of Missouri.

Procedures And Architectures
The ecoevoapps package is an open-source R package and website. The shiny apps use functions in the ecoevoapps package to simulate and visualize model dynamics. Simulations are conducted by functions with the prefix run_ taking parameter values and initial population sizes. The package also includes a series of plotting functions prefixed plot_ which return a ggplot2 object. The apps are freely available online on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers or can be launched locally.

Key Results
At UCLA, 40/51 students reported that the apps were moderately to very helpful for learning models as whole. Students reported a better understanding of concepts like carrying capacity or coexistence after using the apps. Surveys at the University of Missouri showed substantial gains in student confidence. These gains were especially notable among students who express higher interest in related topics.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The interactive apps give everyone easier access to theoretical insights that otherwise take years to grasp. The package can serve as a gateway for users to implement and manipulate mathematical models at the command line. Being open-source, the package is easily accessible and customizable by the EEB community.

Contradictions And Limitations
Simulation-based learning may not provide all the same insights as analytical solutions. Theoretical models remain intimidating for many empirical researchers who lack extensive quantitative training.

Claims
EcoEvoApps provides an open-source platform to facilitate communication and learning of theoretical models in EEB. The package provides a collection of freely available interactive apps. The package includes functions to directly run models through the R console. Simulation-based learning may not provide all the same insights as analytical solutions. The platform can facilitate communication and collaboration between theoretical and empirical researchers.
Interactive simulations significantly improve student confidence and understanding of specific quantitative concepts. Students reported they better understand concepts of 'carrying capacity' or 'coexistence'. Using interactive apps led to substantial gains in student confidence. Theoretical models remain intimidating for many empirical researchers. These apps can be used as a formal instruction tool for teaching mathematical models.

Data And Code Availability
The ecoevoapps package can be installed from GitLab. The shiny apps are freely available online on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers.

Ethical Considerations
Classroom surveys were determined to constitute 'exempt' studies.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the predator-prey dynamics app including Lotka-Volterra and extensions. Figure 2 shows screenshots of the predator-prey dynamics shiny app for the MacArthur-Rosenzweig model. Table 1 lists the models and functions included in the ecoevoapps package. Figure 3A shows that 40/51 students found the apps moderately to very helpful. Figure 3B shows that students better understand concepts of carrying capacity or coexistence.

Three Takeaways
1. EcoEvoApps provides an open-source R package and website with 11 interactive apps for EEB models. 2. At UCLA, 40/51 students found the apps moderately to very helpful for understanding models as a whole. 3. The package will expand to include evolutionary biology and population genetics models.

summary.authors: Shiho Hashiguchi (Fukuoka University); Tomoko Tanaka (Fukuoka University); Ryosuke Mano (Fukuoka University); Seiji Kondo (Fukuoka University); Shohta Kodama (Fukuoka University)
summary.executive_summary: Cellular communication network factor 2 (CCN2), also known as connective tissue growth factor (CTGF), is a well-established matricellular protein and angiogenic factor. While its role in angiogenesis is well-documented, its specific signaling mechanisms in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) remained less clear. This study investigates the role of CCN2 in lymphangiogenesis and identifies its downstream signaling pathways in primary cultured LECs. The researchers found that CCN2 upregulates key lymphatic endothelial markers, including Lyve1, Podoplanin, and Prox1, as well as lymphangiogenic factors such as Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 (Vegfr3). A critical finding is that CCN2 activates the ERK signaling pathway specifically through its interaction with the integrin av receptor. Although CCN2 promotes the phosphorylation of ERK, it also simultaneously enhances the interaction between ERK and the dual-specificity phosphatase DUSP6. These results suggest that CCN2-mediated lymphangiogenesis is governed by a balanced signaling axis between ERK activation and DUSP6-mediated negative feedback. Furthermore, the study highlights that integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 represent potential therapeutic targets in conditions like oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), where CCN2 expression is elevated and associated with lymph node metastasis.

Executive Summary
Cellular communication network factor 2 (CCN2), also known as connective tissue growth factor (CTGF), is a well-established matricellular protein and angiogenic factor. While its role in angiogenesis is well-documented, its specific signaling mechanisms in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) remained less clear. This study investigates the role of CCN2 in lymphangiogenesis and identifies its downstream signaling pathways in primary cultured LECs. The researchers found that CCN2 upregulates key lymphatic endothelial markers, including Lyve1, Podoplanin, and Prox1, as well as lymphangiogenic factors such as Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 (Vegfr3). A critical finding is that CCN2 activates the ERK signaling pathway specifically through its interaction with the integrin av receptor. Although CCN2 promotes the phosphorylation of ERK, it also simultaneously enhances the interaction between ERK and the dual-specificity phosphatase DUSP6. This interaction serves as a regulatory mechanism where DUSP6 acts as a negative modulator, promoting the dephosphorylation of ERK and thereby exerting a weak growth-inhibitory effect on LECs. In vivo experiments using Matrigel plug assays confirmed that exogenous CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis, evidenced by an increase in Podoplanin-positive vessels and the presence of phosphorylated ERK and DUSP6 within these structures. These results suggest that CCN2-mediated lymphangiogenesis is governed by a balanced signaling axis between ERK activation and DUSP6-mediated negative feedback. Furthermore, the study highlights that integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 represent potential therapeutic targets in conditions like oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), where CCN2 expression is elevated and associated with lymph node metastasis.

Research Context
CCN2 is a known matricellular protein. It is a well-known angiogenic factor. However, its roles in LECs remain unclear. CCN2 activates MAPKs such as ERK. Integrins are important cell surface receptors. Previous studies show CTGF enhanced lymphangiogenesis. However, CCN2 signaling in LECs has not been elucidated.

Research Question And Hypothesis
This study investigated the downstream signaling of CCN2. The study specifically looked at primary cultured LECs. The authors sought to determine the intracellular signaling. The research explored how CCN2 activates ERK. It examined whether effects involve interaction with integrins. The study also investigated DUSP6 regulation.

Methodological Details
Primary cultured LECs were utilized. Cells were treated with 0-200 ng/mL of CCN2. Stimulation was performed for 3 hours. Expression levels were analyzed by quantitative RT-PCR. Integrin expression was measured via mRNA. Gene silencing was achieved by siRNA. Protein levels were analyzed by Western blot. Phosphorylation was assessed using a phospho-RTK array. In vivo testing used Matrigel plug assays. Study mice were 8-week-old C57BL/6.

Procedures And Architectures
LECs were cultured using EGM2 medium. Cell proliferation was assessed by crystal violet staining. Absorbance at 590 nm was measured. Total RNA was prepared via a kit. cDNA was prepared using QuantiTect RT Kit. LECs were transfected with 25 pmol siRNA. Samples were separated with SDS-PAGE. Immunoprecipitation used Protein A magnetic beads. Matrigel was mixed with 8.33 $\mu$g CCN2. Mice were euthanized at day 7.

Key Results
Markers Lyve1, Pdpn, and Prox1 were upregulated. The upregulation occurred up to 100 ng/mL. At 200 ng/mL, expression dramatically decreased. Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 expression increased. VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylation was unchanged. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased (p<0.001). Integrin av knockdown decreased phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). CCN2 suppressed LEC growth at 24 h. Suppression was significant at 50 ng/mL (p=0.003) and 100 ng/mL (p=0.02). CCN2 enhanced the ERK-DUSP6 interaction. DUSP6 knockdown increased phospho-ERK levels. CCN2 increased Podoplanin-positive vessels in vivo.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CCN2-induced phospho-ERK is mediated by integrin av. DUSP6 functions as a negative modulator of ERK. CCN2 positively modulated lymphangiogenesis in vivo. DUSP6 might suppress excessive ERK activation. Integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 are potential targets.

Contradictions And Limitations
In vitro growth showed weak suppression. In vivo Matrigel assays showed promotion. Discrepancy may be due to ECM and MMP effects. The results are not contradictory.

Claims
CCN2 upregulates key LEC markers and lymphangiogenic factors in a dose-dependent manner up to 100 ng/mL. Markers Lyve1, Pdpn, and Prox1 were upregulated. Upregulation occurred up to 100 ng/mL. At 200 ng/mL, expression dramatically decreased. CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis.
CCN2 activates ERK signaling specifically through the integrin av receptor. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased (p<0.001). Integrin av knockdown decreased phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Integrin a9 suppression did not decrease phospho-ERK. Integrin av may be a therapeutic target.
CCN2 enhances the binding between ERK and DUSP6, which acts as a negative regulator of ERK signaling. CCN2 enhanced the ERK-DUSP6 interaction. DUSP6 knockdown increased phospho-ERK levels. CCN2 only weakly suppressed cell growth. DUSP6 suppresses excessive activation of ERK.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Integrin av knockdown partially decreased phospho-ERK. Integrin b1 suppression did not alter CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. DUSP6 knockdown significantly increased phospho-ERK levels.

Ethical Considerations
Experiments were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows LEC markers were increased by CCN2. Figure 4A shows CCN2 suppressed cell growth. Figure 6A shows CCN2 increased Podoplanin-positive vessels.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is identifying CCN2-mediated ERK activation via integrin av in LECs. 2. The strongest evidence is that DUSP6 acts as a negative modulator of ERK. 3. The future path involves targeting integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 in OSCC.

summary.title: Tumor PD-L1 selectively suppresses type I interferon in myeloid cells to suppress CTL recruitment to promote lung metastasis
summary.authors: John D Klement, Priscilla S Redd, Chunwan Lu, Alyssa D Merting, Dakota B Poschel, Dafeng Yang, Gang Zhou, David H Munn, Kebin Liu
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the non-canonical role of tumor-expressed PD-L1 (tPD-L1) in promoting lung metastasis, specifically focusing on how it functions through intermediate cell populations rather than direct cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) inhibition. While the traditional paradigm suggests that tPD-L1 acts as a direct molecular shield against CTL lysis, the authors demonstrate that in a pure tumor-CTL environment, tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage to tumor cells. Instead, the research identifies a critical intermediate: myeloid cells. The study reveals that tPD-L1 engages PD-1 on myeloid cells (mPD-1) within the metastatic niche to actively antagonize type I interferon (IFN-I) and STAT1 signaling. This antagonism leads to the repression of chemoattractants Cxcl9 and Cxcl10, which are vital for recruiting CTLs to the site of metastasis. Crucially, this mechanism is independent of primary tumor growth, as PD-L1 knockout did not affect primary tumor size but significantly reduced metastasis. The authors validated this axis using a combination of in vitro co-cultures with RAW264.7 macrophages, in vivo tumor models (4T1 and CT26), and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). They demonstrated that myeloid cell depletion using clodronate liposomes abolished the pro-metastatic effects of tPD-L1. Furthermore, the study establishes a negative feedback circuit where the PD-1/L1 axis is induced by and subsequently attenuates IFN-I signaling. Human patient data from basal cell carcinoma patients further correlates myeloid cell differentiation and IFN-I signaling with responses to PD-1 blockade. By identifying the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis, the study provides a mechanistic basis for why certain tumors remain resistant to standard immunotherapy and suggests new avenues for adjuvant therapies targeting myeloid-mediated interferon suppression. The researchers utilized 4T1 (triple-negative breast cancer) and CT26 (mismatch repair proficient colorectal cancer) cell lines to mimic clinically relevant scenarios where ICB response is often poor. By using 2/20 CTLs, which provide high-fidelity interaction with endogenous antigens, they confirmed that tPD-L1 is not required for local protection against CTL-mediated lysis. The transition from primary tumor to metastatic niche is where tPD-L1 exerts its influence. The discovery that tPD-L1 regulates the 'immunologically cold' status of the lung metastasis through myeloid-mediated repression of chemokine expression provides a significant shift in understanding checkpoint blockade efficacy. It suggests that the success of neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapies depends on overcoming this myeloid-mediated interferon suppression.

Furthermore, the study establishes a negative feedback circuit where the PD-1/L1 axis is induced by and subsequently attenuates IFN-I signaling. Human patient data from basal cell carcinoma patients further correlates myeloid cell differentiation and IFN-I signaling with responses to PD-1 blockade. By identifying the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis, the study provides a mechanistic basis for why certain tumors remain resistant to standard immunotherapy and suggests new avenues for adjuvant therapies targeting myeloid-mediated interferon suppression. The researchers utilized 4T1 (triple-negative breast cancer) and CT26 (mismatch repair proficient colorectal cancer) cell lines to mimic clinically relevant scenarios where ICB response is often poor. By using 2/20 CTLs, which provide high-fidelity interaction with endogenous antigens, they confirmed that tPD-L1 is not required for local protection against CTL-mediated lysis. The transition from primary tumor to metastatic niche is where tPD-L1 exerts its influence. The discovery that tPD-L1 regulates the 'immunologically cold' status of the lung metastasis through myeloid-mediated repression of chemokine expression provides a significant shift in understanding checkpoint blockade efficacy. It suggests that the success of neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapies depends on overcoming this myeloid-mediated interferon suppression.

Research Context
PD-L1 and PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) immunotherapy functions by blocking the engagement of PD-L1 to co-inhibitory receptor PD-1 on cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs). PD-1 engagement on CTLs results in decreased activation and effector functions due to SHP-2 mediated dephosphorylation of the T cell receptor. While much research has focused on tPD-L1 acting as a direct molecular shield, emerging data suggest responses may depend on tumor anatomic sites. Because metastatic growth is the dominant cause of mortality, durable survival benefits from ICB arise from coordinated suppression of metastases. Robust tumor expression of PD-L1 has been shown to promote both micro- and macro-metastatic tumor growth. However, how tPD-L1 might differentially drive metastasis from primary tumor is unknown. While PD-1 expression on myeloid and dendritic cells contributes to immune evasion, how non-T cell-expressed PD-1 connects tPD-L1 to CTL suppression is incompletely understood.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether tPD-L1 directly protects tumor cells or operates through an intermediate cell population. The authors hypothesized that tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage when an antigen-specific effector CTL encounters a tumor cell bearing a cognate peptide-MHC complex. They sought to identify the third factor in the lung metastatic niche necessary for tPD-L1 to exert its indirect protective role. The researchers hypothesized that tPD-L1 targets myeloid cell-expressed PD-1 (mPD-1) to suppress type I IFN expression and function. They predicted this would repress Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 expression in myeloid cells, thereby impairing CTL recruitment to lung metastases. The study aimed to demonstrate that the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis.

Methodological Details
The study utilized 4T1 (triple-negative breast cancer) and CT26 (mismatch repair proficient colorectal cancer) murine cell lines. These cell lines were chosen to mimic clinically relevant cancers that show minimal response to ICB immunotherapy. To study the functional consequences of the PD-1:tPD-L1 interaction, an in vitro CTL-tumor interaction system was utilized using the 2/20 CTL line. The 2/20 line is a tumor-specific CTL line sensitive to PD-1 mediated inhibition that recognizes the H2-Ld-restricted AH1 epitope of the gp70 protein. In vivo experiments were conducted using orthotopic 4T1 tumor models and tail vein injection models to study metastasis. The researchers performed bulk RNA sequencing on lungs colonized by WT and PD-L1-deficient 4T1 cells. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of CD45+ leukocytes was performed on 4T1 WT and PDL1-KO colonized lungs. Approximately 7500 cells were processed using a Chromium Chip B (10x Genomics). In vitro co-cultures were performed with RAW264.7 macrophages to evaluate the impact of tPD-L1 on myeloid cell signaling. To functionally validate the necessity of myeloid cells, clodronate liposomes were used to deplete myeloid cells in tumor-bearing mice. Human patient data from metastatic basal cell carcinoma patients were analyzed using single-cell sequencing. A human lung myeloid cell scRNAseq dataset was used to develop transcriptomic signatures of cluster-identifying genes.

Procedures And Architectures
To generate PD-L1 knockout cell lines, HEK293FT cells were co-transfected with CRISPR lentivirus plasmids. The resulting sgRNA sequences were used to transduce the 4T1 and CT26 tumor cells. Tumor cells were selected with puromycin and sorted for marker-cells using a BD FACSARIA. For in vivo metastasis models, tumor cells were injected into the lateral tail vein of Balb/c mice. Lungs were harvested, inflated with India ink solution, and quantified. For neutralization experiments, 200 µg of anti-CD8α or isotype control were injected i.v. every other day. Flow cytometry was performed using an FACSCalibur or LSRFortessa with BD Diva 8.01. Bulk RNA was extracted from lungs using a Direct-zol RNA microprep kit and sequenced by Novogene. Read alignment was performed using the STARv2.5 aligner and quantification by HTSeqv0.6.1. Leukocytes were positively selected using CD45 magnetic nanobeads and loaded onto a Chromium Chip B. High-quality cells were filtered based on feature count (200 < feature count <4000). Analysis included shared nearest neighbor clustering, UMAP dimensional reduction, and Seurat for cluster annotation. Signature generation involved isolating genes whose expression increased by at least two-fold with a padj < 0.05. Human patient data from the BMS038 dataset was normalized using author-provided scripts. Batch effects in the melanoma cohort were corrected using Harmony.

Key Results
In an in vitro system using 2/20 CTLs, tPD-L1 was shown to confer no survival advantage. Initial orthotopic injection of PD-L1 WT and PD-L1 KO 4T1 cells led to tumor growth at the site of injection. No difference was observed in primary tumor growth between PD-L1 WT and KO 4T1 cells. Similarly, no differences in tumor growth were observed in the WT and PD-L1 KO CT26 tumor at the site of injection. Loss of tPD-L1 in the lung resulted in increased infiltration of CD3+ cells. No difference in initial tumor cell colonization as measured by tumor cell gp70 level in the lungs was seen one day after tail vein injection. PD-L1-deficient and competent 4T1 metastasized equally in adaptive-immune deficient congenic RAGII-KO mice. Genetic ablation of MHC class I antigen presentation and depletion of CD8+ T cells revealed that tPD-L1 drove metastasis by suppressing killing by CTLs. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that expression changes occurred in myeloid cells, but not in CTLs. No change in bulk lung myeloid cell composition was observed, though enhanced antigen presentation machinery was detected in macrophages. Transcriptomic and proteomic analysis identified Pdcd1lg2 as a marker for both type I interferon-stimulated myeloid cells after tPD-L1 loss. Differential expression of PD-L2 was observed in 4T1-colonized lungs as early as one day after injection. Myeloid cell surface PD-1 expression was enhanced following tPD-L1 loss. In co-culture, engagement with 4T1 tPD-L1 enhanced SHP-2 activation and decreased pSTAT1 levels in RAW cells. RAW264.7 PD-1 loss led to increased sensitivity to stimulation by the TLR3 ligand poly(I:C). Disruption of RAW PD-1 expression or 4T1 PD-L1 expression enhanced IFN$ eta$ production. Finally, depletion of myeloid cells diminished tPD-L1 function in promoting tumor growth in the lungs.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The findings indicate that tPD-L1 operates via a non-canonical pathway that uncouples its role at the metastatic site from its role at the primary tumor. The authors demonstrate that tPD-L1 binds to myeloid-expressed PD-1 (mPD-1) to enforce an 'immunologically cold' microenvironment. Specifically, this interaction creates a negative feedback circuit where the PD-1/L1 axis is induced by and subsequently attenuates type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling. By suppressing IFN-I and STAT1 signaling, tPD-L1 represses the expression of chemoattractants Cxcl9 and Cxcl10, which are essential for recruiting CTLs to the lung metastasis. This mechanism explains why certain tumors are resistant to PD-1 blockade; the primary tumor might be 'hot,' but the metastatic niche is kept 'cold' by myeloid cells. Furthermore, the study suggests that low response rates in interferon alpha therapies might be due to compensatory PD-1/L1 upregulation. The identification of the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis provides a clear mechanistic target for improving the efficacy of neoadjuvant and adjuvant immunotherapies.

Contradictions And Limitations
One limitation noted in the study is that the researchers exclusively analyzed lung metastases. Because lung metastases are located in barrier tissue, they may possess a uniquely inflamed microenvironment that differs from other metastatic sites. This could potentially limit the generalizability of the findings to all types of metastatic niches. Additionally, while the study identifies a myeloid-mediated pathway, it does not fully explore the diversity of myeloid subsets beyond macrophages and dendritic cells.

Myeloid cell depletion diminished tPD-L1 function in promoting lung metastasis. tPD-L1 engages mPD-1 to antagonize type I interferon (IFN-I) and STAT1 signaling.  tPD-L1 creates an immunologically cold niche.

Data from the BMS038 dataset was accessed from authors' processed files at https://github.com/riazn/bms038_analysis.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Depletion of myeloid cells via clodronate liposomes diminished tPD-L1 function in promoting lung metastasis. Genetic ablation of MHC class I antigen presentation and antibody-mediated depletion of CD8+ T cells revealed tPD-L1 suppresses CTLs.

Figure 6K and 6L show that myeloid cell depletion diminished tPD-L1 function in promoting metastasis. Figure 7A-C shows myeloid cell PHATE analysis revealing differentiation restriction released by PD-1 blockade.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis regulating CTL infiltration. 2. The strongest evidence is that myeloid cell depletion abolished the pro-metastatic effects of tPD-L1. 3. The future path involves targeting myeloid-mediated interferon suppression to improve neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapies.

summary.executive_summary: This study describes the development of a hydrogel-supported stem cell microarray platform designed to analyze the activity of extracellular glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in growth factor signaling. While GAGs, particularly heparan sulfate (HS), are critical regulators of tissue development, their structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity make establishing structure-function relationships difficult. To address this, the researchers integrated GAG-protein conjugates into a polyacrylamide hydrogel network. They employed a method where GAGs are chemically crosslinked to adhesion proteins (gelatin) using NHS-esters to ensure retention during cell culture while preserving protein-binding specificities. The platform was validated using a specialized model of murine embryonic stem cells (ESCs) lacking the Ext1 enzyme, which ensures that the observed signaling is attributable to the arrayed GAGs rather than endogenous structures. The results demonstrate that NHS-crosslinked heparin provides a 5-to 10-fold higher binding signal for FGF2 compared to non-covalent immobilization, with approximately 40% of binding activity retained after 48 hours of culture. Furthermore, the platform successfully demonstrated dose-responsive MAPK (Erk1/2) signaling activation in response to FGF2 stimulation. This microarray approach offers a rapid, multiplexed tool for profiling the biological activities of well-defined synthetic and recombinant GAGs, accelerating the design of bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based regenerative therapies.
