judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the transcriptional regulation and clinical significance of MicroRNA-196a (miR-196a) in breast cancer, specifically exploring its role as a prognostic biomarker in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) disease. MIR196A is transcribed from two genomic loci (HOXC and HOXB) and is implicated in various cancers as an oncogene. The authors first establish a strong correlation between MIR196A expression and the HOXC gene cluster, particularly HOXC10, in breast tumors. They demonstrate that MIR196A2 is transcriptionally regulated by oestrogen (E2), using GRO-Seq and RNA-Seq to show a dramatic increase in RNA production following E2 treatment. Mechanistically, the research shows that oestrogen-mediated upregulation is controlled by the binding of the estrogen receptor α (ERα) and its pioneer factor FOXA1 to putative promoters (PP1 and PP3) upstream of the MIR196A2 transcription start site. The study further identifies a complex regulatory landscape involving long-range transcriptional regulation, where distal enhancers—including a previously identified HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE) and a novel MIR196A2-enhancer (mE)—physically interact with the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter regions. Additionally, the study finds that MIR196A expression is significantly increased in models of hormone receptor-positive disease resistance, specifically in tamoxifen-resistant and chemotherapeutic-resistant cell lines, coinciding with a loss of DNA methylation in promoter regions. Critically, MIR196A serves as a robust prognostic biomarker; in post-menopausal ER+ patients, high MIR196A expression is associated with poor survival (61% survival at 10 years), while in pre-menopausal women, high expression is associated with a better outcome. These findings suggest that the de-repression and over-activation of MIR196A, mediated by ERα at enhancers and promoters, may facilitate the development of therapeutic resistance and contribute to a stem-cell-like state in cancer.

Research Context
MicroRNAs are potent post-transcriptional regulators involved in all hallmarks of cancer. miR-196a has been implicated in a wide range of developmental and pathogenic processes. Little is known about the regulation of the genes encoding this miRNA. Transcriptional regulation of miRNA is very much in its infancy.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aimed to characterise the expression landscape of MIR196A. They sought to identify factors regulating its expression. They explored potential roles of regulatory elements in breast cancer prognostication. The authors hypothesized that MIR196A2 transcription may be controlled by the oestrogen receptor (ER).

Methodological Details
The study utilized MCF7 cells, including tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR) and fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) sub-lines. Cells were cultured for less than 6 months after authentication. Luciferase reporter assays used 500 ng of modified pGL3 reporter constructs. RNA-Seq was sourced from GSE68815 for ADM and PTX resistance. The METABRIC cohort data was sourced from EGAS00000083. The authors analyzed DNA methylation data from the TCGA cohort.

Procedures And Architectures
Promoters were cloned into the pGL3-Basic luciferase reporter plasmid. GRO-Seq was used to measure nascent RNA production. ChIP-Seq was performed to identify ERα and RNA polymerase II binding. ChIA-PET identified major sites of interaction with MIR196A2 promoters. 3C-qPCR demonstrated physical interaction between enhancer elements and promoter regions.

Key Results
MIR196A expression highly correlates to HOXC genes, particularly HOXC10. E2 addition caused a dramatic increase in RNA production peaking at 40 mins. ERα and FOXA1 bind to two putative promoters, PP1 and PP3. HDE appears to be the most active enhancer in MCF7 cells. High MIR196A expression associates with poor survival in post-menopausal ER+ breast cancer. Survival in the high expression group was 61% at 10 years. MIR196A is significantly increased in tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
MIR196A acts as a possible biomarker for therapeutic resistance. Loss of DNA methylation in promoter regions is associated with increased MIR196A. De-repression of promoter and enhancer elements may facilitate transition to a stem-cell like state.

Contradictions And Limitations
It is currently unclear how dual-encoded miRs are regulated. The association between MIR196A and HOXC genes is limited in normal human breast cells.

Claims
MIR196A is regulated by oestrogen through ERα binding to enhancers and promoters. GRO-Seq showed increased RNA production following E2 treatment. ERα and FOXA1 were found to bind PP1 and PP3. 3C-qPCR confirmed physical interactions between enhancers and promoters. PP3 was not able to increase luciferase expression in a reporter assay. Oestrogen signaling pathways are critical for MIR196A expression levels.
MIR196A is a robust prognostic biomarker for post-menopausal ER+ breast cancer. High expression associates with poor survival. Low expression patients showed >95% survival at 10 years. High expression is associated with a better outcome in pre-menopausal women. MIR196A provides a novel stratification method for resistant breast cancer.

Data And Code Availability
The study used data from GSE68815, GSE14664, GSE27463, and GSE39495.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used tamoxifen-resistant and fulvestrant-resistant cell lines to confirm resistance patterns.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows ChIP-Seq for RNA polymerase II binding. Figure 4A and 4B show MIR196A expression in the METABRIC cohort. Figure 5A shows survival stratification for ER+ tumours.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of MIR196A as an ERα-regulated prognostic biomarker in ER+ breast cancer. 2. The strongest evidence is the survival disparity, with high MIR196A expression correlating to 61% survival at 10 years in post-menopausal patients. 3. The future path involves investigating the functional necessity of increased MIR196A expression in developing therapeutic resistance.

summary.title: Lack of negative density-dependence regulation in a dominant oak tree from a neotropical highland forest
summary.authors: Irene Calderón-Sanou (Universidad de Costa Rica); Luis Diego Ríos; Alfredo Cascante-Marín (Universidad de Costa Rica); Gilbert Barrantes (Universidad de Costa Rica); Eric J Fuchs (Universidad de Costa Rica)
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the mechanisms regulating population dynamics and forest composition in the tropical highland forests of Costa Rica, specifically focusing on the dominance of the oak species Quercus costaricensis. A central theory in forest ecology is Conspecific Negative Density-Dependence (CNDD), where high seedling densities lead to increased mortality from pathogens, herbivores, and competition, thereby promoting biodiversity. However, tropical highland forests are often dominated by a few species, including Q. costaricensis, which represents over 90% of the basal stem area in the Talamanca mountain range. The researchers sought to determine if CNDD regulates the seedling establishment of this dominant oak. Monitoring 3538 seedlings between 2014 and 2017 at the Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station, the study analyzed the effects of seedling density, distance to the nearest adult, herbivory, and Chusquea bamboo density. Executive Summary
This study investigates the mechanisms regulating population dynamics and forest composition in the tropical highland forests of Costa Rica, specifically focusing on the dominance of the oak species Quercus costaricensis. A central theory in forest ecology is Conspecific Negative Density-Dependence (CNDD), where high seedling densities lead to increased mortality from pathogens, herbivores, and competition, thereby promoting biodiversity. However, tropical highland forests are often dominated by a few species, including Q. costaricensis, which represents over 90% of the basal stem area in the Talamanca mountain range. The researchers sought to determine if CNDD regulates the seedling establishment of this dominant oak. Monitoring 3538 seedlings between 2014 and 2017 at the Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station, the study analyzed the effects of seedling density, distance to the nearest adult, herbivory, and Chusquea bamboo density. The results revealed that Q. costaricensis seedlings are spatially aggregated but do not exhibit significant CNDD on survival or recruitment. Instead, seedling survival was found to be significantly reduced by bamboo density and herbivory, while seedling height showed a strong positive effect on survival. Notably, the study found a negative quadratic relationship between seedling survival and distance to the nearest adult, suggesting that ectomycorrhizal (ECM) transfer from adults may facilitate seedling establishment at intermediate distances. Furthermore, seedling recruitment significantly increased with conspecific seedling density, possibly because dense aggregations allow seedlings to escape predation and herbivory. The researchers argue that the lack of intraspecific density regulation at the seedling stage, potentially due to predator satiation and adult facilitation, explains the dominance of Q. costaricensis in these highland forests. Interspecific interactions, particularly the presence of dense Chusquea bamboo, were identified as major factors limiting recruitment and survival through resource competition and physical interference.

Research Context
CNDD is a mechanism proposed to regulate species coexistence. This negative effect likely results from antagonistic plant interactions. CNDD involves mortality from pathogens and herbivores. Tropical montane forests have fewer species compared to lowland forests. These forests are commonly dominated by a few tree species. Processes structuring these low diversity forests are not fully understood. Quercus costaricensis represents over 90% of the basal stem area. Temperate oaks are known to be susceptible to CNDD. Ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults may have a positive effect. Factors regulating recruitment could be species or population specific. Conspecific density could lower survival through competition or increase recruitment. The authors expected to find weak CNDD regulation. They also expected a positive effect of nearby adults.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The main objective was to test for CNDD regulation on Q. costaricensis. Specifically, the study tested seedling density, distance to adults, and herbivory. The effect of bamboo density was also included. These variables were analyzed for seedling recruitment and survival. The researchers hypothesized that CNDD regulation would be weak. They predicted a positive effect of nearby adults. The study aimed to understand mechanisms regulating population dynamics. The study aimed to understand mechanisms regulating forest composition.

Methodological Details
The study was conducted at Cerro de la Muerte. The site is an upper montane tropical forest. Researchers established four 400-m^2 plots in old growth forests. Plots were subdivided into 64 (2.5 x 2.5 m) quadrats. Researchers mapped and tagged 2031 seedlings in 2014. They measured DBH of all adult trees. A total of 3538 seedlings were monitored between 2014 and 2017. Metrics included seedling height, distance to adults, and seedling density. Seedling density was measured in a 1m radius. Leaf damage was estimated using a qualitative index. The number of bamboo stems was counted for each quadrat.

Procedures And Architectures
Spatial analyses were performed using the R statistical language. The spatstat library was used for spatial distribution. Survival was modeled using a generalized linear mixed-effects model. All variables were standardized before being entered in the model. Quadrat and census year were included as random effects. A second-degree polynomial effect for distance to adults was tested. Recruitment was analyzed using a GLMM with a quasi-poisson distribution. Plots were included as a random effect for spatial autocorrelation. The lme4 package in R was used for statistical analyses.

The 2014 seedlings were spatially aggregated at all scales. Over 99% of censused seedlings had leaf damage. Most plants (ca. 71%) had intermediate damage. The lack of CNDD regulation may explain the species dominance. Predator satiation may explain the lack of density dependent regulation. High survivorship could be due to predator satiation. Dense aggregations may allow seedlings to escape seed predation. Dominant species are expected to have weaker CNDD. Abundant species also tend to have low levels of foliar damage. Ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults may provide an advantage. Seedling survival has a negative quadratic relationship with distance to adults. This suggests higher survival due to ECM transfer. Bamboo thickets strongly reduce oak seedling survival. Bamboo limits growth through resource competition.

The results disagree with expectations posed by Janzen-Connell. Survival was unrelated to conspecific density. The study did not examine environmental factors like soil acidity. Harsh conditions could impact CNDD regulation.

Survival was highest at intermediate distances. No specific contradictory evidence was reported. This allows seedlings to escape CNDD.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the acute ecotoxicity of six different types of engineered nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, and SiO2) on the brine shrimp *Artemia sp.*. The researchers utilized two distinct bioassays: a hatching rate test and a standard nauplii toxicity (lethality) test, conducted in high-salinity marine water environments. The study aimed to establish a robust and efficient method for hazard identification of nanomaterials. The nanoparticles were characterized using Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) to understand their physicochemical behavior in both distilled and salt water. Results demonstrated that silver (Ag) and copper oxide (CuO) nanoparticles exhibited the highest toxicity, significantly reducing hatching rates and nauplii viability. Specifically, at a concentration of 100mg/L, hatching rates for Ag and CuO dropped to approximately 29%, with only 50% of the resulting nauplii remaining motile and viable. In the standard toxicity test, silver nanoparticles were identified as the most toxic, with an LC50 of approximately 10.12mg/L at 24 hours. Furthermore, the study revealed a strong inverse correlation (coefficient of -0.7853) between hatching rates and larval mortality, suggesting that hatching assays can serve as a reliable pre-screening tool for nanoparticle toxicity. Morphological assessments showed no gross abnormalities in survivors, but oxidative stress was observed in some nauplii, particularly those exposed to silver. The findings highlight the potential of *Artemia sp.* as a cost-effective, robust model for high-throughput screening of nanomaterial hazards in aquatic ecosystems.

Research Context
Nanomaterials possess unique properties and diverse applications that pose risks to human health and the environment. There is currently a dearth of information regarding the environmental impact of these nanoscale objects. Increasing utility of nanomaterials leads to enhanced ecosystem exposure to unknown risks. Release into the environment can occur via production, applications, weathering, and waste. Nanomaterials behave differently from bulk materials due to specific physicochemical properties. Information on the predictability of their behavior in various conditions is almost negligible. Limited information exists concerning the bioavailability and biopersistence of these particles. The behavior of particles under specific pH and salinity factors is not clearly known. Hazard identification is a critical step for the risk assessment of nanomaterials. Aquatic systems act as inevitable receptacles for materials released into the environment. Many ecotoxicology assays have been tested in bacteria, fishes, and copepods. Artemia sp. is utilized in this study to evaluate nanomaterial toxicity. Artemia is a non-selective filter feeder available in highly saline waters. Due to their distribution and cost-effectiveness, they are excellent model organisms. Early developmental stages of Artemia are highly vulnerable to test materials. Hatching of hydrated cysts has rarely been used as a toxicity end point. Previous studies have shown sensitivity of hatching rates to metals.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to assess the acute toxicity of four metal oxide and two metal nanoparticles. The nanoparticles tested include TiO2, SiO2, CuO, Ag, and Au. The research evaluates these particles on both the hatching of hydrated cysts and the viability of nauplii. Mortality and hatching rates are established as the primary end points. The study explores whether hatching rates show an inverse correlation with larval mortality. This would imply that a hatching bioassay can be developed for hazard assessment.

Methodological Details
The study utilized nanoparticles from the NANOVALID consortium. Source materials included silicon, silver, gold, copper oxide, and zinc oxide. Titanium dioxide particles were synthesized in-house following an existing protocol. Nanoparticle suspensions were prepared at a concentration of 2mg/ml. Suspensions were sonicated at ~30W with a 50% pulse for 10 minutes. Silver nanoparticles were prepared at 4% using PVP as a stabilizer. Gold nanoparticles were prepared in water at a concentration of 0.006%. Working dilutions were prepared in NaCl salt water. Nanoparticles were characterized using TEM and DLS methods. TEM studies involved applying 50µg/ml suspensions to copper grids. Grids were examined in a JEOL 2010 TEM at 100KV. Analysis used a 20µ aperture and GATAN software. DLS measurements were taken at 25µg/ml in milliQ and salt water. The Horiba Nanopartica SZ100 system was used for DLS. Each DLS suspension was analyzed thrice over three days. Artemia cysts used were of the San Francisco Bay strain. The study used 1.0 gram of cysts per 1 litre of culture. Cysts were hydrated in distilled water for 45 minutes. Decapsulation was performed using 20% sodium hypochlorite for 15 minutes. Bleached eggs were washed 6 times with distilled water. Hatching occurred in 25% salt water at pH 8.0. The environmental temperature was maintained at 28°C. Nanoparticle concentrations for the tests were 100mg/l and 10mg/l. Hatching rate was calculated as a percentage of fully hatched Artemia. The hatching experiment was repeated six times. Standard toxicity tests used 10 nauplii per well plate. Toxicity concentrations included 100mg/l, 10mg/l, 1mg/l, 0.1mg/l, and 0.01mg/l. Viability was counted at 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours. LC50 values were calculated using Graphpad software. Oxidative stress was assessed using 10µM DCFDA. Fluorescence imaging was performed using a Zeiss Axiovert imager.

Procedures And Architectures
The nanoparticle source was the NANOVALID consortium. Silica, titanium dioxide, copper oxide, and zinc oxide were 2mg/ml suspensions. A sonication protocol of 30W with 50% pulse was used. Silver nanoparticles were prepared as a 4% PVP suspension. Gold nanoparticles were prepared as a 0.006% water suspension. Dilutions were performed in NaCl salt water. TEM grids were prepared with formvar coating on copper. The JEOL 2010 TEM operated at 100KV. TEM imaging captured approximately 10 images per grid. DLS measurements used the Horiba Nanopartica SZ100 system. DLS samples were analyzed in both milliQ and salt water. Cysts were hydrated under continuous aeration in distilled water. Bleaching was performed for 15 minutes in 20% sodium hypochlorite. Washing steps included 6 cycles with distilled water. Hatching occurred in 25% salt water under continuous light. Temperature was set to the optimum 28°C. Nanoparticles were added at 100mg/l and 10mg/l concentrations. Hatching rate was recorded after a 24-hour period. Three 100µl aliquots were taken from each flask. Counts included motile/immotile nauplii and unhatched cysts. The standard test used six well plates for 10 nauplii. Viability was recorded every 6 hours for the first 24 hours. DCFDA was used as a chemiluminescent probe for ROS. Images were captured using a Zeiss Axiovert imager.

Key Results
The overall order of toxicity was Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2. Normal hatching rate was 74%+5.5 with 97% viability. Hatching rates dropped significantly in the presence of nanoparticles. Silver and copper oxide showed the highest toxicity effects. Hatching rate dropped to about 29% for Ag and CuO at 100mg/L. Viability for these two nanoparticles at 100mg/L was 50%. Hatching rate for silver at 10mg/L was lower, but viability was 85%. Copper oxide showed a hatching rate with 64% viability. Silver nitrate resulted in a 33% hatching rate. Capping agent PVP improved silver hatching to 41%. Other nanoparticles showed hatching rates of 50-60%. Zinc oxide showed a 60% hatching rate with clumping. Titanium dioxide at 100mg/L yielded 41.50% hatching and 67.8% viability. Titanium dioxide at 10mg/L yielded 54% hatching and 90% viability. SiO2 at 10mg/L was equivalent to the control. The LC50 of silver nanoparticles was approximately 10.12mg/L at 24 hours. Silver nitrate solution resulted in 80% mortality in 24 hours. A strong inverse correlation coefficient of -0.7853 was found. The paired T-test showed no significant difference in means (P=0.683).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
A strong correlation exists between hatching rates and larval mortality. This indicates that hatching rate is a sensitive bioassay for metals. The toxicity of Ag and CuO may be due to ionic forms. Even though ionic silver precipitates in salt, it still affects hatching. Silicon nanoparticles at low concentrations were conducive to hatching. Mortality may be caused by nanoparticle clogging in the gut. Hatching assays can serve as a pre-screening tool for toxicity. Artemia cysts provide a cost-effective method for high-throughput hazard identification.

Contradictions And Limitations
Ionic silver precipitates in high salinity but still impacts viability. Some nanoparticles were nontoxic initially but caused death after 30 hours. The study notes that random seeds and train/test splits were not reported. Demographic information regarding the source of cysts was not fully detailed. The correlation was not perfect, with a coefficient of -0.7853. Some nanoparticles were observed to remain stable in seawater for one week.

Claims
Hatching rates of Artemia cysts are a sensitive and viable bioassay for nanoparticle hazard identification. Hatching rates show a good inverse correlation with mortality. Hatching rate was used as a sensitive bioassay. A strong correlation was found between hatching and mortality. Some nanoparticles were nontoxic initially but killed nauplii later. Hatching assays can be used for high-throughput pre-screening.
Silver nanoparticles exhibit the highest acute toxicity among the tested nanomaterials. The order of toxicity is Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2. The most toxic was the silver nanoparticles. LC50 of silver nanoparticles was 10.12mg/L. Silver nitrate showed 80% mortality in 24 hours. Silver remains a high-priority risk for aquatic environments.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The hatching study was repeated six times to ensure validity. The validity criterion was low mortality in the control. The toxicity test validity was mortality below 10% in 24 hours.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 summarizes the hatching rates and viability for all nanoparticles. Figure 3 shows the drastic drop in hatching rates. Figure 4 illustrates the mortality of nauplii across different concentrations. Figure 5 shows the accumulation of nanoparticles in the gut. Figure 6 demonstrates the correlation between hatching and mortality.

Three Takeaways
1. Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles are the most toxic to Artemia sp. hatching and viability. 2. There is a strong inverse correlation (-0.7853) between hatching rates and nauplii mortality. 3. Hatching assays are viable pre-screening tools for high-throughput nanoparticle hazard identification.
